docs.title: Learn steero
docs.text: A hands-on course in sixteen lessons, from your first script to a full test suite. Each lesson teaches one part of steero, runs real code against a practice site on your own machine, and ends with exercises you can check yourself.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Python testers and developers who want to automate Chrome and Firefox: writing end-to-end tests, checking pages before a release, or scripting a browser for a chore. You do not need to know any other browser tool. If you already use Playwright or Selenium, the suggested tracks below skip what you know and point out what is different.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer, and enough Python to write a function and run a script.
  • Chrome or Firefox installed the usual way. Both is better: several lessons compare them.
  • steero installed in a virtual environment. Every lesson shows its example script in full, so you can copy the code from the page.
  • A terminal and an editor. Lessons show PowerShell and bash where the commands differ.

docs.title: How the course works
docs.text:
Every lesson follows the same pattern:

  1. Read the concepts. Each one comes with a short snippet.
  2. Run the worked example from examples/course/NN-topic/. Change it and run it again.
  3. Do the exercises. Each has a collapsed solution: try first, then open it and compare.
  4. Check the common mistakes box before you move on. It lists the errors people actually hit.

Boxes marked Coming from Playwright, Coming from Selenium and Browser support are there for the readers who need them; skip them if they do not apply to you. Conventions explains every box, and how the examples are written.

Every example and solution in the course is run by steero's own test suite in Chrome and Firefox, so the code you see is code that works.

docs.title: The practice site
docs.text:
The lessons drive a small site served from your machine, so nothing depends on the internet and nothing you do can affect a real service. Start it in its own terminal and leave it running:

python examples/course/serve.py

Practice site: http://127.0.0.1:8765/
Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Open that address in your browser to look around. Then run an example from a second terminal:

python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

The examples read three environment variables, so you can change what they do without editing them:

Variable Default Meaning STEERO_COURSE_URL http://127.0.0.1:8765/ Where the practice site is. Set it if you used --port. STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER chrome chrome, firefox or edge. STEERO_COURSE_HEADED not set 1 shows the browser window.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
# Lesson What you learn Time 01 Getting started Install, check your browsers, first script (sync and async), headed and headless, screenshots, reading a failure 30 min 02 Locators Finding elements by role, label, text and test id; chaining and filters; frames and shadow DOM; strictness 45 min 03 Actions and auto-waiting Clicking, typing and forms; what actionability checks; timeouts in seconds; files and drag and drop 45 min 04 Assertions Web-first expect, negation, soft assertions, expect.poll, ARIA snapshots 40 min 05 Visual testing to_have_screenshot, baselines, masks and tolerance, updating snapshots 30 min 06 Contexts and emulation Isolated contexts, devices, locale and time zone, geolocation and permissions, logging in once with storage state 45 min 07 Network Watching requests, routing, mocking, changing real responses, HTTP auth, the API request context 60 min 08 Events, dialogs, downloads and popups Page events, waiting for what an action triggers, dialogs, downloads, new tabs 40 min 09 The pytest plugin Fixtures, options, several browsers, failure artifacts, base URL 45 min 10 Debugging Tracing and steero show-trace, video, pause(), headed runs, reading errors 40 min 11 Recording with codegen steero codegen, the toolbar, how locators are chosen, cleaning up a recording 25 min 12 Self-healing locators Fingerprints and baselines, when healing refuses, fixing the test, strict mode 35 min 13 Browsers and backends Chrome extras over CDP, Firefox specifics, Edge and channels, pinned browser versions 35 min 14 AI agents with MCP steero mcp, connecting a client, the tools, safety 25 min 15 Migrating from Playwright The compatibility layer first, then moving to native steero 40 min 16 Capstone: a ControlLab suite A complete test suite for a real app, with a local gate 90 min

The whole course takes about eleven hours. Lessons 01 to 04 are the core; after them, take the others in any order that suits your work.

docs.title: Suggested tracks
docs.text:
New to browser automation. Take the course in order, and leave the specialist lessons for when you need them:

01, 02, 03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 05, 11, 12, 16. Later, as needed: 13, 14.

Coming from Playwright. Most of the API will look familiar. Learn what differs (seconds, stock browsers, the pytest fixture names), then go straight to the tools:

01, 15, 03, 04, 09, 10, 13, 12, 16. Skim 02, 06, 07 and 08 for their "Coming from Playwright" boxes.

Coming from Selenium. The biggest change is that you stop writing waits. Spend your time on locators, actions and assertions, then on the parts Selenium does not have:

01, 02, 03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 12, 13, 16. See also Migrating from Selenium.

Ready? Start with 01. Getting started.

docs.title: 01. Getting started
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • install steero and check which browsers it can find with steero doctor
  • prepare drivers ahead of time with steero install
  • write and run a first script with the sync API, and the same script with the async API
  • switch between headless and headed runs
  • save screenshots of the viewport, the full page and a single element
  • recognise the errors a first script usually hits, and fix them

Time: about 30 minutes. Before this: nothing; this is the first lesson. Code: examples/course/01-getting-started/

By the end of this lesson you will have driven a real Chrome or Firefox from Python: opened a page, filled in a form, checked the result and saved a picture of it. Every later lesson builds on the script you write here.

docs.title: Install steero
docs.text:
steero is a Python package with one dependency (websockets). It drives the Chrome and Firefox already installed on your machine, so there is no browser to download.

Work in a virtual environment inside your copy of the repository:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -e . pytest

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e . pytest

pip install -e . installs the steero in this checkout, so the library and the course examples always match. (In your own projects, pip install steero is all you need.) Installing steero also installs the steero command:

steero --version

steero 1.0.0rc3

docs.title: Check your browsers
docs.text:
steero doctor reports what steero can find on this machine:

steero doctor

steero 1.0.0rc3 (Python 3.13.5, win32)
cache: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\steero
  chrome   157.0.8103.38    C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe
  firefox  found            C:\Program Files\Mozilla Firefox\firefox.exe
  edge     157.0.4341.42    C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe
  chromedriver cached: none (downloaded on first Chrome launch)

You need at least one of Chrome and Firefox. If one says missing, install it the normal way, or point steero at a browser in an unusual place with STEERO_CHROME_PATH or STEERO_FIREFOX_PATH. The cache is where steero keeps the drivers it downloads and the pinned browser versions you install in lesson 13.

Browser support

Both browsers are driven over WebDriver BiDi, the W3C standard protocol, so the same script works in each. They are reached differently:

  • Firefox speaks BiDi itself. Nothing extra is needed.
  • Chrome is reached through chromedriver, which must match the Chrome version. steero downloads the right one from Chrome for Testing the first time you launch Chrome, and caches it. Lesson 13 shows a second way, backend="chromium-bidi", with no driver.
  • Edge works like Chrome, with msedgedriver.

docs.title: Prepare drivers ahead of time
docs.text:
The first Chrome launch pauses for a few seconds while chromedriver downloads. To do that step now (for example before going offline, or when setting up a build machine), run:

steero install chromedriver

chromedriver for Chrome 157.0.8103.38: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\steero\drivers\chromedriver-157.0.8103.38\chromedriver.exe

steero install also fetches the chromium-bidi mapper (steero install chromium-bidi) and pinned browsers such as steero install chrome@154; lesson 13 covers both.

docs.title: Start the practice site
docs.text:
Every lesson runs against a small site served from your own machine. Open a second terminal, activate the same virtual environment, and start it:

python examples/course/serve.py

Practice site: http://127.0.0.1:8765/
Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Leave it running for the rest of the course. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/login.html in your own browser and sign in once by hand: any user name works, the password must not be empty, and the welcome message appears about half a second after you click. Your first script will do exactly this.

docs.title: Your first script
docs.text:
Here is the whole script. Read it once, then we will go through it.

"""Lesson 01: a first steero script (sync API).

Opens the practice site, signs in, checks the welcome message and saves a screenshot.

    python examples/course/serve.py                                   # terminal 1
    python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py # terminal 2

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        print(f"Running {browser.name} {browser.version}")
        page = browser.new_page()

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        print("Title:", page.title())

        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

        # expect() keeps checking until the text appears (up to 5 seconds), so no sleep is needed.
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")

        page.screenshot("signed-in.png")
        print("Saved signed-in.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it from the repository root, in the terminal that is not running the server:

python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

Running chrome 157.0.8103.38
Title: Sign in - steero practice site
Saved signed-in.png

Open signed-in.png: it shows the form with "Welcome, ada" under the button. Nothing else happened on screen, because the browser ran headless (without a window). Here is what each part does.

The three settings. BASE_URL, BROWSER and HEADLESS come from environment variables, with defaults that suit the practice site. Every example in the course starts this way, so you can switch browser without editing code:

$env:STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER = "firefox"
python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER=firefox python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) starts the browser with a fresh, empty profile and returns a Browser. Used in a with block, it is closed when the block ends, even if something inside fails: the browser process exits and its temporary profile is deleted. Always launch this way (or call browser.close() in a finally), and a script never leaves a browser running behind it.

browser.new_page() opens a tab. page.goto(url) loads a URL and returns once the page's load event has fired.

page.get_by_label("User name") is a locator: a description of how to find an element, here "the control whose label is User name". Building it does not touch the page. Only an action, such as .fill("ada"), finds the element, and it looks again every time. Lesson 02 is all about locators. For now, notice that the script finds things the way a person would describe them (the field labelled "User name", the button called "Sign in") rather than by an id or a CSS class, which change more often than the words on the screen.

.click() waits until the button can be clicked (it exists, is visible, is enabled, is not moving and is not covered by something else) and then clicks it with real mouse events. This is auto-waiting, and it is why the script has no sleep() calls. Lesson 03 explains each check.

expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada") is a web-first assertion: it keeps checking until the text matches or 5 seconds pass. The message appears half a second after the click, and the assertion simply waits for it. If it never appears, the assertion fails with an error saying what it saw instead. Lesson 04 covers assertions.

page.screenshot("signed-in.png") saves a PNG of what is visible in the page.

Coming from Playwright

This will look familiar: the locator, action and expect APIs follow Playwright's names. Three things differ. There is no sync_playwright() object to start first: launch("chrome") or launch("firefox") is the whole setup. The browsers are the stock Chrome and Firefox you have installed, not patched builds. And every timeout is in seconds, so timeout=5 is five seconds, not five milliseconds. Lesson 15 shows how to run existing Playwright code unchanged.

Coming from Selenium

There is no driver to download or start yourself, and no WebDriverWait: actions and assertions wait on their own. A locator is not an element you found earlier, so there is no "stale element" error; it finds the element again on every use.

docs.title: The same script, async
docs.text:
steero is built on asyncio, and the sync API you just used is a thin layer over it. If your program is already async (a web service, a bot, a tool that drives many pages at once), use the async API directly:

"""Lesson 01: the same first script, written with the async API.

    python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script_async.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os

import steero
from steero import expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        print(f"Running {browser.name} {browser.version}")
        page = await browser.new_page()

        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        print("Title:", await page.title())

        await page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        await page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

        await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")

        await page.screenshot("signed-in-async.png")
        print("Saved signed-in-async.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The differences are mechanical:

Sync Async from steero.sync_api import expect, launch import steero and from steero import expect with launch(...) as browser: async with steero.launch(...) as browser: page.goto(...) await page.goto(...) expect(...).to_have_text(...) await expect(...).to_have_text(...) run with main() run with asyncio.run(main())

Building a locator never needs await (it does not touch the page); actions, reads and assertions do. The course uses the sync API first, because most tests and scripts are easier to read without await on every line, and shows async wherever the difference matters.

How the sync API works: each sync Browser runs its own event loop on a background thread, and each call waits for its result. Pick one API per program and stay with it; do not pass objects from one to the other.

docs.title: Headless and headed
docs.text:
Browsers launch headless by default: no window, which is faster and works on machines with no screen, such as a build server. While you are writing a script, it often helps to watch it. Launch headed with headless=False, or, for the course examples, set STEERO_COURSE_HEADED:

$env:STEERO_COURSE_HEADED = "1"
python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py
Remove-Item Env:STEERO_COURSE_HEADED

STEERO_COURSE_HEADED=1 python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

A window opens, the form fills in, and the window closes when the script ends. It runs as fast as it can, so it is over quickly; launch("chrome", headless=False, slow_mo=0.5) waits half a second before each action so you can follow it. Lesson 10 shows how to stop at a point with page.pause() and look around.

launch() takes a few other options you will meet later. The ones worth knowing now:

Option Default Meaning headless True False shows the window window_size (1280, 800) the initial window size timeout 30 seconds allowed for the browser to start ignore_https_errors False accept self-signed certificates executable_path discovered use a specific browser binary

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
page.screenshot() takes a picture of the viewport (what fits in the window). Two variations cover most needs: full_page=True for the whole scrollable page, and locator.screenshot() for a single element.

"""Lesson 01: three kinds of screenshot (viewport, full page, one element).

    python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_screenshots.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    # window_size sets the browser window; the screenshot is of the page area inside it.
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS, window_size=(1024, 700)) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL)

        page.screenshot("home-viewport.png")                  # what fits in the window
        page.screenshot("home-full.png", full_page=True)      # the whole scrollable page
        png = page.locator("table").screenshot("endpoints.png")  # just one element

        # Every screenshot call also returns the PNG bytes, handy for attaching to a report.
        print(f"Saved 3 screenshots; the table alone is {len(png):,} bytes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Each call writes the file when you give it a path, and also returns the PNG as bytes, which is handy when you want to attach the picture to a report instead of saving it. Comparing screenshots against a saved baseline is a different job, covered in lesson 05.

docs.title: Where things go wrong
docs.text:
Most first scripts fail for one of a handful of reasons, and steero's errors say which. It is worth seeing one on purpose. This script asks for a button that does not exist, with a timeout of 2 seconds:

"""Lesson 01: what a failure looks like, so the first real one is not a surprise.

The script looks for a button that does not exist, with a short timeout, and prints the error.

    python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_when_it_fails.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero import SteeroTimeoutError
from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        try:
            # Timeouts are in seconds: this waits up to 2 seconds for a button called "Log in".
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Log in").click(timeout=2)
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
            print("The click timed out, as expected:")
            print("   ", error)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The click timed out, as expected:
    click get_by_role('button', name='Log in'): timed out after 2 s: no element matches

The message names the action, the locator, the time it waited, and the last thing that was wrong. "No element matches" means the locator found nothing: here the button is called "Sign in", not "Log in". Other endings point elsewhere, for example "element is not visible" or "element is covered by <div#overlay>". Lesson 03 lists them all.

The table below is the list to come back to when a script will not run:

What you see What it means What to do LaunchError: ... not found or STEERO_CHROME_PATH points at ..., which does not exist steero cannot find the browser Run steero doctor; install the browser or fix the path variable LaunchError: download failed: ... on the first Chrome launch the chromedriver download failed (offline, proxy, firewall) Run steero install chromedriver where you have access, or use Firefox ProtocolError: browsingContext.navigate: unknown error: net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED nothing is listening at that URL Start the practice site; check STEERO_COURSE_URL matches its port SteeroTimeoutError: ... timed out after 10 s: no element matches the locator finds nothing Check the text, role or label against the page (open it headed) StrictModeViolation: get_by_role('button') matched 2 elements the locator is ambiguous, so steero refuses to guess Make the locator more specific; lesson 02 shows how RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited an async call is missing await Add await; in sync code, import from steero.sync_api AttributeError: 'coroutine' object has no attribute ... the same: a missing await on a call whose result you used Add await before the call

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running, the same way as the examples.

docs.title: Exercise 1: an empty password
docs.text:
Write a script that enters a user name, leaves the password empty and clicks Sign in. Check that the page shows "Password is required" and that the welcome message did not appear.

Hint: page.get_by_text("Password is required") finds the error, and to_be_visible() checks that it is shown.

Solution 
"""Lesson 01, exercise 1: sign in without a password and check the error message.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_text("Password is required")).to_be_visible()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("")
        print("The form refused an empty password")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

to_have_text("") on the status line confirms that no welcome message appeared. It passes at once here, because the form never starts signing in.

docs.title: Exercise 2: just the form
docs.text:
Sign in as grace (any password), but before clicking Sign in, save a screenshot of only the form, as form.png. After the welcome message appears, save a full-page screenshot as welcome-full.png. Open both files and check they show what you expect.

Hint: the form has the id login, so page.locator("#login") finds it. Lesson 02 shows better ways.

Solution 
"""Lesson 01, exercise 2: screenshot only the filled-in form, then the whole page after signing in.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("grace")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("hopper")
        page.locator("#login").screenshot("form.png")

        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, grace")
        page.screenshot("welcome-full.png", full_page=True)
        print("Saved form.png and welcome-full.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 3: async, and the page title
docs.text:
Write an async script that prints the page title, signs in, and then checks that the title changed to "Welcome - steero practice site". Print the title again at the end.

Hint: expect(page).to_have_title(...) is an assertion about the page rather than a locator, and it waits like the others.

Solution 
"""Lesson 01, exercise 3: in async code, sign in and check that the page title changed.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os

import steero
from steero import expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = await browser.new_page()
        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        print("Before:", await page.title())

        await page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        await page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

        # The title changes half a second after the click; to_have_title waits for it.
        await expect(page).to_have_title("Welcome - steero practice site")
        print("After: ", await page.title())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

If you printed await page.title() straight after the click instead of asserting first, you probably saw the old title: the page changes it half a second later. The assertion waits; a plain read does not.

docs.title: Exercise 4: both browsers
docs.text: If you have both Chrome and Firefox, run example_first_script.py in each by setting STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER. Compare the two screenshots: the layout is the same, the fonts are drawn slightly differently. This is why lesson 05 keeps a separate visual baseline per browser.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Running an example before starting the practice site. The script fails with net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED. Start python examples/course/serve.py in another terminal.
  • Starting the server on another port and forgetting to say so. If you used --port, set STEERO_COURSE_URL to the address it printed.
  • Adding time.sleep() to wait for the page. The script gets slower and still fails on a slow day. Use an expect(...) assertion for the thing you are waiting for.
  • Reading a value straight after an action and getting the old one. page.title() or text_content() reads once, right now. Assert with expect when the page may still be changing.
  • Writing timeout=5000 out of habit. steero's timeouts are seconds; that waits 83 minutes.
  • Launching without with. If the script fails before browser.close(), the browser keeps running. Use with launch(...) as browser: (or async with steero.launch(...)).
  • Mixing the two APIs. from steero import expect is the async one; in a sync script, import both launch and expect from steero.sync_api.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• steero doctor shows which browsers steero can use; steero install chromedriver prepares Chrome ahead of time.
  • A script is launch() a browser, new_page(), goto(), then locators, actions and expect assertions.
  • The sync API (steero.sync_api) and the async API (steero) have the same names; async adds await.
  • Runs are headless by default; headless=False (or STEERO_COURSE_HEADED=1) shows the window.
  • Errors name the action, the locator, the time waited and the reason, so read them first.

Next: 02. Locators

docs.title: 02. Locators
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • find elements the way a user sees them: get_by_role, get_by_label, get_by_text, get_by_placeholder, get_by_alt_text, get_by_title
  • use get_by_test_id, CSS and XPath when nothing user-facing is stable
  • narrow and chain: first, nth, filter(has_text=, has=, has_not=), or_, and_, and locators inside locators
  • reach into iframes with frame_locator, and rely on open shadow roots being searched for you
  • explain strictness and read a StrictModeViolation
  • read state from an element (text_content, input_value, count, all) and know when to assert instead

Time: about 45 minutes. Before this: 01. Getting started. Code: examples/course/02-locators/

Every action and every assertion starts with a locator, so the way you find elements decides how readable your scripts are and how often they break. This lesson shows how to describe an element so that the description survives a redesign.

Keep the practice site running (python examples/course/serve.py) for the whole lesson. Most examples use /testsite/form.html, a form with one of everything; open it in your own browser next to the code.

docs.title: Locators are lazy and strict
docs.text:
A locator is a description of how to find elements, not an element you have already found. Building one does not touch the page:

button = page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in")   # nothing happens yet
button.click()                                          # now steero looks, waits, then clicks
button.click()                                          # and looks again, from scratch

Because the search runs again on every use, a locator never goes stale: if the page re-renders the button between two clicks, the second click finds the new one. You can build locators at the top of a script, keep them in variables or page objects, and use them whenever you like.

A locator is also strict. An action needs exactly one element, and when the description matches several, steero raises StrictModeViolation instead of guessing which one you meant. That sounds fussy, but a guess is how a test clicks "Delete" on the wrong row and still passes. You will trigger one on purpose later in the lesson.

Reads that work on many elements at once (count(), all(), all_inner_texts()) are not strict, and neither are assertions about lists such as to_have_count.

docs.title: Prefer what users see
docs.text:
The get_by_* family finds elements by what a person sees or what assistive technology announces:

Locator Finds Example on form.html get_by_role(role, name=...) elements by ARIA role and accessible name get_by_role("button", name="Sign in") get_by_label(text) form controls by their label, aria-label or aria-labelledby get_by_label("User name") get_by_placeholder(text) inputs by placeholder get_by_placeholder("you@example.com") get_by_text(text) the smallest element containing the text get_by_text("Banana") get_by_alt_text(text) images by alt get_by_alt_text("Company logo") get_by_title(text) elements by title get_by_title("Logo")

get_by_role is the one to reach for first. A role is what kind of thing the element is (button, link, textbox, checkbox, radio, combobox, heading, row, cell and so on), and the accessible name is what a screen reader would call it: a button's text, an input's label, an image's alt text. Together they describe an element the way a user would, and they keep working when the markup or the CSS classes change. get_by_role takes a few extra filters, such as level=1 for an <h1>, checked=True for a ticked checkbox and disabled=True for a disabled control:

page.get_by_role("heading", level=1)
page.get_by_role("radio", checked=True)
page.get_by_role("button", disabled=True)

How text is matched. A text argument (name=, or the text of get_by_label, get_by_text and the others) matches a case-insensitive substring by default, with whitespace squashed. So get_by_role("button", name="sign") finds "Sign in". Pass exact=True for a whole, case-sensitive match, or a compiled regular expression for anything else:

page.get_by_text("Banana", exact=True)
page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^ban", re.IGNORECASE))

Why not just CSS? #user or .btn-primary describe how the page is built, and they change whenever someone restructures the HTML or renames a class. "The text box labelled User name" changes only when the page changes for its users too, and then you want the test to notice. Role-based locators also double as a small accessibility check: a button that get_by_role cannot find by name is a button a screen reader cannot announce.

Coming from Selenium

The find_element(By...) calls map like this:

Selenium steero find_element(By.ID, "user") page.locator("#user"), or better page.get_by_label("User name") find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.item") page.locator("li.item") find_element(By.XPATH, "//li[2]") page.locator("xpath=//li[2]") find_element(By.LINK_TEXT, "Docs") page.get_by_role("link", name="Docs") find_elements(By.TAG_NAME, "li") page.locator("li").all() element.find_element(...) locator.locator(...) or locator.get_by_role(...)

The big difference is timing: find_element looks once, now, and hands back an element that can go stale. A locator looks every time it is used and waits for the element to be ready.

docs.title: Test ids, CSS and XPath
docs.text:
Sometimes nothing user-facing is stable: an icon button with no label, a cell in a grid of identical cells, text that is translated. Then use a test id, an attribute added to the markup only for tests:

page.get_by_test_id("user-input")            # <input data-testid="user-input">
page.get_by_test_id("cart", attribute="data-qa")   # a different attribute name

A test id is a promise between the developers and the tests, so it does not change by accident. It says nothing about what the user sees, though, so prefer a role or a label when one exists.

page.locator(selector) takes CSS, or XPath with an xpath= prefix (a selector starting with // is read as XPath too):

page.locator("#items li")
page.locator("xpath=//ul[@id='items']/li[last()]")

CSS selectors in steero also understand three text pseudo-classes that browsers do not: :has-text("x") (contains x, ignoring case), :text("x") (the smallest element containing x) and :text-is("x") (exactly x). They are handy inside a longer selector:

page.locator("label:has-text('Pro') > input")

The locators guide lists every option.

docs.title: Narrowing and chaining
docs.text:
A locator that matches a list can be narrowed:

Narrowing Keeps .first, .last, .nth(i) one match by position (nth(-1) is the last) .filter(has_text="x") matches whose text contains x (has_not_text= drops them) .filter(has=locator) matches that contain an element matching locator (has_not= drops them) .filter(visible=True) visible matches only a.or_(b) elements matching a or b (or both), in document order a.and_(b) elements matching both a and b

And any locator can search inside another, which is called scoping:

table = page.get_by_role("table", name="Products")
rows = table.get_by_role("row")                    # rows in this table only
teapot = rows.filter(has_text="Green teapot")      # the row that mentions the teapot
teapot.get_by_role("button").click()               # the button in that row

Read that as a sentence: "in the Products table, the row with Green teapot, its button". Scoping and filtering are how you deal with repeated structure (table rows, cards, list items) without counting positions. nth(2) breaks as soon as the order changes; "the row with Green teapot" does not.

has= takes a locator built from the page, and steero searches for it inside each candidate:

sold_out = rows.filter(has=page.get_by_role("button", disabled=True))

Coming from Playwright

The locator API is Playwright's, name for name: get_by_role, filter(has=...), or_, and_, nth, first, frame_locator, and the :has-text() pseudo-class all behave the same, and text is matched by the same rules (substring and case-insensitive unless exact=True). One difference to know about: steero computes accessible names with an approximation of the accname algorithm, so in edge cases (nested labels, aria-owns, CSS generated content) a name can differ from the one Playwright computes. If a get_by_role name that works in Playwright finds nothing here, print locator.aria_snapshot() of the surrounding element to see the names steero computed.

docs.title: Frames and shadow DOM
docs.text:
Open shadow roots need nothing special. Web components often hide their markup inside a shadow root, where document.querySelector cannot see it. steero's CSS, text, label and role queries search open shadow roots for you, however deeply they nest. On /testsite/shadow.html the Follow button is two shadow roots deep, and this simply works:

page.get_by_role("button", name="Follow").click()

(Closed shadow roots are closed to every tool by design; nothing can reach into them.)

Iframes must be entered. An iframe holds a separate document, so a locator built from the page does not look inside it. frame_locator(selector) names the iframe, and locators built from it search the document inside:

child = page.frame_locator("#child")
child.get_by_role("button", name="Inner button").click()

For an iframe inside an iframe, chain one frame_locator per level. Exercise 4 does exactly that.

docs.title: Strictness in practice
docs.text:
/testsite/form.html has several text boxes: User name, Password, Notes and the read-only Fixed field (get_by_role("textbox").count() says 4). The file input at the bottom is not one of them: it takes no typed text, and browsers expose it as a button, so steero gives it the button role, as Playwright does. Ask for "the text box" and steero refuses:

StrictModeViolation: get_by_role('textbox') matched 4 elements; use .first, .nth() or a more specific locator

The message names the locator and the number of matches. The fix is almost never .first: that makes the script pick whichever text box happens to come first today, which is the guess strict mode exists to prevent. Say which one you mean instead, with a name (get_by_role("textbox", name="Notes")), a filter, or a scope. Use .first only when any of the matches would do, such as "click any product".

A StrictModeViolation is raised at once, without waiting for the timeout, because waiting would not change the answer.

docs.title: Reading state
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a value from the page, to print it or to use it later in the script. These calls read it:

Call Returns count() how many elements match right now all() a list of locators, one per current match text_content() the element's text, as in the DOM (textContent) inner_text() the text as rendered (hidden text left out, CSS applied) all_inner_texts() the rendered text of every match, as a list input_value() the current value of an input, textarea or select get_attribute(name) an attribute, or None is_visible(), is_enabled(), is_checked() a yes or no 
for item in page.locator("#items li").all():
    print(item.text_content())

There is a catch. count(), all(), all_inner_texts() and is_visible() answer right now, without waiting. On a page that is still loading (the products table arrives a moment after the page does) they can see an empty list. The single-element reads (text_content(), input_value() and so on) wait for the element to exist, but not for its text to change.

So for anything you check, use an assertion instead of a read plus assert:

assert page.locator("#items li").count() == 3          # reads once; fails if the list is late
expect(page.locator("#items li")).to_have_count(3)    # waits until it is true, up to 5 seconds

Reads are for values you need; assertions are for facts you check. Lesson 04 covers assertions in depth.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
This script opens /testsite/form.html and finds its controls in every user-facing way, then by test id, CSS and XPath, printing what each locator found:

"""Lesson 02: find every control on a form the way a user would describe it.

Opens the integration-test form, finds its controls by role, label, placeholder, alt text, title
and test id, and prints what each locator found.

    python examples/course/02-locators/example_user_facing.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import re

from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")

        heading = page.get_by_role("heading", level=1)
        print("Heading:", heading.text_content())

        # Labels, placeholders and test ids all lead to the same User name field.
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        print("By placeholder:", page.get_by_placeholder("you@example.com").input_value())
        print("By test id:    ", page.get_by_test_id("user-input").input_value())

        # A role plus its accessible name is the most precise user-facing locator.
        page.get_by_role("checkbox", name="Remember me").check()
        page.get_by_role("radio", name="Pro").check()
        print("Checked radio: ", page.get_by_role("radio", checked=True).get_attribute("value"))
        print("Country:       ", page.get_by_role("combobox", name="Country").input_value())

        # Images by alt text or title; text by a regular expression.
        print("Logo found:    ", page.get_by_alt_text("Company logo").count(), "by alt,",
              page.get_by_title("Logo").count(), "by title")
        print("Fruit by regex:", page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^ban", re.IGNORECASE)).text_content())

        # CSS and XPath still work when nothing user-facing is stable.
        print("By CSS:        ", page.locator("#items li").count(), "list items")
        print("By XPath:      ", page.locator("xpath=//ul[@id='items']/li[last()]").text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it from the repository root:

python examples/course/02-locators/example_user_facing.py

Heading: Sign in
By placeholder: ada
By test id:     ada
Checked radio:  pro
Country:        in
Logo found:     1 by alt, 1 by title
Fruit by regex: Banana
By CSS:         3 list items
By XPath:       Cherry

The second and third lines prove that three different locators reach the same field: the value filled in through the label is read back through the placeholder and the test id.

Two more scripts cover the rest of the lesson. example_narrowing.py works on the products page (/products.html) with nth, filter(has_text=), filter(has=), scoping and or_:

"""Lesson 02: narrow a list of matches with nth, filter, has, or_ and scoping.

Works on the products page, whose table is filled from /api/products after the page loads.

    python examples/course/02-locators/example_narrowing.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        # The rows arrive a moment after the page loads; wait for them before counting.
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")

        table = page.get_by_role("table", name="Products")
        rows = table.get_by_role("row")                      # scoped: rows inside this table only
        print("Rows, header included:", rows.count())
        print("First data row:", rows.nth(1).inner_text().split("\t")[0])
        print("Last row:      ", rows.last.inner_text().split("\t")[0])

        # filter(has_text=...) keeps rows whose text contains the words.
        teapot = rows.filter(has_text="Green teapot")
        print("Teapot row:    ", teapot.inner_text().replace("\t", " | "))

        # filter(has=...) keeps rows that contain a matching element; has_not drops them.
        sold_out = rows.filter(has=page.get_by_role("button", disabled=True))
        print("Sold out:      ", sold_out.get_by_role("cell").first.text_content())
        buyable = rows.filter(has=page.get_by_role("button", disabled=False))
        print("Can be bought: ", buyable.count(), "rows")

        # A locator inside a locator: the button in the teapot row, found by its role.
        teapot.get_by_role("button").click()
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("cart-count")).to_have_text("1")

        # or_ matches either one, which helps when a page shows one of two states.
        state = page.get_by_text("No products yet").or_(page.get_by_text("3 products"))
        print("Page state:    ", state.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

example_shadow_and_frames.py fills an input inside two shadow roots and clicks a button inside an iframe:

"""Lesson 02: reach elements inside open shadow roots and inside iframes.

Shadow roots need nothing special; iframes are entered with frame_locator.

    python examples/course/02-locators/example_shadow_and_frames.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()

        # The input and the button live two shadow roots deep; the locators do not care.
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/shadow.html")
        page.get_by_placeholder("Say hi").fill("hello")
        print("Shadow input:", page.get_by_placeholder("Say hi").input_value())
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Follow").click()
        expect(page.locator("#result")).to_have_text("followed")
        print("Card name:   ", page.locator(".name").text_content())

        # An iframe is a separate document: enter it first, then locate inside it.
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/frames.html")
        child = page.frame_locator("#child")
        child.get_by_role("button", name="Inner button").click()
        expect(child.locator("#inner-btn")).to_have_text("Inner clicked")
        print("Frame button:", child.locator("#inner-btn").text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Each exercise has a solution script; run it the same way as the examples.

docs.title: Exercise 1: three ways to one button
docs.text:
On /testsite/form.html, find the Sign in button three different ways: by role, by text, and by CSS. Check that all three locate the same element by comparing their bounding_box() (the position and size of the element on the page).

Hint: page.get_by_text("Sign in") matches two elements, because the heading says "Sign in" too. How can you search only inside the form?

Solution 
"""Lesson 02, exercise 1: find the Sign in button three ways and prove they find the same element.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")

        by_role = page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in")
        # The heading also says "Sign in", so text alone matches two elements; scope it to the form.
        by_text = page.locator("#login").get_by_text("Sign in")
        by_css = page.locator("button[type=submit]")

        boxes = [locator.bounding_box() for locator in (by_role, by_text, by_css)]
        for name, box in zip(("role", "text", "CSS"), boxes, strict=True):
            print(f"By {name:<4}: {box}")
        assert boxes[0] == boxes[1] == boxes[2], "the three locators found different elements"
        print("All three locators found the same button")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Scoping the text search to #login leaves out the heading, which is outside the form. Equal boxes mean equal elements here, because two elements cannot occupy exactly the same box on this page.

docs.title: Exercise 2: the row that has it
docs.text:
On /products.html, add the Green teapot to the cart by clicking the button in its row, and check that the cart count shows 1. Then print the names of the products that are still in stock (their button is enabled).

Hint: start from page.get_by_role("row"), and use filter(has_text=...) for the first part and filter(has=...) for the second.

Solution 
"""Lesson 02, exercise 2: add the Green teapot to the cart, then list the products still in stock.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        rows = page.get_by_role("row")

        # Actions wait for the row to appear, so no wait is needed before this click.
        rows.filter(has_text="Green teapot").get_by_role("button", name="Add").click()
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("cart-count")).to_have_text("1")

        # Rows with an enabled button are in stock; the header row has no button at all.
        in_stock = rows.filter(has=page.get_by_role("button", disabled=False))
        expect(in_stock).to_have_count(2)
        # all_inner_texts() reads every match at once; a row's cells are separated by tabs.
        print("In stock:", [text.split("\t")[0] for text in in_stock.all_inner_texts()])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

In stock: ['Blue mug', 'Green teapot']

The header row has no button, so has= leaves it out without any extra work. The to_have_count(2) assertion comes before all_inner_texts() because the read does not wait; after the assertion the rows are certainly there.

docs.title: Exercise 3: a strict mode violation
docs.text:
On /testsite/form.html, call page.get_by_role("textbox").fill("hello"), catch the StrictModeViolation (import it with from steero import StrictModeViolation) and print it. Then fix the locator two ways: once with a better name, once by scoping to a part of the page.

Solution 
"""Lesson 02, exercise 3: trigger a StrictModeViolation, read it, then fix the locator two ways.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (four text boxes: the file input is a button now)
"""

import os

from steero import StrictModeViolation
from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")

        try:
            page.get_by_role("textbox").fill("hello")  # four text boxes on this form
        except StrictModeViolation as error:
            print("Refused:", error)

        # Fix 1: give the role an accessible name, so only one text box qualifies.
        notes = page.get_by_role("textbox", name="Notes")
        notes.fill("hello")
        print("Fix 1, a better name:", notes.input_value())

        # Fix 2: scope the search to the part of the page you mean (the label wraps its input).
        password = page.locator("label", has_text="Password").get_by_role("textbox")
        password.fill("secret")
        print("Fix 2, scoping:      ", password.input_value())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Refused: get_by_role('textbox') matched 4 elements; use .first, .nth() or a more specific locator
Fix 1, a better name: hello
Fix 2, scoping:       secret

The second fix works because the Password label wraps its input, so the text box is inside the label. Catching the error is only for this exercise: in a real script, let it fail.

docs.title: Exercise 4: two frames down
docs.text:
/testsite/frames.html holds an iframe (#child), which holds another iframe (#grandchild) with a button in it. Print the button's text, click it, and check that its text changed to "Deep clicked".

Solution 
"""Lesson 02, exercise 4: read and click the button inside an iframe inside an iframe.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/frames.html")

        # One frame_locator per iframe on the way down: page > #child > #grandchild.
        deep = page.frame_locator("#child").frame_locator("#grandchild").get_by_role("button")
        print("Before:", deep.text_content())
        deep.click()
        expect(deep).to_have_text("Deep clicked")
        print("After: ", deep.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

get_by_role("button") is not ambiguous here, because inside the grandchild frame there is only one button. The locator is scoped by the two frames it entered.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Adding .first to silence a StrictModeViolation. The script now clicks whichever match comes first, and breaks silently when the order changes. Name the element you mean with a role and name, a filter or a scope.
  • Expecting get_by_text to be exact. It matches a case-insensitive substring, so get_by_text("Sign in") also finds "Sign in to continue". Pass exact=True, or use get_by_role with a name.
  • Using count() or all() before the content has loaded. They answer right now and happily return 0 or []. Wait first with an assertion (to_have_count, or to_have_text on a status line), or assert on the list directly.
  • Looking for an element inside an iframe from the page. The locator times out with "no element matches", although you can see the element. Enter the frame with page.frame_locator("#frame") first.
  • Copying a long CSS path from DevTools (div:nth-child(3) > div > span). It breaks on the next layout change. Find a role, a label or a test id instead.
  • Building a locator from an element's current text when the text changes. A button found by name="Save" is gone once it says "Saved". Use a name that stays the same, a test id, or or_ to accept both.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A locator is a lazy description: it is resolved again on every action, so it never goes stale.
  • Locators are strict: an action on several matches raises StrictModeViolation at once; fix the description rather than adding .first.
  • Prefer get_by_role with a name, then labels and text; use test ids, CSS and XPath when nothing user-facing is stable.
  • Narrow with filter, nth, or_ and and_, and scope one locator inside another.
  • Open shadow roots are searched for you; iframes are entered with frame_locator.
  • Reads such as count() answer right now; use expect for anything you check.

Next: 03. Actions and auto-waiting

docs.title: 03. Actions and auto-waiting
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • click, double click, hover, fill, clear, press keys and type key by key
  • check boxes and radios, select options, upload files and drag and drop
  • explain the actionability checks (attached, visible, stable, enabled, editable, receives the click) and read the error that names the failed one
  • set timeouts in seconds per call and per page (set_default_timeout)
  • wait for a condition (wait_for, wait_for_url, wait_for_function) instead of sleeping

Time: about 45 minutes. Before this: 02. Locators. Code: examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/

A locator says which element; an action says what to do with it. This lesson covers every common action and, more importantly, what steero does before each one: it waits until the element is ready. That waiting is why a steero script needs no sleep() calls, and knowing how it works lets you read a timeout error in seconds instead of guessing.

The practice page for this lesson is /testsite/form.html. Open it in your own browser and reload it a few times: a dark overlay covers the page for 0.7 seconds, and a "Late button" appears after 0.6 seconds. Both are there on purpose, to give auto-waiting something to wait for.

docs.title: Your first actions
docs.text:
Most scripts use a handful of actions, and each reads like what a user does:

page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")                          # type into a field
page.get_by_label("Remember me").check()                            # tick a checkbox
page.get_by_label("Pro").check()                                    # choose a radio button
page.get_by_label("Country").select_option(label="United Kingdom")  # pick from a <select>
page.get_by_label("Notes").press("Enter")                           # press one key
page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()                  # click

A few details are worth knowing from the start:

  • fill(value) replaces the whole value of an input, textarea or editable element, then fires input and change events, which frameworks such as React listen for. It does not press individual keys. clear() is fill("").
  • check() and uncheck() are better than click() for checkboxes: they do nothing when the box is already in the state you asked for, and they verify the state afterwards. set_checked(True) is the same with a flag.
  • select_option() takes a value (select_option("uk")), a label=, or an index=, or a list of them for a multi-select, and returns the values it selected.
  • click() sends real mouse events (move, press, release) at the centre of the element. It takes button="right", modifiers=["Shift"], click_count=2 and position={"x": 5, "y": 5} (relative to the element's top-left corner) when you need them.

docs.title: What auto-waiting checks
docs.text:
Before every action, steero finds the element again and runs the actionability checks in the page. If a check fails, it waits a little and tries again, until the checks pass or the timeout runs out. Which checks run depends on the action:

Check Means click fill hover check attached the element is in the DOM yes yes yes yes visible it has a size and is not hidden by CSS yes yes yes yes stable it is not moving (same box over two animation frames) yes yes yes enabled not disabled, not aria-disabled, not in a disabled fieldset yes yes yes editable not read-only yes receives the click nothing else covers its centre point yes yes yes

The last check is the one other tools often miss. On form.html the overlay is a transparent layer over the whole page. A click on the Covered button during the first 0.7 seconds would land on the overlay, not on the button; a script that clicked blindly would "succeed" and the button would never know. steero sees that the point is covered and waits:

page.get_by_role("button", name="Covered button").click()   # waits for the overlay to go

If the timeout passes first, the error names the action, the locator, the time it waited, and the check that was still failing:

click get_by_role('button', name='Covered button'): timed out after 0.2 s: element is covered by <div#overlay>

The ending tells you where to look:

Error ends with What to check no element matches the locator: wrong name, wrong frame, element not created yet element is not visible CSS (display: none, zero size), or the element appears later than the timeout element is not stable (still moving) an animation or transition that never settles element is disabled the app has not enabled it yet: a form not filled in, a request still running element is not editable a read-only field element is covered by <...> an overlay, a cookie banner, a toast, a sticky header

force=True skips the checks (click(force=True)). Use it only when you are sure a check is wrong for your page; usually the check is right and the page is not ready.

Coming from Selenium

There is no WebDriverWait, no expected_conditions and no implicit wait to configure. Each action waits for exactly what it needs. There is also no StaleElementReferenceException: a locator finds the element again on every action, so a re-render between two steps does not break the script. And ElementClickInterceptedException becomes a wait plus, if the page never clears, a timeout that names the element in the way.

docs.title: Timeouts in seconds
docs.text:
Every action waits up to 10 seconds by default. Timeouts in steero are always in seconds, so timeout=2 means two seconds:

page.get_by_role("button", name="Save").click(timeout=2)   # this call only
page.set_default_timeout(5)                                # every action and wait on this page
page.set_default_navigation_timeout(60)                    # goto, reload, wait_for_url

Navigations (goto, reload, wait_for_url) have their own default of 30 seconds, because loading a page usually takes longer than finding a button. Assertions have a third default, 5 seconds, which lesson 04 covers.

When a wait runs out, steero raises SteeroTimeoutError (from steero import SteeroTimeoutError). It is also a Python TimeoutError, so code that already catches TimeoutError works.

Pick timeouts for what the app really does. A longer timeout costs nothing when the page is fast, because steero stops waiting the moment the checks pass; it only matters when something is wrong. Shortening a timeout does not make a script faster.

Coming from Playwright

Same actions, same checks, but seconds, not milliseconds: click(timeout=2) is two seconds. A Playwright habit of timeout=5000 asks for 83 minutes. The default action timeout is 10 seconds (Playwright's is 30); page.set_default_timeout(30) restores Playwright's.

docs.title: Keyboard and mouse
docs.text:
press(key) focuses the element and presses one key or a combination. Key names follow the browser's KeyboardEvent.key values: Enter, Tab, Escape, Backspace, ArrowDown, F2, or a single character. Combinations join keys with +, modifiers first:

notes = page.get_by_label("Notes")
notes.press("Shift+A")             # a capital A
notes.press("ControlOrMeta+A")     # select all: Meta on macOS, Control elsewhere
notes.press_sequentially("hello")  # five separate key presses

fill or press_sequentially? Use fill almost always: it is fast and it sets the value in one step. Use press_sequentially(text) when the page reacts to individual keys, such as an autocomplete box that searches as you type, or an input that formats a card number. It takes a delay= in seconds between keys.

page.keyboard sends keys to whatever has focus, without a locator: page.keyboard.press("Tab") moves focus like a user would, and page.keyboard.type("text") types into the focused field.

For the mouse, the locator actions are usually enough: hover(), click(), dblclick(), and click(button="right") for a context menu. page.mouse works in viewport pixels for the rare case where you need a point rather than an element (drawing on a canvas, for example): page.mouse.move(x, y), down(), up(), click(x, y) and wheel(0, 300). page.mouse does not auto-wait: it acts at that point, whatever is there now.

docs.title: Files and drag and drop
docs.text:
set_input_files() sets the files of an <input type="file">, as if the user had picked them in the file dialog (which never opens):

upload = page.locator("#file")
upload.set_input_files("report.pdf")                    # one file
upload.set_input_files(["report.pdf", "photo.png"])     # several, if the input allows it
upload.set_input_files({"name": "hello.txt", "mimeType": "text/plain", "buffer": b"hi"})  # in memory
upload.set_input_files([])                              # clear the selection

Paths are relative to the current directory. The in-memory form is handy in tests: no file to create and clean up.

drag_to(target) drags one element onto another with real pointer events (press, several moves, release), which works for pages that implement drag with mouse or pointer events and for HTML5 drag and drop:

page.locator("#box").drag_to(page.locator("#target"))
page.drag_and_drop("#box", "#target")                   # the same, with two selectors

Browser support

Firefox starts a native HTML5 drag but does not deliver the final button release to it through WebDriver BiDi, so the page would never see the drop. For elements marked draggable="true" steero replays the HTML5 drag events itself in Firefox. Pages that drag with pointer events, such as /testsite/dnd.html, get real pointer input in both browsers. Your script is the same either way.

docs.title: Waiting for things that are not actions
docs.text:
Actions wait for their own element. Sometimes you need to wait for something else: a spinner to go away, a URL to change, a value in the page to be ready. There is a wait for each:

page.locator("#spinner").wait_for(state="hidden")       # or "visible", "attached", "detached"
page.wait_for_url("**/orders/*")                         # after a click that navigates
page.wait_for_function("() => window.appReady === true") # any JavaScript condition

wait_for_url takes the same patterns as page.route in lesson 07: a glob string (** any text, * any text without a slash; a URL without wildcards must match exactly), a compiled regex such as re.compile(r"/orders/\d+$"), or a function that takes the URL.

wait_for_function returns the truthy value the function produced, so it can also fetch the value you were waiting for. Each takes a timeout= in seconds.

And then there is the wait you should not use. time.sleep(1) (or page.wait_for_timeout(1)) waits a fixed time whatever the page does:

  • when the page is faster than the sleep, the script wastes the rest of the second, on every run;
  • when the page is slower (a busy build machine, a cold cache), the script fails anyway, and you raise the sleep, and every run gets slower.

A condition-based wait stops the moment the condition is true and fails only when it is really not going to happen. Exercise 4 measures the difference. Before you reach for a wait at all, ask whether the next action or an assertion would wait for you; most of the time it does.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
This script fills in every kind of control on /testsite/form.html and submits it. There is no sleep anywhere: the checkbox click waits for the overlay to go, the Late button click waits for the button to appear, and the assertion waits for the status line.

"""Lesson 03: fill in and submit a whole form, with no sleeps anywhere.

The page shows a "Late button" 0.6 seconds after loading and covers everything with an overlay
for 0.7 seconds. Every action below waits for its element to be ready on its own.

    python examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/example_fill_the_form.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import time

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        started = time.monotonic()

        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")                 # text
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")             # password
        page.get_by_label("Remember me").check()                   # checkbox (waits for the overlay)
        page.get_by_label("Pro").check()                           # radio
        page.get_by_label("Country").select_option(label="United Kingdom")
        page.get_by_label("Notes").fill("Two lines\nof notes")     # textarea
        page.locator("#file").set_input_files(
            {"name": "notes.txt", "mimeType": "text/plain", "buffer": b"hello"})

        # Hidden at first, then shown: click() waits until it is visible.
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Late button").click()
        # Under the overlay at first: click() waits until nothing covers it.
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Covered button").click()

        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Signed in as ada")

        print("Status:  ", page.get_by_role("status").text_content())
        print("Country: ", page.get_by_label("Country").input_value())
        print("File:    ", page.locator("#files").text_content())
        print("Buttons: ", page.locator("#late").text_content(), "/", page.locator("#covered").text_content())
        print(f"Done in {time.monotonic() - started:.1f} s, without a single sleep")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it from the repository root:

python examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/example_fill_the_form.py

Status:   Signed in as ada
Country:  uk
File:     notes.txt
Buttons:  Clicked late / Clicked through
Done in 1.4 s, without a single sleep

The time is about the 0.7 seconds the overlay stays, plus the work itself. Run it with STEERO_COURSE_HEADED=1 to watch it: the form fills in while the overlay is still there, because fill does not need to receive a click, and the checkbox waits.

Async version

With the async API several pages can work at once. Here two users fill in the form concurrently with asyncio.gather, in one browser; while one waits for its overlay, the other one keeps working, and the printed lines interleave.

"""Lesson 03: with the async API, actions on several pages run at the same time.

One browser, two users: each fills in the form in a context of its own, concurrently, with
asyncio.gather. Each one waits for the late button and the overlay on its own page, and while one
waits, the other keeps working. The contexts keep the users apart (cookies, storage), as two
separate browser profiles would.

    python examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/example_fill_the_form_async.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (one browser with a context per user, now that background pages no longer stall)
"""

import asyncio
import os

import steero
from steero import expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def sign_in(browser: steero.Browser, user: str) -> str:
    """Fill in the form as ``user`` in a fresh context and return the status text."""
    context = await browser.new_context()  # a clean, separate session for this user
    try:
        page = await context.new_page()
        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        print(f"{user}: page loaded")
        await page.get_by_label("User name").fill(user)
        await page.get_by_label("Remember me").check()              # waits for the overlay
        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Late button").click()  # waits until it is shown
        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text(f"Signed in as {user}")
        print(f"{user}: signed in")
        return str(await page.get_by_role("status").text_content())
    finally:
        await context.close()


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        # gather starts both coroutines and waits for both; their steps interleave.
        results = await asyncio.gather(sign_in(browser, "ada"), sign_in(browser, "grace"))
        print(results)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Each user gets a browser context of its own (browser.new_context()): a separate session with its own cookies and storage, so one user's sign-in can never leak into the other's page. Two pages of one context would share them. Only one tab can be in front at a time, so steero brings a page to the front for the moment it clicks, types or takes a screenshot; the other page's waits keep running in the background.

Two more scripts go with the sections above. example_keyboard_and_mouse.py types, uses key combinations, double-clicks and clicks with page.mouse:

"""Lesson 03: keys, key combinations, typing key by key, double click and hover.

The form page records every key it receives in a paragraph, so you can see the real key events.

    python examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/example_keyboard_and_mouse.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        notes = page.get_by_label("Notes")

        notes.press_sequentially("hello world")      # one real key event per character
        notes.press("ControlOrMeta+A")                # select all (Meta on macOS, Control elsewhere)
        notes.press("Backspace")                      # delete the selection
        expect(notes).to_have_value("")

        page.keyboard.type("typed by page.keyboard")  # keys go to whatever has focus
        expect(notes).to_have_value("typed by page.keyboard")
        print("Keys the page saw:", page.locator("#keys").text_content()[:44], "...")

        # This page has no double-click handler, so add one that writes into the status line.
        heading = page.get_by_role("heading", name="Sign in")
        heading.evaluate("(el) => el.addEventListener('dblclick', "
                         "() => { document.getElementById('status').textContent = 'double-clicked'; })")
        heading.dblclick()                            # two real clicks, close enough to count as one
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("double-clicked")
        print("The heading received a dblclick event")

        # hover() waits until nothing covers the button (the overlay), then moves the pointer there.
        sign_in = page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in")
        sign_in.hover()
        # page.mouse never waits: it acts at viewport pixels, whatever is there right now.
        box = sign_in.bounding_box()
        assert box is not None
        page.mouse.click(box["x"] + box["width"] / 2, box["y"] + box["height"] / 2)
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_contain_text("Signed in")
        print("Clicked Sign in with page.mouse")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

example_waiting.py uses set_default_timeout, wait_for, wait_for_function and wait_for_url:

"""Lesson 03: wait for things that are not actions, and set timeouts in seconds.

    python examples/course/03-actions-and-auto-waiting/example_waiting.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import re
import time

from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.set_default_timeout(5)               # every action and wait on this page: 5 seconds
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        started = time.monotonic()

        # Wait for an element to reach a state: visible, hidden, attached or detached.
        page.locator("#late").wait_for(state="visible")
        print(f"Late button visible after {time.monotonic() - started:.1f} s")
        page.locator("#overlay").wait_for(state="detached", timeout=2)
        print(f"Overlay removed after {time.monotonic() - started:.1f} s")

        # Wait for any condition you can write in JavaScript; the truthy value is returned.
        count = page.wait_for_function("() => document.querySelectorAll('#items li').length")
        print("List items:", count)

        # Wait for the URL after a click that navigates.
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/index.html")
        page.get_by_role("link", name="Second page").click()
        page.wait_for_url(re.compile(r"second\.html$"))
        print("Now at:", page.url.rsplit("/", 1)[-1])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Late button visible after 0.8 s
Overlay removed after 0.8 s
List items: 3
Now at: second.html

docs.title: Exercise 1: read a failed check
docs.text:
Click the Covered button on /testsite/form.html with timeout=0.2, so the click fails while the overlay is still there. Catch the SteeroTimeoutError and print it. Which check failed? Then make the Disabled button and the read-only Fixed field fail too, and compare the three messages. Finally, click the Covered button again with the default timeout and check that it worked.

Solution 
"""Lesson 03, exercise 1: make a click time out on purpose and read which check failed.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero import SteeroTimeoutError
from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        covered = page.get_by_role("button", name="Covered button")

        # 0.2 seconds is shorter than the 0.7 seconds the overlay stays, so this must fail.
        try:
            covered.click(timeout=0.2)
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
            print("Failed as planned:", error)
            assert "covered by <div#overlay>" in str(error)

        # Two other checks failing, for comparison: enabled, then editable.
        try:
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Disabled").click(timeout=0.2)
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
