            print("Failed as planned:", error)
        try:
            page.get_by_label("Fixed").fill("x", timeout=0.2)
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
            print("Failed as planned:", error)

        # With the default timeout the same click simply waits for the overlay to go.
        covered.click()
        # The click renames the button, so check it by id: the name "Covered button" is gone now.
        expect(page.locator("#covered")).to_have_text("Clicked through")
        print("Clicked once the overlay was gone")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Failed as planned: click get_by_role('button', name='Covered button'): timed out after 0.2 s: element is covered by <div#overlay>
Failed as planned: click get_by_role('button', name='Disabled'): timed out after 0.2 s: element is disabled
Failed as planned: fill get_by_label('Fixed'): timed out after 0.2 s: element is not editable
Clicked once the overlay was gone

Notice the last assertion uses #covered, not the covered locator: clicking renames the button to "Clicked through", so a locator that finds it by the name "Covered button" no longer matches anything.

docs.title: Exercise 2: upload two files
docs.text:
Create two small files in the current folder, upload both to the file input on /testsite/form.html (#file) in one call, and check that the page lists both names (it shows them in #files, separated by a comma). Then replace them with a file made in memory.

Solution 
"""Lesson 03, exercise 2: upload two files and check the names the page shows.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
from pathlib import Path

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    # Two small files in the current folder to upload.
    first, second = Path("report.txt"), Path("data.csv")
    first.write_text("quarterly report\n", encoding="utf-8")
    second.write_text("id,name\n1,ada\n", encoding="utf-8")

    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        upload = page.locator("#file")

        upload.set_input_files([first, second])           # paths on this machine
        expect(page.locator("#files")).to_have_text("report.txt,data.csv")
        print("Uploaded:", page.locator("#files").text_content())

        # A file can also be made in memory, without touching the disk.
        upload.set_input_files({"name": "hello.txt", "mimeType": "text/plain", "buffer": b"hi"})
        expect(page.locator("#files")).to_have_text("hello.txt")
        print("Replaced with:", page.locator("#files").text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Each call to set_input_files replaces the selection, as picking files in the dialog again would.

docs.title: Exercise 3: drag and drop
docs.text:
On /testsite/dnd.html, drag the blue box onto the dashed target and check that the state line says "dropped". Then reload the page and do the same with page.drag_and_drop.

Solution 
"""Lesson 03, exercise 3: drag the box onto its target and check the page noticed.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/dnd.html")
        state = page.locator("#state")
        expect(state).to_have_text("idle")

        page.locator("#box").drag_to(page.locator("#target"))
        expect(state).to_have_text("dropped")
        print("State after drag_to:", state.text_content())

        # page.drag_and_drop does the same with two selectors.
        page.reload()
        page.drag_and_drop("#box", "#target")
        expect(state).to_have_text("dropped")
        print("State after drag_and_drop:", state.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The page reports "missed" when the box is released outside the target, so "dropped" proves the pointer really ended on it.

docs.title: Exercise 4: remove a sleep
docs.text:
Here is a script someone wrote while the Late button was giving them trouble:

page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
time.sleep(1)  # wait for the late button
page.locator("#late").click()

Replace the sleep with the right wait (or with none at all), and measure both versions with time.monotonic().

Solution 
"""Lesson 03, exercise 4: replace a fixed sleep with the right wait, and measure the difference.

This is the one script in the course that sleeps on purpose, to show what it costs.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import time

from steero.sync_api import Page, expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def with_sleep(page: Page) -> float:
    """The given script: sleep long enough for the late button, then click it."""
    started = time.monotonic()
    page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
    time.sleep(1)  # "should be enough": too long on a fast day, too short on a slow one
    page.locator("#late").click()
    expect(page.locator("#late")).to_have_text("Clicked late")
    return time.monotonic() - started


def with_auto_wait(page: Page) -> float:
    """The fix: no sleep at all; click() waits until the button is visible."""
    started = time.monotonic()
    page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
    page.locator("#late").click()
    expect(page.locator("#late")).to_have_text("Clicked late")
    return time.monotonic() - started


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        slow = with_sleep(page)
        fast = with_auto_wait(page)
        print(f"With time.sleep(1): {slow:.2f} s")
        print(f"With auto-waiting:  {fast:.2f} s")
        assert fast < slow, "auto-waiting should not be slower than a fixed sleep"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

With time.sleep(1): 1.54 s
With auto-waiting:  0.98 s

Your numbers will differ, but the gap will not: the sleep always costs its full second, while click() waits only the 0.6 seconds the button takes to appear. No separate wait is needed, because the click already waits for the button to be visible. This is the one script in the course that sleeps, and it does so only to be measured.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Sleeping before an action. The script gets slower and still fails on a slow day. Delete the sleep: the action waits on its own. If it must wait for something else, use wait_for, wait_for_url or an assertion.
  • timeout=5000. Timeouts are seconds; that is 83 minutes. Write timeout=5.
  • Reaching for force=True when a click times out. The check was usually right: something covers the element, or it is disabled. Read the end of the error message and fix the cause, such as closing the cookie banner first.
  • Using click() on a checkbox. It toggles, so it unticks a box that was already ticked. Use check() and uncheck(), which go to the state you name.
  • Typing with press_sequentially everywhere. It is slower and fires a key event per character. Use fill unless the page reacts to each key.
  • Finding a button by a name the click changes. After get_by_role("button", name="Follow").click() the button may say "Following", and the same locator then finds nothing. Check the result with a locator that does not depend on the old text.
  • Expecting page.mouse to wait. It acts at a point right now. Use locator actions, or wait for the element first.
  • Running concurrent users in one context. Pages of one context share cookies and storage, so the second sign-in replaces the first. Give each concurrent user its own context.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Actions (click, fill, check, select_option, press, set_input_files, drag_to) wait for their element to be attached, visible, stable, enabled, editable and not covered, as each one needs.
  • A timeout error names the action, the locator, the seconds it waited and the check that failed.
  • Timeouts are seconds: per call with timeout=, per page with set_default_timeout; actions default to 10 seconds and navigations to 30.
  • Wait for conditions (wait_for, wait_for_url, wait_for_function, assertions), never for a fixed time.

Next: 04. Assertions

docs.title: 04. Assertions
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • write web-first assertions with expect for locators, pages and responses
  • use the common matchers: text, value, visibility, count, URL, title, attribute, enabled and checked
  • negate with not_ (or not_to_*) and set a timeout per assertion or for all of them
  • collect several failures at once with expect.soft, and assert on any value with expect.poll
  • check structure with aria_snapshot and to_match_aria_snapshot

Time: about 40 minutes. Before this: 03. Actions and auto-waiting. Code: examples/course/04-assertions/

A script that clicks through a page proves only that nothing crashed. Assertions are what turn it into a test: they say what the page must show. This lesson teaches steero's expect, which checks the page the way the actions in lesson 03 act on it, by waiting until the page is ready.

docs.title: Why web-first assertions
docs.text:
Here are two ways to check the welcome message on the sign-in page:

page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()

assert page.get_by_role("status").text_content() == "Welcome, ada"   # reads once
expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")      # waits until true

The first line reads the text once, straight after the click. The page answers half a second later, so the read sees "Signing in..." and the assert fails, although nothing is wrong. The usual "fix" is a sleep before the read, with all the problems lesson 03 described.

The second line is a web-first assertion. expect(locator) builds an assertion about what the locator finds, and to_have_text(...) keeps checking, about ten times a second, until the text matches or 5 seconds pass. On a fast page it returns at once; on a slow one it waits as long as needed; and when the text really is wrong, it fails with both values:

AssertionError: expect(get_by_role('status')).to_have_text: expected 'Welcome, ada', got 'Signing in...' after 5 s

State assertions name the states instead, for example expect(get_by_text('Saved')).to_be_hidden: expected hidden, got visible after 5 s, or got no element matches when the locator found nothing.

expect comes from the same import as launch:

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

It takes a locator, a page (expect(page).to_have_title(...)) or a response (expect(response).to_be_ok(), for lesson 07).

docs.title: The everyday matchers
docs.text:
Matcher Passes when to_have_text(text) the element's whole text equals text (whitespace squashed; a regex is searched) to_contain_text(text) the text contains text to_have_value(value) an input, textarea or select has this value to_be_visible(), to_be_hidden() the element is shown; or hidden or absent to_have_count(n) exactly n elements match to_be_enabled(), to_be_disabled() the control can, or cannot, be used to_be_checked() a checkbox or radio is ticked (checked=False: it is not) to_be_editable(), to_be_empty(), to_be_focused() accepts typing; has no text or value; has focus to_have_attribute(name, value) an attribute has this value to_have_class(...), to_contain_class(...) the class attribute is exactly, or includes, these classes expect(page).to_have_url(url) the page's URL equals url (or matches a regex) expect(page).to_have_title(title) the document title equals title

A few notes on using them well:

  • Text matchers take a string or a compiled regex. A string compares the whole text (to_have_text) or a part (to_contain_text); re.compile(r"Welcome, \w+") is searched. ignore_case=True makes either kind case-insensitive.
  • A list checks several elements at once. expect(page.locator("li")).to_have_text(["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]) passes only when there are exactly three items with those texts, in that order. Exercise 1 uses this.
  • Assertions are strict, like actions. to_have_text("x") on a locator that matches several elements raises StrictModeViolation. to_have_count and the list forms are made for several.
  • Hidden includes absent. to_be_hidden() passes when nothing matches, which is what you want for "the spinner has gone".

The visual comparison guide lists the less common matchers (to_have_values, to_have_role, to_have_accessible_name, to_have_css, and others).

docs.title: Negation and timeouts
docs.text:
Every matcher can be turned around with .not_, which then waits until the condition is false:

expect(page.get_by_role("alert")).not_.to_be_visible()
expect(page.get_by_role("status")).not_.to_have_text("Signing in...")

Playwright's spelling works too: not_to_be_visible(), not_to_have_text(...), and so on for every matcher. Pick one style per project.

The 5-second default can be changed per assertion, for every assertion made afterwards, or for a named group:

expect(page.locator("#report"), timeout=30).to_be_visible()   # this assertion: 30 seconds
expect.set_options(timeout=10)                                  # every expect() from now on
slow = expect.configure(timeout=60)                             # a separate expect with its own default
slow(page.locator("#export")).to_have_text("Export finished")

As everywhere in steero, timeouts are seconds. And as with actions, a long timeout costs nothing when the page is quick: the assertion returns as soon as it passes.

Coming from Playwright

expect and its matchers have Playwright's names and behaviour, including the 5-second default, .not_, expect.soft, expect.poll, expect.configure and the custom message. The differences: timeouts are seconds (timeout=10, not timeout=10_000), and soft failures are raised by expect.raise_soft_failures() (or by the pytest plugin in lesson 09) rather than by a test runner you cannot see.

Coming from Selenium

You may be used to WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.text_to_be_present_in_element(...)) followed by a plain assert. expect(...) is both in one: the wait and the check, with a failure message that says what was expected and what the page showed.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
A failure says what was checked, but not why. When a script has many similar checks, add a message as the second argument of expect; it is printed above the details:

expect(page.get_by_test_id("cart-count"), "cart updated after adding the teapot").to_have_text("1")

AssertionError: cart updated after adding the teapot
expect(get_by_test_id('cart-count')).to_have_text: expected '1', got '0' after 5 s

Write the message as the step's purpose, not a restatement of the matcher: "cart updated after adding the teapot" helps the person reading a failure at midnight; "cart count is 1" does not.

docs.title: Soft assertions
docs.text:
Normally the first failed assertion stops the script, which is right when later steps depend on it. Some pages have several independent things to check, though, such as the fields of a profile page, and you would like to see every wrong one in a single run. That is what soft assertions are for:

expect.soft(page.get_by_label("Name")).to_have_value("Ada")
expect.soft(page.get_by_label("Email")).to_have_value("ada@example.com")
expect.soft(page.get_by_label("City")).to_have_value("London")
expect.raise_soft_failures()

A failed expect.soft(...) waits as usual, then records the failure and lets the script go on. expect.raise_soft_failures() raises one AssertionError listing everything recorded, and clears the list; it does nothing when every check passed:

AssertionError: 2 soft assertion(s) failed:
  1. expect(get_by_label('Email')).to_have_value: expected 'ada@example.com', got 'ada@example.org' after 5 s
  2. expect(get_by_label('City')).to_have_value: expected 'London', got '' after 5 s

Always end a group of soft checks with raise_soft_failures(); without it, the failures are collected and never reported, and the script passes.

docs.title: Polling any value
docs.text:
expect(...) works on things in a page. For anything else (a row in a database, a file a job writes, a count an API returns) use expect.poll(fn). It calls fn again and again until the matcher holds or the timeout passes:

expect.poll(lambda: len(api.get("api/orders").json()), timeout=10).to_equal(3)

The poll matchers are to_be, to_equal, to_be_truthy, to_be_falsy, to_be_none, to_be_greater_than (and _or_equal), to_be_less_than (and _or_equal), to_contain, to_match and to_have_length, each with .not_. In the sync API, fn is called on your own thread, so it can use any sync code; it waits a little longer between calls each time (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, then 1 second; change it with intervals=[...]).

docs.title: ARIA snapshots
docs.text:
Checking a whole form one matcher at a time gets long. An ARIA snapshot describes the structure of a part of the page as assistive technology sees it: roles, names and states, in a small YAML-like format. locator.aria_snapshot() prints it:

print(page.locator("#login").aria_snapshot())

- form:
  - text: User name
  - textbox "User name"
  - alert
  - text: Password
  - textbox "Password"
  - alert
  - checkbox "Remember me"
  - text: Remember me
  - button "Sign in"

Each line is a role, then the accessible name in quotes, then states in brackets ([checked], [disabled], [level=1]). Children are indented under their parent. Plain containers such as div and span are left out, and so is hidden content.

expect(locator).to_match_aria_snapshot(template) compares the snapshot against a template in the same format. The template is partial, which makes it robust:

  • the nodes it lists must appear in that order, but the page may have more;
  • a role without a name (- textbox) matches any name;
  • states are checked only when you write them;
  • a name written as /regex/ is searched instead of compared.
expect(page.locator("#login")).to_match_aria_snapshot("""
    - textbox "User name"
    - textbox "Password"
    - checkbox "Remember me"
    - button "Sign in"
""")

That one assertion checks that the form has these four controls, with these names, in this order. When it fails, the error includes the actual snapshot, so you can see at a glance what changed.

Browser support

Snapshots are computed by steero's own script inside the page, so Chrome and Firefox produce the same text for the same page. The accessible names are an approximation of the W3C algorithm; in rare cases (nested labels, aria-owns, CSS generated content) they can differ from Playwright's, so write templates against what steero prints.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The script signs in on the practice site, then checks the result five ways: the welcome text, the page title, that the URL did not change, that the button is usable again, and the form's structure. Three details that do not depend on each other are checked softly, and reported together.

"""Lesson 04: sign in, then check the result five ways, with one group of soft checks.

    python examples/course/04-assertions/example_check_sign_in.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        button = page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in")

        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        button.click()

        # 1 to 4: each assertion waits (up to 5 seconds) for the half-second round trip.
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")
        expect(page).to_have_title("Welcome - steero practice site")
        expect(page).to_have_url(BASE_URL + "login.html")          # signing in did not navigate
        expect(button).to_be_enabled()

        # 5: the structure of the form, as assistive technology sees it (a partial template).
        expect(page.locator("#login")).to_match_aria_snapshot("""
            - textbox "User name"
            - textbox "Password"
            - checkbox "Remember me"
            - button "Sign in"
        """)

        # Soft checks: independent details, all reported together at the end.
        expect.soft(page.get_by_label("User name")).to_have_value("ada")
        expect.soft(page.get_by_label("Remember me")).not_.to_be_checked()
        expect.soft(page.get_by_role("alert").first).to_be_empty()
        expect.raise_soft_failures()                                # raises if any of them failed
        print("Signed in, and all checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/04-assertions/example_check_sign_in.py

Signed in, and all checks passed

A passing run says little, so break it on purpose: change "Welcome, ada" to "Welcome, Ada" and run it again to see a hard failure; then change the soft to_have_value("ada") to to_have_value("grace") to see the soft report.

example_matchers.py uses most of the matchers in the table above, plus not_, the not_to_* spelling and a per-assertion timeout, on /testsite/form.html:

"""Lesson 04: the everyday matchers, their negations and per-assertion timeouts.

    python examples/course/04-assertions/example_matchers.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import re

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")

        # The page
        expect(page).to_have_title("Form")
        expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r"/testsite/form\.html$"))

        # Visibility: both assertions wait for the page's timers.
        expect(page.locator("#late")).to_be_visible()                # shown after 0.6 seconds
        expect(page.locator("#overlay")).to_be_hidden()              # removed after 0.7 seconds
        expect(page.locator("#overlay")).not_.to_be_visible()        # the same check, negated

        # Text: to_have_text is the whole text, to_contain_text a part of it.
        expect(page.get_by_role("heading", level=1)).to_have_text("Sign in")
        expect(page.locator("#items")).to_contain_text("Banana")
        expect(page.locator("#items li")).to_have_count(3)

        # Values, states and attributes of form controls
        user = page.get_by_label("User name")
        user.fill("ada")
        expect(user).to_have_value("ada")
        expect(user).to_have_attribute("placeholder", "you@example.com")
        expect(page.get_by_label("Free")).to_be_checked()
        expect(page.get_by_label("Pro")).not_to_be_checked()          # Playwright's spelling of not_
        expect(page.get_by_role("button", name="Disabled")).to_be_disabled()
        expect(page.get_by_label("Fixed")).to_be_editable(editable=False)

        # A shorter timeout for one assertion, in seconds.
        expect(page.get_by_role("status"), timeout=1).to_be_empty()
        print("Every assertion passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 1: a whole list in one assertion
docs.text:
On /testsite/form.html, check that the fruit list (#items li) has exactly three items, "Apple", "Banana" and "Cherry", with a single to_have_text([...]) call. Then check that the list contains "Banana" with to_contain_text, and that "Cherry" does not come before "Apple".

Solution 
"""Lesson 04, exercise 1: check a whole list in one assertion.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/form.html")
        fruit = page.locator("#items li")

        # A list checks every match, in order: exactly three items, Banana second.
        expect(fruit).to_have_text(["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"])
        print("The list is Apple, Banana, Cherry")

        # to_contain_text with a list: these texts appear in this order, other items allowed.
        expect(fruit).to_contain_text(["Banana"])
        expect(fruit).not_.to_contain_text(["Cherry", "Apple"])     # wrong order
        print("Banana is in it, and Cherry does not come before Apple")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

With a list, to_contain_text looks for each text in order, skipping elements in between, so ["Cherry", "Apple"] fails (and .not_ passes) because Apple comes first.

docs.title: Exercise 2: read the message
docs.text:
On the practice sign-in page (login.html), enter a user name but no password and click Sign in. Assert that the status says "Welcome, ada" with a timeout of 1 second: it never will. Catch the AssertionError and print it. Then do the same with a message saying what the step was for, and compare the two outputs.

Solution 
"""Lesson 04, exercise 2: read a failing assertion's message, then add your own.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()     # no password, so this never signs in
        status = page.get_by_role("status")

        # Catching AssertionError is only for this exercise, so both messages can be printed.
        try:
            expect(status, timeout=1).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("Without a message:\n ", error)

        try:
            expect(status, "signing in as ada with an empty password", timeout=1).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("With a message:\n ", str(error).replace("\n", "\n  "))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Without a message:
  expect(get_by_role('status')).to_have_text: expected 'Welcome, ada', got '' after 1 s
With a message:
  signing in as ada with an empty password
  expect(get_by_role('status')).to_have_text: expected 'Welcome, ada', got '' after 1 s

The details are the same; the message says which step of the test they belong to. Catching the error is only for this exercise.

docs.title: Exercise 3: poll an API
docs.text:
The practice site serves its product list at /api/products. Without opening a browser, use expect.poll to wait until the API reports three products, with a message and a timeout of 10 seconds. Count how many times your function was called.

Hint: from steero.sync_api import request, then with request.new_context(base_url=BASE_URL) as api: gives you api.get("api/products"), whose .json() is the list. Lesson 07 covers the request API properly.

Solution 
"""Lesson 04, exercise 3: poll a value that is not on any page, here an API's product count.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, request

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    # No browser needed: a request context sends HTTP requests straight from Python.
    with request.new_context(base_url=BASE_URL) as api:
        calls = 0

        def product_count() -> int:
            nonlocal calls
            calls += 1
            return len(api.get("api/products").json())

        # Calls product_count until it returns 3, for up to 10 seconds.
        expect.poll(product_count, "the catalogue has three products", timeout=10).to_equal(3)
        expect.poll(product_count).to_be_greater_than(0)
        print(f"The API reports 3 products ({calls} calls)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Here the count is right on the first call. In a real system the value would change over time (a background job importing products), and the poll would keep asking until it did.

docs.title: Exercise 4: a template that ignores the errors
docs.text:
On the sign-in page, write an ARIA snapshot template for the form that passes both before and after clicking Sign in on the empty form, when the two error messages appear. Print aria_snapshot() first to see what you are matching.

Hint: after the click, the snapshot shows textbox "User name User name is required", because the error text sits inside the label.

Solution 
"""Lesson 04, exercise 4: a partial ARIA snapshot template that ignores the error messages.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

# Unlisted nodes (the alert spans, the label texts) are ignored. The names are regular
# expressions, because an error inside a label becomes part of the field's accessible name.
TEMPLATE = """
- form:
  - textbox /^User name/
  - textbox /^Password/
  - checkbox "Remember me"
  - button "Sign in"
"""


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        form = page.locator("#login")
        print(form.aria_snapshot())

        expect(form).to_match_aria_snapshot(TEMPLATE)               # before: no errors shown

        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()         # empty form: both errors appear
        expect(page.get_by_text("Password is required")).to_be_visible()
        expect(form).to_match_aria_snapshot(TEMPLATE)               # after: still matches
        print("The template matches with and without the error messages")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Leaving the alert lines out makes the template ignore them, because templates are partial. The regular expressions /^User name/ and /^Password/ accept the name with or without the error text appended.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • assert locator.text_content() == ... after an action. It reads once and fails while the page is still updating. Use expect(locator).to_have_text(...).
  • Forgetting expect.raise_soft_failures(). Soft failures are recorded and never reported, and the script passes. End every group of soft checks with it.
  • Using to_have_text for a part of the text. It compares the whole text, so "Welcome" does not match "Welcome, ada". Use to_contain_text, or a regex.
  • Asserting on a locator that matches several elements. to_have_text("x") raises StrictModeViolation. Narrow the locator, or use the list form or to_have_count.
  • timeout=5000. Seconds, so that is 83 minutes. Write timeout=5.
  • Mixing the sync and async expect. from steero import expect is the async one (it needs await); a sync script imports expect from steero.sync_api.
  • Checking a moment that passes. A state that lasts half a second (a "Saving..." label, a disabled button during a request) may be over before the assertion first looks. Assert on the end state instead.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• expect(locator), expect(page) and expect(response) start assertions that retry until they pass or 5 seconds go by, so there is no need to wait before checking.
  • The common matchers cover text, values, visibility, counts, states, attributes, URL and title; .not_ (or not_to_*) inverts any of them.
  • Timeouts are seconds: per assertion, with expect.set_options, or with expect.configure.
  • expect.soft collects failures until expect.raise_soft_failures(); expect.poll asserts on any value; to_match_aria_snapshot checks a whole structure with a partial template.

Next: 05. Visual testing

docs.title: 05. Visual testing
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • compare a page or an element against a baseline with to_have_screenshot
  • know where baselines live, why the first run fails, and how to update them with STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1
  • hide changing content with mask and allow small differences with threshold, max_diff_pixels and max_diff_pixel_ratio
  • read the -actual.png and -diff.png files a failure leaves

Time: about 30 minutes. Before this: 04. Assertions. Code: examples/course/05-visual-testing/

The assertions in lesson 04 check what you thought to check. A broken stylesheet, a button that turned white on white, or a card that slid under another passes all of them. A visual test compares a screenshot with a saved picture of how the page should look, and catches the changes you did not think of.

This lesson uses a new practice page, /dashboard.html: four fixed-size cards, one with a clock that ticks every second and one with a spinning progress indicator. Open it in your browser before you start.

docs.title: Screenshots as assertions
docs.text:
to_have_screenshot is an assertion like the ones in lesson 04, about a page or a locator:

expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard.png")                      # the viewport
expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard-full.png", full_page=True) # the whole page
expect(page.get_by_test_id("orders-card")).to_have_screenshot("orders-card.png")  # one element

It takes a screenshot and compares it, pixel by pixel, with a baseline: a PNG saved earlier under the name you gave. When they match, it passes. When they do not, it takes another screenshot and compares again, until one matches or the timeout passes (5 seconds, like every assertion), so a page that is still settling does not fail the test.

An element screenshot is usually the better choice. It ignores the rest of the page, so a change in the header does not fail the test for a card, and it keeps the baseline small.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
Where they live. Baselines are files, named after the name you gave plus the browser and the operating system:

dashboard-chrome-win32.png
dashboard-firefox-win32.png
dashboard-chrome-linux.png

The folder is chosen in this order:

  1. expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=...), if your code set one;
  2. the STEERO_SNAPSHOT_DIR environment variable;
  3. in a pytest test, __snapshots__/<test file name>/ next to the test file;
  4. otherwise __snapshots__/ in the current directory.

In a real project you commit the baselines next to the tests, so everyone compares against the same pictures. The examples in this lesson put theirs in a new temporary folder on every run (each prints where), so they always start from scratch and never write into your checkout.

The first run fails. When there is no baseline, steero takes a screenshot, saves it as the baseline, and then fails the assertion:

AssertionError: expect(page).to_have_screenshot: no baseline existed; wrote ...\dashboard-chrome-win32.png. Check it and run again (or set STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 to write baselines).

That is deliberate. If a missing baseline passed, a test with a typo in the name, or a folder that was never committed, would pass forever without comparing anything. So: run once, open the new PNG and check it shows what the page should look like, then run again.

Updating. When the page changes on purpose (a new design, a new card), the baselines must change too. Run the tests with STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1, and every to_have_screenshot it reaches rewrites its baseline and passes:

$env:STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS = "1"
pytest tests/visual
Remove-Item Env:STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS

STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 pytest tests/visual

Then look at the changed PNGs (your version control shows which ones) before you commit them. An update run accepts whatever the page shows, bugs included.

docs.title: Making screenshots stable
docs.text:
A visual test is only useful if the same page gives the same picture on every run. Three things get in the way, and steero handles two of them for you:

  • Animations. By default to_have_screenshot stops CSS animations and transitions for the capture (animations="disabled"): finite ones jump to their end, infinite ones are cancelled. The dashboard's spinner needs nothing from you.
  • The text caret. A blinking cursor in a focused input is hidden (caret="hide").
  • Content that changes on every run: clocks, dates, random ids, ads, avatars. steero cannot know which parts those are, so you tell it with mask:
clock = page.locator("#clock")
expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard.png", mask=[clock])

Each element the mask locators match is painted over with a solid box (magenta, or mask_color="#000") before the screenshot is taken, in the baseline and in every comparison, so the box is equal even when the clock under it is not.

Also fix the size. A screenshot of the viewport depends on the window size, and an element can change size with it. Set it explicitly before visual checks:

page.set_viewport_size({"width": 800, "height": 400})

docs.title: Tolerance
docs.text:
By default every pixel must match, within a small colour tolerance. Three options loosen that:

Option Default Meaning threshold 0.2 how different one pixel's colour may be and still count as equal, 0 (exact) to 1 (anything) max_diff_pixels 0 how many pixels may differ max_diff_pixel_ratio none which share of the pixels may differ, 0 to 1

threshold is about how much each pixel changed: 0.2 lets through the faint colour shifts of image scaling but not a real colour change. The other two are about how many pixels changed. With both max_diff_pixels and max_diff_pixel_ratio, the smaller limit wins.

Why allow anything at all? The same page can be drawn very slightly differently from one run to the next: font smoothing at the edges of letters, a GPU rounding a gradient. steero does not try to detect anti-aliasing, so a few dozen pixels of slack (max_diff_pixels=50) on a text-heavy element is normal. Keep the slack as small as works: a big tolerance hides real regressions.

docs.title: When a visual test fails
docs.text:
On a failure steero writes two files next to the baseline:

  • <name>-actual.png, the screenshot it took last;
  • <name>-diff.png, the baseline faded out, with every differing pixel in red.

and the error says how many pixels differed and where the files are:

AssertionError: expect(locator('#login')).to_have_screenshot('login-form.png'): 734 pixels (1.39%) differ; diff written to ...\login-form-chrome-win32-diff.png; baseline ...\login-form-chrome-win32.png, actual ...\login-form-chrome-win32-actual.png after 1 s

Open the diff first: the red shows where to look. Then decide which of two things happened:

  • A regression: the page changed and should not have. Fix the page; the test passes again against the old baseline.
  • An intended change: the new look is right. Check the -actual.png, then rewrite the baseline with STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1.

A size difference (the element grew by a pixel) is reported as size differs: expected 200x110, got 200x111 with no diff image, since the two cannot be laid over each other. The -actual.png and -diff.png files are removed again by the next passing run.

Coming from Playwright

to_have_screenshot follows Playwright: the same options (mask, mask_color, threshold, max_diff_pixels, max_diff_pixel_ratio, animations, caret, full_page), the same failing first run, and per-browser, per-platform baseline names. The differences: update with the STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 environment variable rather than --update-snapshots, the timeout is in seconds, and the comparison is pure Python with no anti-aliasing detection, so allow a little max_diff_pixels where text edges vary.

Coming from Selenium

Selenium has screenshots but no comparison: projects add a library (and a baseline folder convention, and a diff tool) on top. Here it is one assertion, with no extra dependency.

Browser support

Chrome and Firefox draw text and form controls differently, so a baseline from one never matches the other. That is why the browser is part of the file name: each browser keeps its own baselines, and a suite run in both browsers keeps two sets. The operating system is in the name for the same reason (fonts differ between Windows, macOS and Linux), so record baselines on the platform your tests run on, such as the build machine. Exercise 3 shows the two names.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The script opens the dashboard and does the same comparison twice: once with the clock masked, once without. Each baseline is recorded first (the expected first-run failure is caught by a small helper), then the script waits for the clock to tick and compares again.

"""Lesson 05: compare a page with a live clock against a baseline, with and without a mask.

Baselines go to a new temporary folder on every run (printed at the start), so each run starts
with none and nothing is written into the repository.

    python examples/course/05-visual-testing/example_mask_the_clock.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile
from typing import Any

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def record_baseline(target: Any, name: str, **options: Any) -> None:
    """With no baseline, steero writes one and fails the assertion; here that failure is expected."""
    try:
        expect(target).to_have_screenshot(name, **options)
    except AssertionError as error:
        if "no baseline existed" not in str(error):
            raise


def main() -> None:
    snapshots = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="steero-lesson05-")
    expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=snapshots)
    print("Baselines in", snapshots)

    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.set_viewport_size({"width": 800, "height": 400})     # same size on every run
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "dashboard.html")
        clock = page.locator("#clock")

        # Masked: the clock is painted over, so the page looks the same every second.
        record_baseline(page, "dashboard-masked.png", mask=[clock])
        expect(clock).not_.to_have_text(clock.text_content())    # wait for the next tick
        expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard-masked.png", mask=[clock])
        print("Masked:   matches its baseline after the clock moved on")

        # Unmasked: the baseline holds one second, and the next screenshot shows another.
        record_baseline(page, "dashboard-unmasked.png")
        expect(clock).not_.to_have_text(clock.text_content())
        try:
            expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard-unmasked.png", timeout=2)
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("Unmasked: fails, as it must:\n ", str(error).split(";")[0])
        else:
            raise AssertionError("the unmasked screenshot should not have matched")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/05-visual-testing/example_mask_the_clock.py

Baselines in C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Temp\steero-lesson05-qgasuj8_
Masked:   matches its baseline after the clock moved on
Unmasked: fails, as it must:
  expect(page).to_have_screenshot('dashboard-unmasked.png'): 82 pixels (0.03%) differ

The masked comparison passes although a second has gone by: the clock is under the box. The unmasked one fails because one second is all it takes. Open the folder the script printed and look at dashboard-unmasked-...-diff.png: only the clock's digits are red. The spinner was animating the whole time and caused no difference, because animations are stopped for the capture.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a baseline of the form only
docs.text:
On login.html, record a baseline of the sign-in form (#login) alone, and check that a second comparison passes. Then change the "User name" label to "Username" with page.evaluate and compare again. Print the error and list the files in the snapshot folder. Open the diff.

Solution 
"""Lesson 05, exercise 1: a baseline of the sign-in form only, then a changed label and its diff.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    snapshots = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="steero-lesson05-"))
    expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=snapshots)

    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        form = page.locator("#login")

        # First run: steero writes the baseline, then fails so a missing file never passes.
        try:
            expect(form).to_have_screenshot("login-form.png")
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("First run:", str(error).split(";")[0])
        expect(form).to_have_screenshot("login-form.png")
        print("Second run: matches")

        # Change the label text, as a careless edit to the page might.
        page.evaluate("() => { document.querySelector('label').firstChild.textContent = 'Username '; }")
        try:
            expect(form).to_have_screenshot("login-form.png", timeout=1)
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("After the change:", str(error).split(";")[0])

        for file in sorted(snapshots.iterdir()):
            print("  ", file.name)
        assert any(file.name.endswith("-diff.png") for file in snapshots.iterdir())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

First run: expect(locator('#login')).to_have_screenshot: no baseline existed
Second run: matches
After the change: expect(locator('#login')).to_have_screenshot('login-form.png'): 227 pixels (0.26%) differ
   login-form-chrome-win32-actual.png
   login-form-chrome-win32-diff.png
   login-form-chrome-win32.png

The -actual.png shows the new label and the -diff.png marks only the changed letters in red: the rest of the form did not move. An element screenshot keeps the diff this focused.

docs.title: Exercise 2: allow a one-pixel border change
docs.text:
On the dashboard, record a baseline of the Orders card (get_by_test_id("orders-card")). Change the colour of its top border with evaluate, see the comparison fail, then make it pass with max_diff_pixels, allowing no more pixels than the border has.

Hint: the top border is one pixel tall and as wide as the card; bounding_box() gives the width.

Solution 
"""Lesson 05, exercise 2: tolerate a one-pixel border change with max_diff_pixels.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="steero-lesson05-"))

    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "dashboard.html")
        card = page.get_by_test_id("orders-card")

        # Record the baseline (this first assertion fails by design: there was none).
        try:
            expect(card).to_have_screenshot("orders-card.png")
        except AssertionError:
            print("Baseline recorded")

        # Recolour the card's top border: one row of pixels, as wide as the card.
        card.evaluate("(el) => { el.style.borderTopColor = 'rgb(220, 0, 0)'; }")
        box = card.bounding_box()
        assert box is not None
        border_pixels = round(box["width"])

        try:
            expect(card).to_have_screenshot("orders-card.png", timeout=1)
        except AssertionError as error:
            print("No tolerance:", str(error).split(";")[0].split(": ", 1)[1])

        # Allow exactly that many pixels to differ, and the comparison passes.
        expect(card).to_have_screenshot("orders-card.png", max_diff_pixels=border_pixels)
        print(f"With max_diff_pixels={border_pixels}: passes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Baseline recorded
No tolerance: 200 pixels (0.91%) differ
With max_diff_pixels=200: passes

Allowing exactly the border's pixels documents what the test tolerates. A larger number "just to be safe" would also let through a change to the card's text.

docs.title: Exercise 3: one baseline per browser
docs.text:
Record a masked baseline of the dashboard named dashboard.png in Chrome and in Firefox (launch each in turn in the same script), then list the files in the snapshot folder. Why are there two, and why do their sizes differ?

Solution 
"""Lesson 05, exercise 3: record the same baseline in Chrome and in Firefox, and compare the names.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero import LaunchError
from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    snapshots = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="steero-lesson05-"))
    expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=snapshots)

    for name in ("chrome", "firefox"):
        try:
            browser = launch(name, headless=HEADLESS)
        except LaunchError as error:  # only one browser installed: say so and carry on
            print(f"{name}: not available ({error})")
            continue
        with browser:
            page = browser.new_page()
            page.set_viewport_size({"width": 800, "height": 400})
            page.goto(BASE_URL + "dashboard.html")
            try:
                expect(page).to_have_screenshot("dashboard.png", mask=[page.locator("#clock")])
            except AssertionError:
                print(f"{name}: baseline recorded")

    # One name in the test, one file per browser (and per operating system) on disk.
    for file in sorted(snapshots.iterdir()):
        print("  ", file.name, f"{file.stat().st_size:,} bytes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chrome: baseline recorded
firefox: baseline recorded
   dashboard-chrome-win32.png 12,417 bytes
   dashboard-firefox-win32.png 12,450 bytes

One name in the code gives one file per browser, because the two browsers render the same page differently (fonts, anti-aliasing, form controls), and comparing a Firefox screenshot with a Chrome baseline would always fail. The platform part of the name keeps Windows and Linux baselines apart for the same reason. If you have only one browser, the script says so and records one file.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Thinking the first failure is a bug. "No baseline existed" means steero just wrote one. Check the PNG, then run again.
  • Updating baselines without looking at them. STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 accepts whatever the page shows, bugs included. Look at every changed PNG before committing it.
  • Leaving STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 set. Every visual test then passes, because each one rewrites its baseline. Unset it after the update run.
  • A clock, a date or an avatar in the screenshot. The test fails on every run. Mask it, or screenshot a smaller element that does not include it.
  • Not fixing the viewport size. Baselines from a 1280 pixel window fail in a 1024 pixel one with "size differs". Call set_viewport_size before visual checks.
  • Raising the tolerance until the test passes. A big max_diff_pixel_ratio hides real regressions. Find what changes (open the diff) and mask it instead.
  • Recording baselines on your laptop and running on Linux. The platform is in the file name, so the build machine finds no baseline. Record them where the tests run.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• expect(page_or_locator).to_have_screenshot("name.png") compares against a baseline and retries until it matches or the timeout passes.
  • Baselines are named <name>-<browser>-<platform>.png; set the folder with expect.set_options(snapshot_dir=...) or STEERO_SNAPSHOT_DIR.
  • A missing baseline is written and the assertion fails; STEERO_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 rewrites baselines on purpose.
  • Animations and the caret are frozen for you; mask what changes, fix the viewport size, and keep threshold, max_diff_pixels and max_diff_pixel_ratio as small as works.
  • A failure leaves -actual.png and -diff.png next to the baseline: open the diff, then fix the page or update the baseline.

Next: 06. Contexts and emulation

docs.title: 06. Contexts and emulation
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • explain what a browser context is, and use one per user or per test
  • emulate a device with devices[...], and set the viewport, locale, time zone and color scheme
  • grant permissions and set a geolocation
  • work with cookies (add_cookies, cookies, clear_cookies), extra headers and init scripts
  • log in once and reuse the session with storage_state

Time: about 45 minutes. Before this: 05. Visual testing. Code: examples/course/06-contexts-and-emulation/

So far every script has used one browser and one page. Real tests need more: a clean session for each test, two users at once, a phone instead of a laptop, a visitor from Berlin, a user who is already signed in. All of these are one idea, the browser context, plus a handful of options you pass when you create it.

docs.title: What a context is
docs.text:
A browser context is an isolated session inside one browser, like a private window. Each context has its own cookies, localStorage, cache and permissions. What one context stores, no other context can see, even though they all run in the same browser process.

with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
    context = browser.new_context()      # a fresh, empty session
    page = context.new_page()            # a tab inside it
    page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
    context.close()                      # closes its pages and throws its data away

Creating a context takes milliseconds; launching a browser takes a second or more. That is why the usual pattern is one browser per test run and one context per test: every test starts with no cookies and no storage, and none of them pays for a new browser. The pytest plugin in lesson 09 does exactly this for you.

Every browser also has a default context, browser.contexts[0]. browser.new_page() with no arguments opens a tab there, which is what lessons 01 to 05 did. The default context lives as long as the browser and cannot be closed, so use browser.new_context() whenever isolation matters.

Coming from Playwright

The same model and names: browser.new_context(...), context.new_page(), context.close(), browser.contexts. browser.new_page(locale="de-DE") with any context option also works: the page gets a context of its own, closed together with the page.

Coming from Selenium

Selenium has one session per driver, so isolating two users means two browsers. A context gives you the same isolation without a second browser: open as many as you like.

docs.title: Two users at once
docs.text:
Because contexts do not share anything, two users can be signed in side by side: an admin and a guest, a buyer and a seller, or a chat between two people. This script signs Ada in, leaves a guest signed out, and checks what the Who am I page (whoami.html) tells each of them:

"""Lesson 06: two users at once, in two contexts of one browser.

Ada signs in in one context; a guest browses in another. Neither sees the other's
cookies or localStorage, although both pages run in the same browser process.

    python examples/course/06-contexts-and-emulation/example_two_users.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        ada = browser.new_context()
        guest = browser.new_context()
        ada_page = ada.new_page()
        guest_page = guest.new_page()

        ada_page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        ada_page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        ada_page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        ada_page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(ada_page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")

        ada_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        guest_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        expect(ada_page.get_by_test_id("user")).to_have_text("ada")
        expect(guest_page.get_by_test_id("user")).to_have_text("nobody")

        print("Ada's cookies:  ", [c["name"] for c in ada.cookies()])
        print("Guest's cookies:", [c["name"] for c in guest.cookies()])
        print("Open pages:", len(browser.pages), "in", len(browser.contexts), "contexts (one is the default)")

        ada.close()  # closes Ada's page and throws her cookies and storage away
        guest.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Ada's cookies:   ['session']
Guest's cookies: []
Open pages: 3 in 3 contexts (one is the default)

The guest's page never sees Ada's session cookie or her localStorage entry. Three pages are open: the blank tab the browser started with in the default context, and one tab in each new context. context.pages lists only the pages of one context.

docs.title: Devices and viewports
docs.text:
The same page can look completely different on a phone. Context options tell the browser what kind of device to pretend to be:

Option What the page sees viewport={"width": 390, "height": 664} the size of the visible area, in CSS pixels screen={"width": 390, "height": 844} what window.screen reports device_scale_factor=3 window.devicePixelRatio user_agent="..." the User-Agent header and navigator.userAgent is_mobile=True honour <meta name=viewport> the way a phone does (Chrome only) has_touch=True a touch screen, navigator.maxTouchPoints (Chrome only) color_scheme="dark" prefers-color-scheme: dark in CSS and matchMedia

Setting all of these by hand is tedious, so steero has device presets: devices maps a name to the options of a real device.

from steero.sync_api import devices

print(devices["Pixel 7"]["viewport"])         # {'width': 412, 'height': 839}
context = browser.new_context(**devices["Pixel 7"], color_scheme="dark")

There are iPhones, iPads, Pixel and Galaxy phones and tablets (each also as "<name> landscape") and desktop presets such as "Desktop Chrome"; list(devices) prints them all. The ** spreads the preset into keyword arguments, so you can add more options next to it.

page.viewport_size reads the size back: the context's viewport (from the options or the preset), or None when the browser window decides. To resize a page that is already open, use page.set_viewport_size:

page = context.new_page()
print(page.viewport_size)                               # {'width': 412, 'height': 839}
page.set_viewport_size({"width": 1024, "height": 768})
print(page.viewport_size)                               # {'width': 1024, 'height': 768}

Browser support

Firefox cannot emulate is_mobile or has_touch over WebDriver BiDi, so passing a phone preset there raises UnsupportedOnBrowser, naming the option. desktop_only drops those two keys and keeps the viewport, screen, scale factor and user agent, which is enough for most responsive layouts:

from steero.api.devices import desktop_only

phone = devices["Pixel 7"]
if browser.name == "firefox":
    phone = desktop_only(phone)

The other Chrome-only options are java_script_enabled=False, reduced_motion and forced_colors. steero never quietly ignores an option: if the browser cannot apply it, you get the error. The full table is in Emulation.

docs.title: Locale, time zone, geolocation and permissions
docs.text:
locale sets the language the page sees (navigator.language, the Accept-Language header) and how Intl formats dates and numbers. timezone_id sets the clock's time zone, with an IANA name such as "Europe/Berlin" or "Asia/Tokyo". Together they let you test the page a visitor from another country sees, from your own machine:

context = browser.new_context(locale="ja-JP", timezone_id="Asia/Tokyo")

Permissions are what a browser normally asks the user about: location, notifications, the clipboard. A test cannot click "Allow" in a browser prompt, so grant the permission up front. geolocation is the position the Geolocation API then reports:

context = browser.new_context(
    geolocation={"latitude": 48.8584, "longitude": 2.2945},
    permissions=["geolocation"],
)
context.set_geolocation({"latitude": 51.5007, "longitude": -0.1246})  # move, later
context.grant_permissions(["clipboard-read"])                          # grant more, later
context.clear_permissions()                                            # back to "ask"

A position without the permission is useless: the page asks, nobody answers. Grants apply to every origin the context visits; pass origin="https://example.com" to grant to one only.

docs.title: Cookies, headers and init scripts
docs.text:
You can read and change a context's cookies directly:

context.add_cookies([{"name": "theme", "value": "dark", "url": BASE_URL}])
print(context.cookies())          # [{'name': 'theme', 'value': 'dark', 'domain': '127.0.0.1', ...}]
context.clear_cookies()           # all of them; or clear_cookies(name="theme")

A cookie needs a name, a value, and either a url or a domain (with an optional path). Adding cookies before the first page loads is a quick way to set a preference or a consent banner's "already answered" flag.

Two more tools change every page of a context:

context.set_extra_http_headers({"X-Test-Run": "lesson-06"})       # sent with every request
context.add_init_script("localStorage.setItem('user', 'grace')")  # runs before the page's own scripts

An init script runs in every new document, before any script of the page itself. Use it to seed storage, stub a browser API, or switch on a test mode the page checks for. page has the same two methods, for one page only.

docs.title: Log in once
docs.text:
Signing in through the form at the start of every test is slow, and it tests the login page a hundred times instead of once. The better pattern: sign in once, save the session, and start every later context from it.

A site remembers you in cookies and in localStorage. context.storage_state() returns both, and with path= also writes them to a JSON file. new_context(storage_state=...) takes the file (or the dict) and starts a context with that state already in place:

state = context.storage_state(path=state_file)     # after signing in
signed_in = browser.new_context(storage_state=state_file)

The file uses Playwright's storage-state format, so files move between the two tools. localStorage is read from the origins of the pages open at the moment you call storage_state(), so call it while the signed-in page is still open.

Keep the state file private

The file holds a live session cookie: anyone with the file is signed in as that user. Write it to a temporary or gitignored folder, never into the repository.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
This script signs Ada in on the practice login page, saves the storage state to a file in a temporary folder, and closes that context. Then it opens a new context from the file: the Who am I page shows Ada as the stored user with her session cookie, and the login page greets her as a returning user. A third context without the file is a stranger.

"""Lesson 06: log in once, save the storage state, and start a second context already signed in.

Signs in on the practice site in one context, saves its cookies and localStorage with
``context.storage_state()``, then opens a fresh context from that file and shows the page
already knows the user.

    python examples/course/serve.py                                          # terminal 1
    python examples/course/06-contexts-and-emulation/example_log_in_once.py  # terminal 2

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    # The state file holds a live session: keep it out of the repository.
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder, launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        state_file = Path(folder) / "state.json"

        # 1. Sign in once, in a context of its own, and save what the site stored.
        context = browser.new_context()
        page = context.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")
        state = context.storage_state(path=state_file)
        context.close()
        print(f"Saved {len(state['cookies'])} cookie(s) and localStorage for "
              f"{len(state['origins'])} origin(s)")

        # 2. Any later context can start from the file, already signed in.
        signed_in = browser.new_context(storage_state=state_file)
        page = signed_in.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("user")).to_have_text("ada")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("cookies")).to_have_text("session=ada")
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("returning")).to_have_text("Welcome back, ada. You are already signed in.")
        print("The new context is signed in as", page.evaluate("() => localStorage.getItem('user')"))

        # 3. A context without the state is a stranger.
        guest = browser.new_context()
        page = guest.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("user")).to_have_text("nobody")
        print("A fresh context is signed in as nobody")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it with the practice site running:

python examples/course/06-contexts-and-emulation/example_log_in_once.py

Saved 1 cookie(s) and localStorage for 1 origin(s)
The new context is signed in as ada
A fresh context is signed in as nobody

In a test suite you would sign in once per run (in a session fixture, lesson 09), keep the file for the rest of the run, and pass storage_state= to every test's context. When the session expires, delete the file and the next run signs in again.

Async version

The same three steps with the async API; only the awaits differ:

context = await browser.new_context()
page = await context.new_page()
# ... sign in ...
await context.storage_state(path=state_file)
await context.close()
signed_in = await browser.new_context(storage_state=state_file)

A second example puts several options together: a Pixel 7 in Tokyo, in Japanese, with a dark theme. On Firefox it uses desktop_only, as the note above explains.

"""Lesson 06: emulate a phone with a locale, a time zone and a dark color scheme.

Opens the "Who am I" page in a context built from the Pixel 7 device preset, set to
Japanese in Tokyo with a dark theme, and prints what the page sees.

    python examples/course/06-contexts-and-emulation/example_emulation.py

Firefox cannot emulate a phone's mobile viewport or touch screen, so on Firefox the
script drops those two settings with ``desktop_only`` and keeps the rest.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.api.devices import desktop_only
from steero.sync_api import devices, expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        phone = devices["Pixel 7"]
        if browser.name == "firefox":
            phone = desktop_only(phone)  # no is_mobile or has_touch on Firefox

        context = browser.new_context(**phone, locale="ja-JP", timezone_id="Asia/Tokyo", color_scheme="dark")
        page = context.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")

        expect(page.get_by_test_id("locale")).to_have_text("ja-JP")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("timezone")).to_have_text("Asia/Tokyo")
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("scheme")).to_have_text("dark")
        # The page shows a menu button instead of links below 600 pixels wide.
        expect(page.get_by_role("button", name="Menu")).to_be_visible()

        for field in ("viewport", "dpr", "touch", "date"):
            print(f"{field:>8}:", page.get_by_test_id(field).text_content())

        # Resize the running page: wide enough for the desktop links again.
        page.set_viewport_size({"width": 1024, "height": 768})
        expect(page.get_by_role("button", name="Menu")).to_be_hidden()
        print("At 1024 pixels wide the menu button is hidden")
        context.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

viewport: 412 x 839
     dpr: 2.625
   touch: 5
    date: 2026年11月7日土曜日 21:00
At 1024 pixels wide the menu button is hidden

On Firefox, touch prints 0, because has_touch was dropped. The date is the same moment in every run (12:00 UTC on 7 November 2026), so the only thing that changes it is the context's locale and time zone: 21:00 in Tokyo.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a German visitor
docs.text:
Open whoami.html in a context with locale="de-DE" and timezone_id="Europe/Berlin". Check that the page reports the language de-DE, and print the date it formats.

Hint: the date field has the test id date. What time is 12:00 UTC in Berlin in November?

Solution 
"""Lesson 06, exercise 1: the same moment, formatted for a German user in Berlin.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        context = browser.new_context(locale="de-DE", timezone_id="Europe/Berlin")
        page = context.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")

        expect(page.get_by_test_id("locale")).to_have_text("de-DE")
        # 12:00 UTC is 13:00 in Berlin in November (CET, one hour ahead).
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("date")).to_have_text("Samstag, 7. November 2026 um 13:00")
        print("Berlin sees:", page.get_by_test_id("date").text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The page formats the date with Intl and no explicit language, so the context's locale decides the words ("Samstag") and the time zone decides the hour (13:00, one hour ahead of UTC in winter). Nothing on your machine had to change.

docs.title: Exercise 2: the phone layout
docs.text:
The Who am I page shows its own links on wide screens and a Menu button below 600 pixels. Open it once in a normal page and once in an "iPhone 13" context, and assert that the Menu button is hidden on the first and visible on the second. Make the script work on Firefox too.

Solution 
"""Lesson 06, exercise 2: emulate a phone and check that the page switched to its narrow layout.

On Firefox the phone preset loses ``is_mobile`` and ``has_touch`` (``desktop_only``), which
Firefox cannot emulate; the narrow viewport is enough for the layout to switch.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.api.devices import desktop_only
from steero.sync_api import devices, expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        phone = devices["iPhone 13"]
        if browser.name == "firefox":
            phone = desktop_only(phone)

        desktop_page = browser.new_page()
        desktop_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        expect(desktop_page.get_by_role("button", name="Menu")).to_be_hidden()

        phone_context = browser.new_context(**phone)
        phone_page = phone_context.new_page()
        phone_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        expect(phone_page.get_by_role("button", name="Menu")).to_be_visible()
        site_nav = phone_page.get_by_role("navigation", name="Site")
        expect(site_nav.get_by_role("link", name="Products")).to_be_hidden()
        print("Desktop shows links, the phone shows a Menu button")
        print("Phone viewport:", phone_page.get_by_test_id("viewport").text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The header also has a Products link, so the solution looks for the hidden one inside the page's "Site" navigation. On Firefox, desktop_only keeps the 390 pixel viewport, which is what the CSS media query reacts to.

docs.title: Exercise 3: cookies stay home
docs.text:
Create two contexts. Add a cookie theme=dark to the first only, open whoami.html in both, and check that the first page sees the cookie and the second does not. Then clear the first context's cookies and check that it sees none either.

Solution 
"""Lesson 06, exercise 3: a cookie added to one context is invisible to another.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        first = browser.new_context()
        second = browser.new_context()
        # "url" sets the domain and path from an address; "domain" and "path" work too.
        first.add_cookies([{"name": "theme", "value": "dark", "url": BASE_URL}])

        first_page = first.new_page()
        second_page = second.new_page()
        first_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        second_page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")

        expect(first_page.get_by_test_id("cookies")).to_have_text("theme=dark")
        expect(second_page.get_by_test_id("cookies")).to_have_text("none")
        assert [c["name"] for c in first.cookies()] == ["theme"]
        assert second.cookies() == []
        print("First context has theme=dark, the second has no cookies")

        first.clear_cookies()
        first_page.reload()
        expect(first_page.get_by_test_id("cookies")).to_have_text("none")
        print("After clear_cookies() the first context has none either")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The page reads document.cookie when it loads, so after clear_cookies() the solution reloads it before checking again.

docs.title: Exercise 4: where am I?
docs.text:
Start a context at the Eiffel Tower (latitude 48.8584, longitude 2.2945) with the geolocation permission. Click Show my location and assert the coordinates. Then move the context to Big Ben (51.5007, -0.1246) and check again.

Solution 
"""Lesson 06, exercise 4: set a geolocation, read it back, then move.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

EIFFEL_TOWER = {"latitude": 48.8584, "longitude": 2.2945}
BIG_BEN = {"latitude": 51.5007, "longitude": -0.1246}


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        # Without the permission the page is never told where it is.
        context = browser.new_context(geolocation=EIFFEL_TOWER, permissions=["geolocation"])
        page = context.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "whoami.html")
        locate = page.get_by_role("button", name="Show my location")
        location = page.get_by_test_id("location")

        locate.click()
        expect(location).to_have_text("48.8584, 2.2945")
        print("In Paris:", location.text_content())

        context.set_geolocation(BIG_BEN)
        locate.click()
        expect(location).to_have_text("51.5007, -0.1246")
        print("In London:", location.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

set_geolocation changes the position of a running context; the page sees it the next time it asks.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Using browser.new_page() and expecting a clean session. Pages without options share the default context, so cookies from one test leak into the next. Create a context per test (or per user) with browser.new_context().
  • Passing a phone preset on Firefox. It raises UnsupportedOnBrowser: is_mobile is not supported on firefox. Wrap the preset in desktop_only(...) when browser.name is "firefox".
  • Setting geolocation without permissions=["geolocation"]. The page asks for the position and is never answered: Chrome refuses it ("User denied Geolocation") and Firefox keeps waiting for a prompt nobody sees. Grant the permission too.
  • Calling storage_state() after closing the page. localStorage is read from the pages that are open, so the file has the cookies but no origins. Save the state while the signed-in page is still open.
  • Committing state.json. It is a working session. Write it to a temporary or gitignored folder.
  • Adding a cookie with only a name and a value. add_cookies raises ValueError: cookie 'theme' needs 'domain' or 'url'. Give it the site's url.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A context is an isolated session (cookies, storage, cache, permissions) inside one browser: cheap to create, so use one per test or per user.
