  • browser.new_context(...) takes the emulation options: viewport, locale, time zone, color scheme, geolocation, permissions, user agent; devices[...] fills in a whole device.
  • Firefox lacks is_mobile, has_touch, java_script_enabled=False, reduced_motion and forced_colors; steero raises UnsupportedOnBrowser rather than ignoring them.
  • add_cookies, cookies, clear_cookies, set_extra_http_headers and add_init_script shape what every page of a context starts with.
  • Log in once: context.storage_state(path=...), then new_context(storage_state=...).

Next: 07. Network

docs.title: 07. Network
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • watch requests and responses with page events
  • wait for the response an action triggers with expect_response
  • mock an endpoint with page.route and route.fulfill, block requests with route.abort, and change requests with route.continue_
  • change a real response with route.fetch, and pass a request on with route.fallback
  • answer HTTP authentication, and call APIs directly with steero.request and context.request

Time: about 60 minutes. Before this: 06. Contexts and emulation. Code: examples/course/07-network/

A web page is mostly a conversation with servers. Being able to listen to that conversation, and to answer in the server's place, lets you test what a page does when the API is empty, slow, broken or offline, without changing the server at all. This lesson uses the Products page (products.html), which loads its table from /api/products.

docs.title: Seeing the traffic
docs.text:
Every request a page makes fires a request event, and every answer a response event. A request that fails without an answer (a refused connection, a blocked request) fires requestfailed instead. Listen with page.on:

page.on("request", lambda request: print(">>", request.method, request.url))
page.on("response", lambda response: print("<<", response.status, response.url))
page.on("requestfailed", lambda request: print("failed:", request.url, request.failure))
page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")

A Request has url, method, headers, resource_type and, once answered, response. A Response has url, status, ok (true for 200 to 299), headers and its request. Header names are lower case in headers; headers_array() keeps them as sent.

Lesson 08 covers events in general. For now, one rule: a listener only sees what happens after you register it, so register it before goto.

docs.title: Waiting for a response
docs.text:
Often you want one particular response: the one a click causes. page.expect_response(url) wraps the action in a with block. It starts listening when the block starts, so a fast response cannot slip past, and when the block ends it waits (up to 30 seconds) for a matching response:

with page.expect_response("**/api/products") as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
response = waiter.value
print(response.status)          # 200

The pattern is a glob: ** matches any text, * any text without a slash, ? one character, and {a,b} either alternative. You can also pass a compiled regex (re.compile(r"/api/products$")) or a function that takes the URL and returns True or False. The same patterns work everywhere in this lesson. expect_request is the same for requests.

Coming from Playwright

page.goto() returns the main document's Response, as in Playwright (None for about:blank and other pages with no response), so page.goto(url).status works. To wait for any other response, wrap the action in expect_response, as the worked example does. Timeouts are in seconds: expect_response("**/api/*", timeout=5).

docs.title: Response bodies
docs.text:
A browser does not keep response bodies around for scripts unless asked, because they can be large. Call browser.collect_response_bodies() once, before the requests you care about, and then response.body(), text() and json() work:

browser.collect_response_bodies()
with page.expect_response("**/api/products") as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
products = waiter.value.json()

The same collector keeps request bodies, so request.post_data() and request.post_data_json() return what the page sent. Here is all of it in one script:

"""Lesson 07: watch the traffic a page makes, and wait for the response a click triggers.

Logs every request and response of the products page, then reloads the product list with the
Reload button and reads the JSON the page received.

    python examples/course/serve.py                     # terminal 1
    python examples/course/07-network/example_traffic.py # terminal 2

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        browser.collect_response_bodies()  # keep bodies, so response.json() works
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.on("request", lambda request: print(">>", request.method, request.url.replace(BASE_URL, "/")))
        page.on("response", lambda response: print("<<", response.status, response.url.replace(BASE_URL, "/")))

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")

        # Subscribe first, then act: the waiter catches the response the click causes.
        with page.expect_response("**/api/products") as waiter:
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
        response = waiter.value
        products = response.json()
        print(f"Reload answered {response.status} with {len(products)} products:",
              ", ".join(p["name"] for p in products))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

>> GET /products.html
<< 200 /products.html
>> GET /course.css
<< 200 /course.css
>> GET /api/products
<< 200 /api/products
>> GET /api/products
<< 200 /api/products
Reload answered 200 with 3 products: Blue mug, Green teapot, Red kettle

The order of the lines can differ between runs and browsers, because the browser fetches in parallel; Firefox also asks for /favicon.ico.

docs.title: Mocking with route
docs.text:
page.route(pattern, handler) intercepts every matching request before it leaves the browser. The handler receives a Route and decides what happens. route.fulfill(...) answers the request itself, so the server never sees it:

page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.fulfill(json=[]))             # an empty list
page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.fulfill(status=500))          # a server error
page.route("**/api/user", lambda route: route.fulfill(json={"name": "Ada"}))    # any JSON
page.route("**/logo.png", lambda route: route.fulfill(path="tests/logo.png"))   # a file

fulfill takes status, headers, body (text or bytes), json (any value, sent as JSON with the right content type), content_type and path. Three rules decide which handler runs:

  • The newest matching route wins. Add a new route for the same pattern and it takes over.
  • Unmatched requests go to the network as usual.
  • page.unroute(pattern) removes a route, page.unroute_all() removes them all.

context.route(...) works the same for every page of a context; a page's own routes are tried first.

A one-call handler fits in a lambda, as above. A handler that has to do several things (look at the request, decide, then answer) is an ordinary function:

def products_or_error(route: Route) -> None:
    if route.request.headers.get("x-break") == "1":
        route.fulfill(status=500)
    else:
        route.continue_()

page.route("**/api/products", products_or_error)

In the sync API the handler gets a sync Route and runs on a worker thread, so it can call route.fetch(), route.fulfill() or any other sync method, as many times as it needs. With the async API, write the handler as an async def and await each call; the async version of the worked example shows one.

docs.title: Blocking and changing requests
docs.text:
route.abort() fails the request as if the network were down. Blocking images, fonts, analytics or third-party scripts makes a test faster and keeps it away from servers you do not control:

page.route(re.compile(r"\.(png|jpe?g|svg)$"), lambda route: route.abort())
page.route("**/analytics/**", lambda route: route.abort())

route.continue_(...) sends the request to the network, optionally changed: a different url, method, headers or post_data. (The trailing underscore is because continue is a Python keyword.)

page.route("**/api/**", lambda route: route.continue_(
    headers={**route.request.headers, "x-test-run": "lesson-07"}))

docs.title: Changing a real response
docs.text:
Sometimes you want the real data with one thing changed: an extra product, a feature flag switched on, an error in one field. route.fetch() performs the request and returns the real response without answering the page; you then fulfill with it, changing what you need:

def add_product(route: Route) -> None:
    response = route.fetch()                             # the real answer
    products = response.json()
    products.append({"id": 4, "name": "Yellow cup", "price": 6.25, "stock": 9})
    route.fulfill(response=response, json=products)      # same status and headers, new body

fulfill(response=...) keeps the fetched status and headers unless you override them. route.fetch() is made by Python's own HTTP client with the page's headers and cookies, not by the browser, so it does not use the browser's cache or proxy.

route.fallback() passes the request on to the next matching handler: an older route of the page, then the context's routes. That lets a general route set a default and a specific one step aside:

context.route("**/api/**", lambda route: route.fulfill(json={"mocked": True}))   # default for every page
page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.fallback())                     # this page: let the context decide

fallback takes the same changes as continue_ (headers=, url=, ...), applied when a later handler continues the request. If no handler is left, the request goes to the network.

docs.title: HTTP authentication
docs.text:
Some pages are protected by HTTP authentication: the server answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header, and a browser would show a sign-in dialog. A test answers it with credentials instead, for a whole context or for one page:

context = browser.new_context(http_credentials={"username": "ada", "password": "secret"})
page.set_http_credentials({"username": "ada", "password": "secret"})    # one page only

The practice site's /api/basic-auth accepts user ada with password secret. Credentials that the server refuses are not retried: the page gets the 401 response, which on the practice site is a page saying "Sign-in required". With no credentials at all the challenge is cancelled the same way, so the page shows the 401 rather than a sign-in dialog. Page credentials win over the context's when both are set. Browsers remember credentials that worked for the rest of the session, so test the failure case in a context of its own.

docs.title: The API request context
docs.text:
Not every check needs a page. steero.request is an HTTP client with no browser at all: it is the quickest way to set up test data, call an API, or check one directly.

from steero.sync_api import expect, request

with request.new_context(base_url=BASE_URL) as api:
    response = api.post("api/echo", data={"name": "Ada"})   # a dict or list is sent as JSON
    expect(response).to_be_ok()
    print(response.json())

It has get, post, put, patch, delete, head and fetch. data= sends JSON, form= a form, params= a query string. A 404 or 500 comes back as a response (check response.ok or response.status) rather than raising, unless you pass fail_on_status_code=True. expect(response).to_be_ok() fails with the status and the URL.

context.request is the same client attached to a browser context: it shares the context's cookies. Sign in through the API and the context's pages are signed in too, which is faster than filling in a form:

"""Lesson 07: sign in through the API with context.request, and the pages are signed in too.

``context.request`` sends HTTP requests from Python that share the context's cookies. The
script posts to /api/login, then opens a page in the same context: it already has the cookie.

    python examples/course/07-network/example_api_request.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        context = browser.new_context(base_url=BASE_URL)

        refused = context.request.post("api/login", data={"user": "ada", "password": ""})
        print("Without a password:", refused.status, refused.json())

        response = context.request.post("api/login", data={"user": "ada", "password": "lovelace"})
        expect(response).to_be_ok()
        print("Signed in through the API:", response.json())

        page = context.new_page()
        page.goto("whoami.html")  # relative to base_url
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("cookies")).to_have_text("session=ada")
        print("The page has the cookie:", page.get_by_test_id("cookies").text_content())
        print("The API agrees:", context.request.get("api/me").json())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Without a password: 401 {'error': 'user and password are required'}
Signed in through the API: {'user': 'ada'}
The page has the cookie: session=ada
The API agrees: {'user': 'ada'}

base_url= on the context makes page.goto("whoami.html") and context.request.post("api/login") relative to the practice site.

Coming from Selenium

Selenium cannot see or change network traffic without a proxy or CDP-only extras. In steero events, routes and context.request are part of the core API and work the same in Chrome and Firefox, because they are WebDriver BiDi commands.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The products page shows a table when /api/products returns products, "No products yet" for an empty list, and an error message when the request fails or returns an error status. Testing those states against a real server would mean emptying its database or breaking it. With route, each state is one line. The script:

  1. loads the page normally, waits for the real /api/products response, and checks the table;
  2. routes the endpoint to an empty list and reloads;
  3. routes it to a 500, which replaces the empty list because the newest route wins;
  4. aborts it, so the page sees a network failure;
  5. removes every route, and the real data comes back.
"""Lesson 07: mock an API with page.route and check every state the page can show.

The products page loads /api/products. The script checks the real answer first, then answers
the same request itself: with an empty list, with a server error, and with a network failure.

    python examples/course/07-network/example_mock_products.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        state = page.get_by_role("status")

        # 1. The real server: wait for its response, then for the page to show it.
        with page.expect_response("**/api/products") as waiter:
            page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        print("Real API answered", waiter.value.status)
        expect(state).to_have_text("3 products")

        # 2. An empty list, without touching the server.
        page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.fulfill(json=[]))
        page.reload()
        expect(state).to_have_text("No products yet")
        print("Empty list:", state.text_content())

        # 3. A server error. The newest matching route wins, so this one replaces the empty list.
        page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.fulfill(status=500))
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
        expect(state).to_have_text("Could not load products (HTTP 500)")
        print("Server error:", state.text_content())

        # 4. No answer at all: the request fails as a network error.
        page.route("**/api/products", lambda route: route.abort())
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
        expect(state).to_contain_text("Could not load products")
        print("Network failure:", state.text_content())

        # Remove every route: the real server answers again.
        page.unroute_all()
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
        expect(state).to_have_text("3 products")
        print("Routes removed:", state.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/07-network/example_mock_products.py

Real API answered 200
Empty list: No products yet
Server error: Could not load products (HTTP 500)
Network failure: Could not load products (Failed to fetch)
Routes removed: 3 products

The network failure text comes from the browser: Chrome says "Failed to fetch", Firefox "NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.", which is why that step checks with to_contain_text.

Async version

Here the route handler is an async def that counts the requests and answers each one differently: an empty list first, then a 503.

"""Lesson 07: the routing example with the async API and async route handlers.

A handler that does more than one thing (look at the request, decide, answer) reads best as an
``async def``. This one sends an empty list for the first request and a server error after that.

    python examples/course/07-network/example_mock_products_async.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os

import steero
from steero import expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = await browser.new_page()
        calls = 0

        async def products(route: steero.Route) -> None:
            nonlocal calls
            calls += 1
            print(f"Request {calls}: {route.request.method} {route.request.url.replace(BASE_URL, '/')}")
            if calls == 1:
                await route.fulfill(json=[])
            else:
                await route.fulfill(status=503)

        await page.route("**/api/products", products)
        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        state = page.get_by_role("status")
        await expect(state).to_have_text("No products yet")
        print("First load:", await state.text_content())

        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Reload").click()
        await expect(state).to_have_text("Could not load products (HTTP 503)")
        print("Reload:", await state.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The handler awaits route.fulfill(...). A handler that returns without fulfilling, continuing or aborting is continued for you, so a mistake in a handler cannot hang the page.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running.

docs.title: Exercise 1: no pictures
docs.text:
The Gallery page (gallery.html) shows three pictures and a line saying how many loaded. Block every image with one route, check that the page reports "0 of 3 pictures loaded", and that its Like button still works. Print the names of the blocked files.

Hint: the pictures are .svg files; a regex can match several extensions at once.

Solution 
"""Lesson 07, exercise 1: block every image with one route and check the page still works.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import re

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        blocked: list[str] = []
        page.on("requestfailed", lambda request: blocked.append(request.url.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]))
        # A regex matches anywhere in the URL; this one catches the usual image types.
        page.route(re.compile(r"\.(png|jpe?g|gif|webp|svg)$"), lambda route: route.abort())

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "gallery.html")
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("0 of 3 pictures loaded")

        # The rest of the page still works without its pictures.
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Like").click()
        expect(page.get_by_test_id("likes")).to_have_text("1")
        print("Blocked:", ", ".join(sorted(blocked)))
        print("The Like button still works")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Every aborted request fires requestfailed, which is how the solution collects the names.

docs.title: Exercise 2: one more product
docs.text:
Use route.fetch to get the real product list, add a fourth product to it, and fulfil the request with the changed list. Check that the page shows "4 products" and the new row.

Hint: the handler fetches, changes and fulfils: three calls in one ordinary function. Each row has the test id product-<id>.

Solution 
"""Lesson 07, exercise 2: fetch the real product list and add a fourth product to it.

``route.fetch()`` gets the real response; ``route.fulfill(response=..., json=...)`` sends it on
with a changed body. The handler does three steps, so it is an ordinary function: in the sync
API it gets a sync ``Route`` and runs on a worker thread, so each call simply blocks.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (a plain sync handler now that sync route handlers get a sync Route)
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import Route, expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

YELLOW_CUP = {"id": 4, "name": "Yellow cup", "price": 6.25, "stock": 9}


def add_product(route: Route) -> None:
    response = route.fetch()  # the real answer from the server
    products = response.json()
    products.append(YELLOW_CUP)
    route.fulfill(response=response, json=products)  # same status and headers, new body


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.route("**/api/products", add_product)
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")

        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("4 products")
        row = page.get_by_test_id("product-4")
        expect(row).to_contain_text("Yellow cup")
        expect(row).to_contain_text("$6.25")
        print("The page shows 4 products, the last one:", row.get_by_role("cell").first.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The first three products come from the server, so if someone changes them there, this test still checks the real data plus the one you added.

docs.title: Exercise 3: an echo, no browser
docs.text:
Post the JSON {"product": "Blue mug", "quantity": 2} to /api/echo with steero.request, and assert that the server echoes the method, the body and the Content-Type it received. Add an X-Course header to every request of the client and check that it arrives too. Then show that /api/status/404 comes back as a response with status 404.

Solution 
"""Lesson 07, exercise 3: post JSON to /api/echo with steero.request, no browser at all.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, request

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with request.new_context(base_url=BASE_URL, extra_http_headers={"X-Course": "lesson-07"}) as api:
        order = {"product": "Blue mug", "quantity": 2}
        response = api.post("api/echo", data=order)  # a dict is sent as JSON
        expect(response).to_be_ok()

        echoed = response.json()
        assert echoed["method"] == "POST"
        assert echoed["body"] == order
        headers = {name.lower(): value for name, value in echoed["headers"].items()}
        assert headers["content-type"] == "application/json"
        assert headers["x-course"] == "lesson-07"
        print("The server echoed:", echoed["body"])

        missing = api.get("api/status/404")  # 4xx and 5xx come back as responses, not errors
        assert missing.status == 404 and not missing.ok
        print("A 404 is a response too:", missing.status)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The echo shows header names as the client sent them, so the solution compares them in lower case.

docs.title: Exercise 4: members only
docs.text:
Open /api/basic-auth once with the wrong password and once with the right one (ada / secret). Assert the 401 and the "Sign-in required" heading the first time, and the 200 and "Welcome, ada" the second time.

Solution 
"""Lesson 07, exercise 4: HTTP basic authentication, refused and accepted.

Each attempt uses a context of its own, because a browser remembers credentials that worked.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        for password, status, heading in (("wrong", 401, "Sign-in required"), ("secret", 200, "Welcome, ada")):
            context = browser.new_context(http_credentials={"username": "ada", "password": password})
            page = context.new_page()
            with page.expect_response("**/api/basic-auth") as waiter:
                page.goto(BASE_URL + "api/basic-auth")
            assert waiter.value.status == status, waiter.value.status
            expect(page.get_by_role("heading")).to_have_text(heading)
            print(f"Password {password!r}: {status} {heading}")
            context.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Each attempt gets a fresh context, so the browser cannot reuse credentials that worked earlier.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Starting expect_response after the click. The response may already have arrived, and the waiter times out with no 'response' event within 30 s. Put the action inside the with block.
  • response.json() raises UnsupportedOnBrowser: response bodies are off. Bodies are only kept after browser.collect_response_bodies(); call it before the request is made.
  • A route that never matches. "/api/products" is compared with the full URL (http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/products) and matches nothing. Start globs with **/, or use a regex.
  • Two routes for one URL, and the older one seems ignored. The newest matching route wins. Remove the newer one with unroute, or have it call route.fallback().
  • Mixing the two APIs in a handler. A sync handler (def or lambda) gets a sync Route and calls it without await. An async def handler gets the async Route, even when you register it with the sync API, and must await every call; forgetting one sends the request to the real server.
  • Expecting a sign-in dialog for a protected page. A test never sees one: with no credentials steero cancels the challenge and the page shows the 401 response. Assert that response, or give credentials.
  • Expecting route.fetch() to go through the browser's proxy or cache. It is made from Python. Use route.continue_() when the browser itself must send the request.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• page.on("request" / "response" / "requestfailed") shows the traffic; expect_response waits for the one an action causes, if you start it before the action.
  • page.route(pattern, handler) intercepts requests: fulfill answers, abort fails, continue_ sends on (changed), fallback passes to the next handler. The newest route wins.
  • route.fetch() plus fulfill(response=..., json=...) changes a real response.
  • http_credentials (context) and set_http_credentials (page) answer HTTP authentication.
  • steero.request calls APIs with no browser; context.request shares the context's cookies.

Next: 08. Events, dialogs, downloads and popups

docs.title: 08. Events, dialogs, downloads and popups
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • listen to page events with on, once and remove_listener
  • wait for what an action triggers with the expect_* waiters, subscribing before the action
  • accept, dismiss and answer dialogs, and know what steero does without a listener
  • save a download with expect_download and save_as
  • work with popups and several tabs (expect_popup, context.expect_page, browser.pages)

Time: about 40 minutes. Before this: 07. Network. Code: examples/course/08-events-dialogs-downloads/

Not everything a page does is a change you can see in the DOM. It writes to the console, throws errors nobody catches, stops to ask the user a question, starts a download, opens another window. A script has to notice these things, and sometimes answer them, or it will miss bugs or get stuck. This lesson uses the Events page (events.html), where each control does one of these things.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
A page (and a context, and the browser) emits events: named notifications with a payload. You subscribe with on(name, handler); the handler is called with the payload every time the event fires.

page.on("console", lambda message: print(message.type, message.text))
page.on("pageerror", lambda error: print("uncaught:", error))

The page events you will use most:

Event Payload Fires when console ConsoleMessage (type, text, args) the page calls console.log, error, warn and so on pageerror JavaScriptError an exception nobody catches dialog Dialog alert, confirm, prompt or a "leave page?" question opens download Download the page starts a download popup Page the page opens a new tab or window request, response, requestfailed Request or Response network traffic (lesson 07) load Page the page's load event fires close Page the page is closed

once(name, handler) calls the handler for the next event only. remove_listener(name, handler) stops a handler; pass the same function you registered, so give it a name rather than a lambda when you plan to remove it.

In the sync API, handlers run on a worker thread, with sync objects, so a handler may call the sync API itself (dialog.accept(), for example). Keep handlers short: record what happened in a list or print it, and make your checks in the main script.

Coming from Selenium

Selenium makes you poll for these things: switch_to.alert, the browser log, the window handle list. In steero they arrive as events, the moment they happen, in Chrome and Firefox alike.

docs.title: Waiters
docs.text:
A listener collects everything. Often you want just the one event an action causes: the error a click logs, the download a link starts. Each expect_* method is a waiter, used as a with block around the action:

with page.expect_console_message() as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Log a message").click()
print(waiter.value.text)        # Hello from the page

The waiter starts listening when the block starts and, when the block ends, waits (30 seconds by default) for the event; waiter.value is its payload. The order matters. If you clicked first and started listening afterwards, a fast event could already be over, and the waiter would wait for a second one that never comes. Subscribe before the action is the rule for every waiter.

The waiters are expect_console_message, expect_dialog, expect_download, expect_popup, expect_request and expect_response, plus the general expect_event(name, predicate), which waits for any event and can filter it:

with page.expect_event("console", lambda message: message.type == "error") as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Log a message").click()   # ignored: not an error
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Log an error").click()
print(waiter.value.text)        # Something went wrong

All of them take timeout= in seconds.

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text:
alert(), confirm() and prompt() open dialogs, which block the page until someone answers. A script answers with a dialog listener. The listener receives a Dialog with type ("alert", "confirm", "prompt" or "beforeunload"), message and default_value, and must call one of:

  • dialog.accept(): OK. For a prompt, dialog.accept("Ada") types the answer first.
  • dialog.dismiss(): Cancel (or close an alert).
page.once("dialog", lambda dialog: dialog.accept("Ada"))
page.get_by_role("button", name="Rename").click()
expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Hello, Ada")

Register the listener before the action that opens the dialog. The click itself does not finish until the dialog is answered, so code after the click is too late.

Without a listener, steero dismisses every dialog. A stray alert() never hangs a run: an alert is closed, a confirm answers Cancel (false), a prompt answers Cancel (null). That is the safe default, and it means a test that forgot its listener fails on a wrong result ("Item kept") instead of waiting forever.

expect_dialog() tells you a dialog appeared and what it said, but it cannot answer it: the block ends only after the click, and the click waits for the answer. Use it together with a listener:

page.once("dialog", lambda dialog: dialog.dismiss())
with page.expect_dialog() as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Delete item").click()
print(waiter.value.message)     # Delete the item?

Coming from Playwright

The same defaults as Playwright: no listener means dismissed, and a listener must accept or dismiss. In steero's sync API the handler runs on a worker thread, so lambda dialog: dialog.accept() just works.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
When a page starts a download (a link to a file the server sends as an attachment, or a link with a download attribute), the browser saves it into the browser profile and fires download. Wait for it with expect_download, then copy the file somewhere with save_as:

with page.expect_download() as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("link", name="Download the report").click()
download = waiter.value
print(download.suggested_filename)                  # report.csv
saved = download.save_as(Path(folder) / "report.csv")

save_as waits for the download to finish (60 seconds by default), creates missing folders, and returns the path. Copy the file before the browser closes: the profile, and the original file in it, are deleted then. download.url is where it came from, and download.failure() returns why a download did not complete, or None.

Save downloads to a temporary folder (the examples use tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()), so a run never leaves files in your repository.

docs.title: Popups and tabs
docs.text:
A link with target="_blank" opens a new tab; window.open() opens a new window. To steero both are a new Page and a popup event on the page that opened it. Catch it with expect_popup:

with page.expect_popup() as waiter:
    page.get_by_role("link", name="Help in a new tab").click()
help_tab = waiter.value
expect(help_tab).to_have_title("Help - steero practice site")
help_tab.close()

expect_popup hands the popup over once it has committed its URL, so help_tab.url is already the real address. The document may still be loading, though: check it with web-first assertions and locators (which wait), or call help_tab.wait_for_load_state() before a single read such as help_tab.title().

Two other ways to find pages:

  • context.expect_page() waits for any new page in a context, whichever page or script opened it.
  • browser.pages lists every open page, context.pages those of one context.

Each page is a separate object, so "switching tabs" is just using the other variable; there is no current tab to switch. page.bring_to_front() makes a tab the active one when that matters for a headed run. Closing a popup (popup.close(), or the page calling window.close()) fires its close event and leaves the other pages untouched.

Coming from Selenium

No window_handles and no switch_to.window: the popup is a Page of its own, and the opener keeps working the whole time.

docs.title: Async handlers
docs.text:
In the async API, a handler may be a plain function or a coroutine. An async def handler can await the API directly, which is the natural way to answer a dialog:

async def answer(dialog: steero.Dialog) -> None:
    await dialog.accept("Ada")

page.on("dialog", answer)

A plain function that needs to call the async API can schedule it instead: page.once("dialog", lambda dialog: asyncio.ensure_future(dialog.accept())). The waiters are async with blocks, and waiter.value is awaited:

async with page.expect_download() as waiter:
    await page.get_by_role("link", name="Download the report").click()
download = await waiter.value

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
This script goes through the events page from top to bottom. It prints every console message and uncaught error, answers a confirm and a prompt with one named listener (and removes it afterwards), saves the CSV report to a temporary folder, and opens and closes the help page in a new tab.

"""Lesson 08: handle everything the events page can throw at a script (sync API).

Console messages and an uncaught error, a confirm and a prompt, a download and a new tab.

    python examples/course/serve.py                                      # terminal 1
    python examples/course/08-events-dialogs-downloads/example_events.py # terminal 2

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero.sync_api import Dialog, expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def answer(dialog: Dialog) -> None:
    """Accept every dialog; give a prompt a name."""
    print(f"Dialog ({dialog.type}): {dialog.message}")
    dialog.accept("Ada" if dialog.type == "prompt" else None)


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.on("console", lambda message: print(f"Console {message.type}: {message.text}"))
        page.on("pageerror", lambda error: print("Page error:", error))
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")
        result = page.get_by_role("status")

        # Console messages and an uncaught error arrive as events.
        with page.expect_console_message():
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Log a message").click()
        with page.expect_event("pageerror"):
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Throw an error").click()

        # Dialogs: the listener answers each one while the click waits for it.
        page.on("dialog", answer)
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Delete item").click()
        expect(result).to_have_text("Item deleted")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Rename").click()
        expect(result).to_have_text("Hello, Ada")
        page.remove_listener("dialog", answer)

        # A download: wait for it, then copy it out of the browser's profile.
        with page.expect_download() as waiter:
            page.get_by_role("link", name="Download the report").click()
        download = waiter.value
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
            saved = download.save_as(Path(folder) / download.suggested_filename)
            print(f"Downloaded {download.suggested_filename}: {len(saved.read_text().splitlines())} lines")

        # A link with target=_blank opens a new tab: a popup of this page.
        with page.expect_popup() as waiter:
            page.get_by_role("link", name="Help in a new tab").click()
        help_tab = waiter.value
        expect(help_tab.get_by_role("heading")).to_have_text("Help")
        print("New tab:", help_tab.title(), "| open tabs:", len(browser.pages))
        help_tab.close()
        print("Closed it | open tabs:", len(browser.pages))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/08-events-dialogs-downloads/example_events.py

Console log: Hello from the page
Page error: Error: Boom
Dialog (confirm): Delete the item?
Dialog (prompt): What is your name?
Downloaded report.csv: 4 lines
New tab: Help - steero practice site | open tabs: 2
Closed it | open tabs: 1

The waiters around "Log a message" and "Throw an error" make the script wait for those events before it moves on; their payloads are printed by the listeners.

Async version

The same page with the async API: a plain-function console listener next to a coroutine dialog handler, and the waiters as async with blocks.

"""Lesson 08: the events example with the async API.

Handlers may be plain functions or coroutines; an ``async def`` handler can await
``dialog.accept()`` directly.

    python examples/course/08-events-dialogs-downloads/example_events_async.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import steero
from steero import expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def answer(dialog: steero.Dialog) -> None:
    """Accept every dialog; give a prompt a name."""
    print(f"Dialog ({dialog.type}): {dialog.message}")
    await dialog.accept("Ada" if dialog.type == "prompt" else None)


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = await browser.new_page()
        page.on("console", lambda message: print(f"Console {message.type}: {message.text}"))  # plain function
        page.on("dialog", answer)                                                              # coroutine
        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")
        result = page.get_by_role("status")

        async with page.expect_console_message() as waiter:
            await page.get_by_role("button", name="Log an error").click()
        print("Waited for:", (await waiter.value).text)

        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Rename").click()
        await expect(result).to_have_text("Hello, Ada")

        async with page.expect_download() as waiter:
            await page.get_by_role("link", name="Download the report").click()
        download = await waiter.value
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
            saved = await download.save_as(Path(folder) / download.suggested_filename)
            print("Downloaded", saved.name)

        async with page.expect_popup() as waiter:
            await page.get_by_role("link", name="Help in a new tab").click()
        help_tab = await waiter.value
        await expect(help_tab).to_have_title("Help - steero practice site")
        await help_tab.close()
        print("Opened and closed the help tab")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running.

docs.title: Exercise 1: no errors allowed
docs.text:
Collect every console error and every uncaught page error into a list. Click Log a message and assert the list is empty. Then click Log an error and Throw an error, and check that both were caught.

Hint: message.type is "error" for console.error. The events arrive a moment after the click, so use expect.poll(lambda: len(problems)).to_be(2) rather than checking at once.

Solution 
"""Lesson 08, exercise 1: fail when the page logs a console error or throws an uncaught one.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        problems: list[str] = []
        # Register before goto, so errors logged while the page loads are caught too.
        page.on("console", lambda message: problems.append(message.text) if message.type == "error" else None)
        page.on("pageerror", lambda error: problems.append(str(error)))
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")
        result = page.get_by_role("status")

        page.get_by_role("button", name="Log a message").click()
        expect(result).to_have_text("Logged a message")
        assert problems == [], f"the page reported errors: {problems}"
        print("A plain log message is not a problem")

        page.get_by_role("button", name="Log an error").click()
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Throw an error").click()
        # Events arrive a moment after the click; poll the list instead of sleeping.
        expect.poll(lambda: len(problems)).to_be(2)
        print("Caught:", problems)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

pageerror and console are separate events: an uncaught exception is not a console message, so a check that only watches the console misses it. In a test suite, register both in a fixture and assert the list is empty at the end of every test.

docs.title: Exercise 2: your name, please
docs.text:
Answer the Rename prompt with your name using once, and assert the page greets you. Click Rename again without a listener and check what the page says.

Solution 
"""Lesson 08, exercise 2: answer a prompt with a name, then see what happens with no listener.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")
        rename = page.get_by_role("button", name="Rename")
        result = page.get_by_role("status")

        # once(): answer the next dialog only, then the listener is gone.
        page.once("dialog", lambda dialog: dialog.accept("Grace"))
        rename.click()
        expect(result).to_have_text("Hello, Grace")
        print("With a listener:", result.text_content())

        # No listener: steero dismisses the prompt, as if Cancel was pressed.
        rename.click()
        expect(result).to_have_text("No name given")
        print("Without one:", result.text_content())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

After once has fired, no listener is left, so steero dismisses the second prompt and the page reads null: "No name given".

docs.title: Exercise 3: the report
docs.text:
Download the CSV report, save it to a temporary folder, and assert it is called report.csv and has four lines: a header and three products.

Solution 
"""Lesson 08, exercise 3: download the CSV report and check it has a header and three rows.

The file is saved to a temporary folder, never into the repository.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import csv
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser, tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")

        with page.expect_download() as waiter:
            page.get_by_role("link", name="Download the report").click()
        download = waiter.value
        assert download.suggested_filename == "report.csv", download.suggested_filename

        saved = download.save_as(Path(folder) / "report.csv")  # waits for the download to finish
        lines = saved.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        assert len(lines) == 4, lines
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(lines))
        assert [row["name"] for row in rows] == ["Blue mug", "Green teapot", "Red kettle"]
        print(f"{download.suggested_filename}: {len(lines)} lines, header {lines[0]!r}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 4: the help window
docs.text:
Click Open help window (it calls window.open), check the popup's title and that it knows a script opened it, then click its Close this window button. Wait for the popup to close, and show that the events page still works.

Hint: popup.expect_event("close") waits for the page to close.

Solution 
"""Lesson 08, exercise 4: open the help popup window, read it, close it, and carry on.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (popups are handed over once their URL commits)
"""

# (the default Chrome backend handles popups since the chromedriver popup repair)

import os

from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "events.html")

        with page.expect_popup() as waiter:
            page.get_by_role("button", name="Open help window").click()
        popup = waiter.value
        # The popup has its URL already; assertions wait for the page to finish loading.
        expect(popup).to_have_title("Help - steero practice site")
        expect(popup.get_by_test_id("opener")).to_have_text("a script (window.open)")
        print("Popup heading:", popup.get_by_role("heading").text_content())
        print("Open pages:", len(browser.pages))

        # The page closes itself; the "close" event tells us it is gone.
        with popup.expect_event("close"):
            popup.get_by_role("button", name="Close this window").click()
        print("Popup closed:", popup.is_closed(), "| open pages:", len(browser.pages))

        # Back on the first page, which never stopped working.
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Opened help")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Log a message").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Logged a message")
        print("The events page still works")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The help page closes itself with window.close(), which only a window opened by a script may do. Afterwards the popup object still answers is_closed() (now True); do not act on it any more.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Clicking first and waiting afterwards. page.click(...) and then with page.expect_download(): waits for a second download and fails with no 'download' event within 30 s. Put the action inside the with block.
  • Reading waiter.value inside the with block. The event may not have arrived yet; steero raises the event has not arrived yet; read .value after the 'with' block.
  • Registering the dialog listener after the click. The click waits for the dialog to be answered, and with no listener steero dismisses it, so the page sees Cancel. Register on("dialog") or once("dialog") first.
  • Removing a lambda listener. page.remove_listener("dialog", lambda d: d.accept()) is a new function, so nothing is removed. Keep a reference to the handler, or use once.
  • Checking a list filled by a listener straight after the action. Events arrive a moment later, on another thread. Use a waiter, or expect.poll(...).
  • Reading a popup's title at once. The URL is set, but the page may still be loading. Use expect(popup).to_have_title(...) or a locator, which wait, or popup.wait_for_url("**/help.html") (a glob, as in page.route) or popup.wait_for_load_state().
  • Saving downloads into the working directory. Use a temporary folder. And call save_as before the browser closes: the browser's own copy is deleted with its profile.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• on, once and remove_listener subscribe to events such as console, pageerror, dialog, download, popup and close; sync handlers run on a worker thread.
  • Waiters (expect_console_message, expect_dialog, expect_download, expect_popup, expect_event) go around the action, so a fast event is never missed.
  • A dialog listener must accept() or dismiss(); without one, steero dismisses every dialog so nothing hangs.
  • expect_download then download.save_as(path) copies a finished download out of the profile.
  • A popup or new tab is a Page; get it with expect_popup or context.expect_page, and close it when you are done.

Next: 09. The pytest plugin

docs.title: 09. The pytest plugin
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • write tests with the steero_page, steero_context and steero_browser fixtures
  • run one suite in several browsers with --browser (or --steero-browser)
  • use the options that matter day to day: headed, timeout, base URL, screenshots, video and tracing
  • find and read the failure artifacts (screenshot, HTML, diagnostics)
  • customise launch options and add your own fixtures in conftest.py

Time: about 45 minutes. Before this: 08. Events, dialogs, downloads and popups. Code: examples/course/09-pytest-plugin/

Up to now every lesson has been a script: launch, do something, close. A real test suite has dozens of tests that each need a clean browser state, run in more than one browser, and leave evidence behind when they fail. steero's pytest plugin does all of that for you, so a test is only the part you care about.

docs.title: Your first test
docs.text:
Installing steero also installs a pytest plugin; there is nothing to enable. A test asks for a page by naming the steero_page fixture as an argument:

from steero.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_sign_in(steero_page: Page) -> None:
    steero_page.goto("http://127.0.0.1:8765/login.html")
    steero_page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
    steero_page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
    steero_page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")

Save it as test_sign_in.py and run pytest test_sign_in.py. pytest finds the function because its name starts with test_, sees that it wants steero_page, and asks the plugin for one. The plugin launches Chrome (headless), opens a page, runs the test, and closes everything afterwards. There is no launch() and no with block in the test.

Tests use the sync API (from steero.sync_api import ...), like the scripts in earlier lessons. The plugin's fixtures are sync objects, so there is no await anywhere.

Coming from Playwright

pytest-playwright calls its fixtures page, context and browser. steero prefixes its own with steero_ so that both plugins can be installed side by side without fighting over page. If you prefer the short name, add a one-line alias (shown in Configuring). For an existing pytest-playwright suite, lesson 15 shows the opt-in plugin -p steero.compat.playwright.pytest, which provides Playwright's exact fixture names and millisecond timeouts.

Coming from Selenium

You do not write a driver fixture with yield and driver.quit(): the plugin owns the browser's lifetime, and it always closes it, even when a test fails or you press Ctrl+C.

docs.title: The fixtures
docs.text:
The plugin provides a small family of fixtures. Each has a scope: how long one instance lives before pytest makes a new one.

Fixture Scope What you get steero_browser session one browser, shared by every test in the run (per browser chosen) steero_context test a fresh, isolated browser context: its own cookies, storage and cache steero_page test a page in that context, with the default action timeout set steero_launch_options session the keyword arguments passed to launch(); override it to customise steero_healer test a self-healing helper for steero_page (lesson 12)

Starting a browser takes a second or two, so it happens once per session. A context is cheap (milliseconds), so every test gets a new one. That gives you isolation for free: a test that signs in cannot leave a cookie or a localStorage entry behind for the next test, and tests can run in any order.

When a test needs two pages in the same context (a popup, say), ask for steero_context and call steero_context.new_page(). When it needs two separate users at once, ask for steero_browser and create a second context with steero_browser.new_context(); close that one yourself at the end of the test.

docs.title: Several browsers
docs.text:
Choose browsers on the command line, once per browser:

pytest --browser chrome --browser firefox

The plugin parametrizes every steero test over the browsers, so each test runs once per browser and its test id ends with the browser in square brackets:

tests/test_shop.py::test_products_table_loads[chrome] PASSED
tests/test_shop.py::test_products_table_loads[firefox] PASSED

Use the id to run one combination, for example pytest "tests/test_shop.py::test_products_table_loads[firefox]", or -k firefox for every Firefox run. Without any --browser, tests run in Chrome.

To skip one browser in one test, ask for steero_browser_name, the name the current run was parametrized with:

import pytest


def test_print_to_pdf(steero_browser_name: str, steero_page: Page) -> None:
    if steero_browser_name != "chrome":
        pytest.skip("printing to PDF is a Chrome-only feature")
    ...

Browser support

--browser accepts chrome, firefox and edge, plus Playwright's spellings chromium (meaning Chrome) and msedge (meaning Edge). --browser webkit is a usage error rather than a silent skip: Safari has no WebDriver BiDi, so steero cannot drive it. Add --steero-backend chromium-bidi to reach Chrome without chromedriver (lesson 13).

docs.title: Options worth knowing
docs.text:
All of these are command-line options. The table shows pytest-playwright's names, which steero accepts too, with the --steero- spelling that always works:

Option Meaning --browser NAME / --steero-browser NAME browser to run in; repeat for several --headed / --steero-headed show the browser window --steero-timeout 10 default action timeout for steero_page, in seconds --base-url URL / --steero-base-url URL relative goto() URLs resolve against it --screenshot on\|off\|only-on-failure save a screenshot when each test ends --video on\|off\|retain-on-failure record a video of each test --tracing on\|off\|retain-on-failure record a trace of each test (lesson 10) --output DIR where those per-test files go (default test-results)

--base-url is the one to adopt first. With it, a test says steero_page.goto("login.html") and the same suite runs against your laptop, a test server or staging by changing one option.

--steero-timeout sets how long each action on steero_page (a click, a fill) may wait. It is 10 seconds by default; assertions keep their own default of 5 seconds.

--screenshot, --video and --tracing each record something per test into --output/<test id>/: test-failed-1.png or test-finished-1.png, a video/ folder, and trace.zip. only-on-failure and retain-on-failure record every test but keep the file only when the test failed, which is the setting you want on a build server.

Put options you always use in your project's configuration rather than typing them each time:

# pytest.ini
[pytest]
addopts = --browser chrome --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/ --screenshot only-on-failure

When pytest-playwright is installed too

The plain names (--browser, --headed, --base-url, --screenshot and the rest) are registered by steero only when pytest-playwright is not installed; when it is, those names belong to pytest-playwright and steero registers only its --steero- spellings. --base-url likewise belongs to pytest-base-url if that is installed. The course's example scripts use the --steero- spellings so they work either way.

docs.title: When a test fails
docs.text:
A failing test that used steero_page gets a folder of evidence under steero-artifacts/ (change it with --steero-artifacts DIR), named after its test id:

File What it holds screenshot.png the whole page, at the moment the test failed page.html the page's HTML at that moment diagnostics.json the page URL, console messages, uncaught page errors and failed requests

The folder's path is printed in the failure report, in a section headed steero, so you do not have to search for it. diagnostics.json is often the fastest clue: an uncaught JavaScript error or a request that failed with a 500 usually explains a test that "suddenly" cannot find a button.

These failure artifacts are always on; --screenshot, --video and --tracing add the per-test files in --output on top.

docs.title: Configuring
docs.text:
pytest loads a file called conftest.py automatically for every test in its folder and below. Fixtures defined there are available to those tests without an import. Three things people usually put there:

A short page name. A fixture that returns another fixture is an alias:

import pytest
from steero.sync_api import Page


@pytest.fixture
def page(steero_page: Page) -> Page:
    return steero_page

Launch options. Override steero_launch_options and build on the plugin's own value, which already carries --headed and --steero-backend:

from typing import Any


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def steero_launch_options(steero_launch_options: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {**steero_launch_options, "window_size": (1024, 768)}

A fixture may ask for the fixture it replaces, by the same name: pytest gives it the plugin's version. The override must keep the plugin's session scope.

A fixture that does the boring part. Most tests of an app start signed in, so put the signing in into a fixture and let tests ask for signed_in_page. Exercise 4 builds exactly that. When signing in is slow (a real login page, two-factor), do it once per session instead: sign in, save the context's storage state with context.storage_state(path=...), and start each test's context with steero_browser.new_context(storage_state=...). Lesson 06 covers storage state.

docs.title: Parallel runs
docs.text:
pytest-xdist runs tests in several processes at once: pip install pytest-xdist, then pytest -n 4. It works with steero unchanged. Each worker is a separate Python process with its own session, so each launches its own browser and its tests get their own contexts, as before. Self-healing baselines (lesson 12) are written to one file per worker and merged when the run ends, so workers never overwrite each other.

Because every test already gets a fresh context, a suite that passes in order passes in parallel, as long as the tests do not share something outside the browser (a database row, a file).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The lesson's folder holds a small suite, tests/test_shop.py: three tests against the practice site, where the last one is written to fail.

"""Lesson 09: a small test suite for the practice site, run by ``example_run_tests.py``.

Three tests use the ``steero_page`` fixture. The last one is written to fail, so a run shows
what the plugin saves for a failing test. URLs are relative: ``--base-url`` supplies the rest.

    pytest examples/course/09-pytest-plugin/tests --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

from steero.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_home_page_lists_the_course_pages(steero_page: Page) -> None:
    steero_page.goto("index.html")
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("heading", name="Practice site")).to_be_visible()
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("heading", name="Course pages")).to_be_visible()


def test_products_table_loads(steero_page: Page) -> None:
    steero_page.goto("products.html")
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("row")).to_have_count(4)  # the header row and three products


def test_deliberately_wrong_title(steero_page: Page) -> None:
    steero_page.goto("login.html")
    steero_page.evaluate("console.log('checking the title')")  # shows up in diagnostics.json
    # The real title is "Sign in - steero practice site", so this fails after 2 seconds.
    expect(steero_page, timeout=2).to_have_title("Log in - steero practice site")

Next to it, pytest.ini marks the lesson folder as a project of its own, so pytest does not pick up steero's own test settings from the repository's pyproject.toml.

You can run the suite yourself, with the practice site running in another terminal:

pytest examples/course/09-pytest-plugin/tests -v --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/

The course test runs every example_*.py and solution_*.py file as a script, so the worked example is a script that runs pytest for you, exactly as you would in a terminal, and then checks the result. It uses a small helper, pytest_run.py, that runs python -m pytest in a child process with a JUnit XML report and reads the pass and fail counts back from it. All output goes to a steero-course folder in your temporary directory.

"""Lesson 09: run the lesson's test suite with the steero pytest plugin, and check what it did.

Runs ``tests/test_shop.py`` in the course browser against the practice site, then checks that two
tests passed, one failed, and that the plugin saved artifacts for the failure. Everything is
written to a ``steero-course`` folder in your temporary directory, never into the repository.

    python examples/course/09-pytest-plugin/example_run_tests.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from pytest_run import run_pytest

# course: timeout=180

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "steero-course" / "09-pytest-plugin"


def main() -> None:
    shutil.rmtree(OUT, ignore_errors=True)
    args = [str(HERE / "tests"), "-v", "--tb=short",
            "--steero-browser", BROWSER, "--steero-base-url", BASE_URL,
            "--steero-screenshot", "only-on-failure", "--steero-output", str(OUT / "test-results"),
            "--steero-artifacts", str(OUT / "steero-artifacts")]
    if not HEADLESS:
        args.append("--steero-headed")
    outcome = run_pytest(*args, out=OUT)

    print(f"exit code {outcome.exit_code}: {outcome.passed} passed, {outcome.failures} failed")
    assert (outcome.passed, outcome.failures, outcome.errors) == (2, 1, 0), outcome
    assert outcome.exit_code == 1, "pytest exits 1 when a test failed"

    # The plugin's failure artifacts: one folder per failed test, named after its test id.
    (failure,) = (OUT / "steero-artifacts").iterdir()
    print("Failure artifacts:", failure)
    for file in sorted(failure.iterdir()):
        print("   ", file.name)
    assert {"screenshot.png", "page.html", "diagnostics.json"} <= {f.name for f in failure.iterdir()}

    # --screenshot only-on-failure: one more picture, in the per-test --output folder.
    (screenshot,) = (OUT / "test-results").glob("*/test-failed-1.png")
    print("Per-test screenshot:", screenshot)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/09-pytest-plugin/example_run_tests.py

tests/test_shop.py::test_home_page_lists_the_course_pages[chrome] PASSED [ 33%]
tests/test_shop.py::test_products_table_loads[chrome] PASSED             [ 66%]
tests/test_shop.py::test_deliberately_wrong_title[chrome] FAILED         [100%]
...
E   AssertionError: expect(page).to_have_title: expected 'Log in - steero practice site', got 'Sign in - steero practice site' after 2 s
...
========================= 1 failed, 2 passed in 9.48s =========================
exit code 1: 2 passed, 1 failed
Failure artifacts: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Temp\steero-course\09-pytest-plugin\steero-artifacts\tests_test_shop.py_test_deliberately_wrong_title_chrome
    diagnostics.json
    page.html
    screenshot.png
Per-test screenshot: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Temp\steero-course\09-pytest-plugin\test-results\tests_test_shop.py_test_deliberately_wrong_title_chrome\test-failed-1.png

Notice three things. The test ids end in [chrome]. pytest's exit code is 1 because a test failed, which is what makes a build server mark the run red. And the failing test got two sets of files: the always-on failure artifacts, and the test-failed-1.png that --screenshot only-on-failure asked for.
