Every positional or id-based CSS locator became a user-facing one. #user has a data-testid, so the test id wins over its label.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Nothing is recorded. The recorder is paused (the toolbar shows Record), or a pick or assert mode is still on. Click Record, or press Escape.
  • The script has a goto you did not type. The page navigated by itself late (a redirect, a timed refresh) and the timing rule read it as yours. Delete the line.
  • A recorded test passes but proves nothing. Recordings hold actions, not checks. Add at least one expect(...) for the outcome the test is about.
  • set_input_files fails with a missing file. Only the file names were recorded; put the files next to the script or fix the paths.
  • The recorded locator uses .nth(1). Nothing about the element was unique. Add a test id or an accessible name to the page if you can; otherwise check the position is really stable.
  • generate_locator raises StrictModeViolation. The locator you passed matched more than one element; it needs exactly one.
  • <coroutine object generate_locator ...> is printed instead of a locator. generate_locator is async: call it with await inside async def, as in the examples.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• steero codegen <url> records what you do in a visible browser and streams a runnable script; --target python-pytest --output test_x.py writes a test.
  • The toolbar pauses, picks locators and adds to_be_visible, to_contain_text and to_have_value assertions.
  • Locators are chosen in a fixed order (test id, role and name, label, ...) and only if steero's engine resolves them to exactly that element; generated ids and classes are never used.
  • generate_locator(locator) gives the same choice from code.
  • A recording is a draft: remove noise, add the checks, replace data, and name the test.

Next: 12. Self-healing locators

docs.title: 12. Self-healing locators
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • explain what self-healing does and, just as important, when it refuses
  • wrap locators in a healer with stable keys and a FingerprintStore
  • use the steero_healer fixture and --steero-strict-heal in pytest
  • read a heal event and its suggested replacement, and fix the test
  • tune HealConfig, and use risk="destructive" for dangerous actions

Time: about 35 minutes. Before this: 11. Recording with codegen. Code: examples/course/12-self-healing/

A redesign lands, and half the suite fails. Not because anything is broken for users, but because an id was renamed and a class changed. Self-healing keeps such a test running when the answer is clear, tells you exactly which locator to fix, and refuses when the answer is not clear. The second half matters more than the first: a healer that guesses clicks the wrong button, and a wrong click is worse than a red test.

docs.title: Why tests break
docs.text:
Lesson 02 recommended user-facing locators because markup changes more often than what users see. Real suites still contain brittle ones: #submit-btn, .btn.btn-primary, div > form > button:nth-child(3), written before anyone knew better or copied from a browser's "copy selector". When the page is redesigned:

  • an id is renamed (#submit-btn becomes #login-submit);
  • classes are restyled (btn btn-primary becomes button button--primary);
  • a wrapper <div> appears, so a positional path no longer leads anywhere.

For the user, nothing changed: the button still says "Sign in" in the same place. For the test, the locator matches nothing and every test that signs in fails.

docs.title: How healing decides
docs.text:
Healing works in two phases.

While the locator still works, steero records a fingerprint of the element it finds, under a key you choose, such as login.submit. A fingerprint is everything that describes the element apart from the locator: tag, id, test id, role, accessible name, label, classes, the headings and landmarks around it, and its position on the page.

When the locator matches nothing, for at least 1 second (heal_after), steero scores every visible element on the page against the fingerprint. Each feature gives a similarity from 0 to 1, and the score is their weighted average. Then a fixed rule decides:

Rule Default Why best score at least warn_threshold 0.65 below that, nothing on the page is really like the original best leads the runner-up by at least margin 0.10 two close candidates means the healer would be guessing best score at least auto_threshold 0.80 heal silently (auto); between 0.65 and 0.80, heal with a SelfHealWarning (warn)

If the rule accepts, the action goes ahead on the healed element and a heal event records what happened. If not, nothing is guessed: the action times out as it would have without healing, and its error says why healing refused.

The rule is deterministic: the same page and the same fingerprint give the same decision every time. There is no model and no network call involved.

docs.title: Using a healer
docs.text:
Wrap each locator you want healed, with a key that stays the same when the markup changes:

from steero.heal import FingerprintStore
from steero.sync_api import healer

with FingerprintStore(".steero/baselines") as store:    # saved when the block ends
    heal = healer(page, store)
    submit = heal.locator("login.submit", page.locator("#submit-btn"))
    submit.click()

heal.locator(...) returns an ordinary locator: you call click(), fill() and expect(...) on it as before. It only behaves differently when the original stops matching.

The FingerprintStore keeps fingerprints by key. Given a folder, it reads fingerprints.json from it when created. New fingerprints are kept in memory until they are saved: the with block saves them into fingerprints.json when it ends (even if the code inside failed), or call store.save() yourself. The pytest plugin saves for you at the end of a session, with one shard per pytest-xdist worker. FingerprintStore() with no folder keeps everything in memory.

A fingerprint is recorded the first time a key's locator matches exactly one element, and is not overwritten afterwards, so the baseline stays what the page looked like when the test was known good. Pass update_baselines=True to healer() (or --steero-update-baselines in pytest) to re-record after a redesign you have accepted.

Async version 
from steero.heal import FingerprintStore, Healer

with FingerprintStore(".steero/baselines") as store:
    heal = Healer(page, store)
    submit = heal.locator("login.submit", page.locator("#submit-btn"))
    await submit.click()

Coming from Playwright

Playwright has no built-in self-healing. Healing in steero is opt-in per locator: a plain page.locator(...) never heals, so nothing changes in a suite until you wrap a locator.

Coming from Selenium

Selenium healing tools usually heal any find_element and pick the best match automatically. steero heals only the locators you name, and refuses rather than picks when two candidates are close. Expect fewer heals and no silent wrong clicks.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
There are three kinds of refusal, and each one is the healer doing its job.

Ambiguous. Two candidates are about equally good, for example two identical "Save" buttons. The error ends with:

self-healing refused: ambiguous: best 0.91 vs runner-up 0.90 (margin 0.10)

Low score. Nothing on the page is similar enough, for example the button was removed:

self-healing refused: best score 0.41 below warn threshold 0.65

Destructive. A locator wrapped with risk="destructive" heals only to an element with the same id or the same data-testid as the original. Use it for Delete, Pay, Send and anything else you could not undo:

delete = heal.locator("account.delete", page.locator("#delete-btn"), risk="destructive")

self-healing refused: destructive action: no exact id/data-testid match

A lookalike Delete button is never clicked, however high it scores.

One more message is not a refusal: self-healing never ran: it waits 1 s for the original locator before trying, so give this action a longer timeout. An action with a timeout shorter than heal_after gives up before healing starts.

docs.title: Fixing the test
docs.text:
A heal is a warning, not a fix. Every decision is a heal event; heal.report() returns them as dictionaries:

Field Meaning key the stable name, login.submit locator the original locator, locator('#submit-btn') outcome healed or refused band auto, warn or refused score, runner_up the best and second-best scores reason why the decision was made suggestion a robust replacement, such as page.get_by_role('button', name='Sign in') url the page the decision was made on

The suggestion is the code to paste into the test, in place of the brittle locator. It follows the same preference as codegen: test id, then role and name, then label.

docs.title: In pytest
docs.text:
The plugin provides a steero_healer fixture for steero_page:

def test_sign_in(steero_page: Page, steero_healer: Healer) -> None:
    steero_page.goto("login.html")
    steero_healer.locator("login.submit", steero_page.locator("#submit-btn")).click()

Baselines live in --steero-baselines (default .steero/baselines) and are saved when the session ends. After a run with heals, pytest prints a summary and writes steero-artifacts/heal-report.json:

========================= steero self-healing =========================
HEALED  login.submit [warn 0.74] locator('#submit-btn') -> page.get_by_role('button', name='Sign in')
report: steero-artifacts/heal-report.json

--steero-strict-heal fails any test that needed healing, after it ran. Use it in your release gate: day to day the suite stays green through a redesign, and the gate makes sure someone replaces each healed locator before release. Commit fingerprints.json with the tests, so every machine heals from the same baselines.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
HealConfig holds the numbers from the table above:

from steero.heal import HealConfig

config = HealConfig(auto_threshold=0.85, warn_threshold=0.70, margin=0.15, heal_after=2.0)
heal = healer(page, store, config)

Raising the thresholds trades heals for safety; lowering them does the opposite, and some of the extra heals will be wrong clicks. Change them only when you have measured on your own app, as below.

docs.title: Measured on ControlLab
docs.text:
steero's own suite includes ControlLab, a larger single-page app with 279 tests written against version 1 with deliberately brittle locators. Versions 2 and 3 apply 18 catalogued changes: renamed ids, moved markup, reordered columns, a removed button, a relabelled delete. (The practice site serves all three at /controllab/v1/, /controllab/v2/ and /controllab/v3/.) With fingerprints from a v1 run and the default thresholds, on Chrome:

App Healing off Healing on v2 1 test passes (every test signs in, and the sign-in button's id changed) 235 of 279 pass v3 252 pass 270 pass

What still fails is the useful part of the result:

  • Changes that are not about locators. A menu that moved under a submenu (the old element exists but is hidden, so healing never runs), a <select> that became a custom listbox (select_option cannot work on a button). The test needs updating, not healing.
  • Correct refusals. The relabelled Delete button is refused as destructive, the removed Export button has nothing to heal to, two row checkboxes that became indistinguishable are refused as ambiguous (1.00 against 0.97).
  • Real misses. A few elements scored just under the 0.65 floor. Lowering the floor would rescue some and misclick others, which is why it is a setting.
  • Positional locators that still match. After the grid columns were reordered, td:nth-child(7) still finds a cell, just the wrong one. No healer can notice, because nothing failed to match: only a user-facing locator would have avoided it.

The self-healing guide has the details and the commands to reproduce the numbers.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The script signs in on /testsite/heal/v1.html with brittle #id locators wrapped in a healer, which records three fingerprints and saves them to a baseline folder in your temporary directory. Then it runs the same sign-in on v2.html, the redesign, where every id and class changed, with a fresh store read from that folder. All three locators match nothing; the healer finds each element again and the sign-in succeeds.

"""Lesson 12: a sign-in script survives a redesign that renamed every id and class.

Run 1 signs in on ``/testsite/heal/v1.html`` with brittle id locators wrapped in a healer, which
records a fingerprint of each element and saves them to a baseline folder. Run 2 uses the same
script on ``v2.html``, where the ids changed: the locators match nothing, the healer finds each
element again by its fingerprint, and the script prints every heal and its suggested locator.

    python examples/course/12-self-healing/example_heal_redesign.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (the store saves itself in a with block)
"""

import os
import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from steero.heal import FingerprintStore
from steero.sync_api import Browser, expect, healer, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

BASELINES = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "steero-course" / "12-self-healing" / "baselines"


def sign_in(browser: Browser, version: str) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Sign in on heal/<version>.html with id locators; return the healer's events."""
    page = browser.new_context().new_page()
    # Reads fingerprints.json from earlier runs; saves what this run recorded when the block ends.
    with FingerprintStore(BASELINES) as store:
        heal = healer(page, store)
        user = heal.locator("login.user", page.locator("#username"))
        password = heal.locator("login.password", page.locator("#password"))
        submit = heal.locator("login.submit", page.locator("#submit-btn"))

        page.goto(BASE_URL + f"testsite/heal/{version}.html")
        user.fill("ada")
        password.fill("lovelace")
        submit.click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("signed in")
    page.context.close()
    return heal.report()


def main() -> None:
    shutil.rmtree(BASELINES, ignore_errors=True)  # start with no baselines
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        events = sign_in(browser, "v1")
        print(f"v1: signed in, {len(events)} heal events; baselines in {BASELINES}")
        assert events == []

        events = sign_in(browser, "v2")
        print(f"v2: signed in after {len(events)} heals:")
        for event in events:
            print(f"  {event['key']:15} {event['band']:5} {event['score']:.2f}  "
                  f"{event['locator']} -> {event['suggestion']}")
        assert {e["key"] for e in events if e["outcome"] == "healed"} == {"login.user", "login.password",
                                                                           "login.submit"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

v1: signed in, 0 heal events; baselines in C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Temp\steero-course\12-self-healing\baselines
SelfHealWarning: healed login.password (score 0.77 (warn)); use page.get_by_role('textbox', name='Password')
SelfHealWarning: healed login.submit (score 0.74 (warn)); use page.get_by_role('button', name='Sign in')
v2: signed in after 3 heals:
  login.user      auto  0.82  locator('#username') -> page.get_by_role('textbox', name='User name')
  login.password  warn  0.77  locator('#password') -> page.get_by_role('textbox', name='Password')
  login.submit    warn  0.74  locator('#submit-btn') -> page.get_by_role('button', name='Sign in')

The user name field heals in the auto band. The password field and the button heal in the warn band, so Python prints a SelfHealWarning for each: they changed more (new id, new classes and a new wrapper) and the healer wants a person to look. The suggestions are what the test should have said in the first place.

A second example shows tuning. The same Sign in button heals at the default thresholds, and is refused with warn_threshold=0.80, because its score of 0.74 is now under the floor:

"""Lesson 12: the same redesign under two ``HealConfig`` settings, the default and a stricter one.

Records fingerprints on ``/testsite/heal/v1.html``, then clicks the renamed Sign in button on
``v2.html`` twice: with the default thresholds it heals (score 0.74, in the warn band), and with
``warn_threshold=0.80`` the same candidate is below the floor, so the click is refused.

    python examples/course/12-self-healing/example_heal_config.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os
import warnings

from steero import SteeroTimeoutError
from steero.heal import FingerprintStore, HealConfig, SelfHealWarning
from steero.sync_api import Browser, healer, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def click_sign_in(browser: Browser, config: HealConfig) -> str:
    """Record on v1, click on v2 under ``config``; return the outcome and reason."""
    page = browser.new_context().new_page()
    heal = healer(page, FingerprintStore(), config)
    submit = heal.locator("login.submit", page.locator("#submit-btn"))
    page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/heal/v1.html")
    submit.click()
    page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/heal/v2.html")
    try:
        submit.click(timeout=10)  # healing starts after 1 s; leave it time to run
    except SteeroTimeoutError:
        if not heal.report():
            raise  # healing never got to decide: that is a real failure
        # otherwise it refused, and the event below says why
    page.context.close()
    (event,) = heal.report()
    return f"{event['outcome']} ({event['reason']})"


def main() -> None:
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", SelfHealWarning)  # the events say the same thing
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        default = click_sign_in(browser, HealConfig())
        strict = click_sign_in(browser, HealConfig(auto_threshold=0.90, warn_threshold=0.80))
    print("default thresholds:", default)
    print("warn_threshold 0.80:", strict)
    assert default.startswith("healed") and strict.startswith("refused")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

default thresholds: healed (score 0.74 (warn))
warn_threshold 0.80: refused (best score 0.74 below warn threshold 0.80)

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running.

docs.title: Exercise 1: two lookalikes
docs.text:
The practice page heal-lookalikes.html has one Save button, #save. Its version 2, heal-lookalikes.html?v=2, renamed the id and added a second, identical Save button. Wrap #save in a healer, click it on version 1, then try again on version 2. What happens, and which button was clicked?

Solution 
"""Lesson 12, exercise 1: two lookalike buttons, and a healer that refuses to pick one.

Version 1 of ``heal-lookalikes.html`` has one Save button, ``#save``; the healer records it.
Version 2 renamed the id and added a second, identical Save button. Both candidates score the
same, so the click is refused and times out with the reason, and nothing is saved.

    python examples/course/12-self-healing/solution_1_ambiguous_refusal.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero import SteeroTimeoutError
from steero.heal import FingerprintStore
from steero.sync_api import expect, healer, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    store = FingerprintStore()  # in memory: this script records and heals in one run
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        heal = healer(page, store)
        save = heal.locator("notes.save", page.locator("#save"))

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "heal-lookalikes.html")
        save.click()  # works, and records the fingerprint
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Saved by #save")

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "heal-lookalikes.html?v=2")
        try:
            save.click(timeout=10)  # healing waits 1 s before it tries, so allow well more than that
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
            print("Refused, as it should be:")
            print("   ", error)
        else:
            raise AssertionError("the healer guessed between two identical buttons")
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("")  # neither button was clicked

        (event,) = heal.report()
        print(f"{event['outcome']}: best {event['score']:.2f}, runner-up {event['runner_up']:.2f}")
        assert event["outcome"] == "refused" and "ambiguous" in event["reason"], event


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Refused, as it should be:
    click locator('#save'): timed out after 10 s: no element matches; self-healing refused: ambiguous: best 0.91 vs runner-up 0.90 (margin 0.10)
refused: best 0.91, runner-up 0.90

Neither button was clicked. Both score high (0.91 is well inside auto), but they are only 0.01 apart, so choosing one would be a coin toss. The click is given 10 seconds, well over the 1 second healing waits before it tries.

docs.title: Exercise 2: a destructive action
docs.text:
On /testsite/heal/v1.html, wrap the Delete account button (#delete-btn) twice: once normally, once with risk="destructive". On v2.html the button has a new id and a new data-testid. Show that the normal locator heals (without clicking it) and that the destructive one refuses to click.

Solution 
"""Lesson 12, exercise 2: a Delete button marked ``risk="destructive"`` is never healed to a lookalike.

On ``/testsite/heal/v2.html`` the Delete account button has a new id and a new data-testid. A
normal healing locator finds it again (here only asked whether it is enabled, so nothing is
deleted). The same locator marked destructive refuses, because neither the id nor the test id
matches exactly, and the click times out with the reason.

    python examples/course/12-self-healing/solution_2_destructive.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero import SteeroTimeoutError
from steero.heal import FingerprintStore
from steero.sync_api import expect, healer, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        heal = healer(page, FingerprintStore())
        normal = heal.locator("danger.delete.normal", page.locator("#delete-btn"))
        destructive = heal.locator("danger.delete", page.locator("#delete-btn"), risk="destructive")

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/heal/v1.html")
        assert normal.is_enabled() and destructive.is_enabled()  # both record a fingerprint

        page.goto(BASE_URL + "testsite/heal/v2.html")
        print("Normal locator healed, enabled:", normal.is_enabled(timeout=10))
        try:
            destructive.click(timeout=10)
        except SteeroTimeoutError as error:
            print("Destructive locator refused:")
            print("   ", error)
        else:
            raise AssertionError("a destructive action was healed to a different element")
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("")  # the account was not deleted

        outcomes = {e["key"]: e["outcome"] for e in heal.report()}
        print(outcomes)
        assert outcomes == {"danger.delete.normal": "healed", "danger.delete": "refused"}, outcomes


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Normal locator healed, enabled: True
Destructive locator refused:
    click locator('#delete-btn'): timed out after 10 s: no element matches; self-healing refused: destructive action: no exact id/data-testid match
{'danger.delete.normal': 'healed', 'danger.delete': 'refused'}

The normal heal is probably right here, it is the same button renamed. But "probably" is not good enough for deleting an account, and risk="destructive" makes that a rule.

docs.title: Exercise 3: strict mode in pytest
docs.text:
Write a pytest test that signs in through steero_healer, with the page version taken from an environment variable. Run it on v1 to record baselines, on v2 to see it heal, and on v2 again with --steero-strict-heal. Explain the third result.

Solution

The test, heal_tests/test_heal_sign_in.py:

"""Lesson 12, exercise 3: a pytest test that signs in through the ``steero_healer`` fixture.

The page version comes from ``HEAL_VERSION`` (``v1`` or ``v2``), so the same test can record
baselines on v1 and then heal on v2. Run by ``solution_3_strict_heal.py``.

    HEAL_VERSION=v1 pytest examples/course/12-self-healing/heal_tests --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import os

from steero.sync_api import Healer, Page, expect


def test_sign_in(steero_page: Page, steero_healer: Healer) -> None:
    steero_page.goto(f"testsite/heal/{os.environ.get('HEAL_VERSION', 'v1')}.html")
    steero_healer.locator("login.user", steero_page.locator("#username")).fill("ada")
    steero_healer.locator("login.password", steero_page.locator("#password")).fill("lovelace")
    steero_healer.locator("login.submit", steero_page.locator("#submit-btn")).click()
    expect(steero_page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("signed in")

The script that runs it three times:

"""Lesson 12, exercise 3: ``steero_healer`` in pytest, and why ``--steero-strict-heal`` fails a healed test.

Runs ``heal_tests/test_heal_sign_in.py`` three times, all writing to your temporary directory:

1. on v1: the test passes and the plugin records baselines in ``--steero-baselines``;
2. on v2: the test passes by healing, and the plugin writes ``heal-report.json``;
3. on v2 with ``--steero-strict-heal``: the test body passes, but the healer fixture then fails
   it, so a heal can never slip through a gate unnoticed.

    python examples/course/12-self-healing/solution_3_strict_heal.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

# course: timeout=240

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "steero-course" / "12-self-healing" / "pytest"


def run(version: str, *extra: str) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
    """Run the healing test on one page version and print pytest's summary line."""
    command = [sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", str(HERE / "heal_tests"), "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider",
               "--steero-browser", BROWSER, "--steero-base-url", BASE_URL,
               "--steero-baselines", str(OUT / "baselines"), "--steero-artifacts", str(OUT / "artifacts"), *extra]
    if not HEADLESS:
        command.append("--steero-headed")
    env = dict(os.environ, HEAL_VERSION=version, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1")
    result = subprocess.run(command, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace",
                            check=False)
    print(f"{' '.join([version, *extra])}: exit {result.returncode}: {result.stdout.strip().splitlines()[-1]}")
    return result


def main() -> None:
    shutil.rmtree(OUT, ignore_errors=True)
    assert run("v1").returncode == 0
    print("    baselines:", sorted(json.loads((OUT / "baselines" / "fingerprints.json").read_text())))

    healed = run("v2")
    assert healed.returncode == 0 and "HEALED" in healed.stdout, healed.stdout
    for event in json.loads((OUT / "artifacts" / "heal-report.json").read_text()):
        print(f"    {event['key']}: use {event['suggestion']}")

    strict = run("v2", "--steero-strict-heal")
    assert strict.returncode == 1 and "--steero-strict-heal: locators needed healing" in strict.stdout, strict.stdout
    print("    strict mode turned the heals into an error, as a release gate should")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

v1: exit 0: 1 passed in 5.00s
    baselines: ['login.password', 'login.submit', 'login.user']
v2: exit 0: 1 passed, 2 warnings in 7.22s
    login.user: use page.get_by_role('textbox', name='User name')
    login.password: use page.get_by_role('textbox', name='Password')
    login.submit: use page.get_by_role('button', name='Sign in')
v2 --steero-strict-heal: exit 1: 1 passed, 2 warnings, 1 error in 11.17s
    strict mode turned the heals into an error, as a release gate should

In strict mode the test itself passes (the heals worked), and then the steero_healer fixture fails it while tearing down, which pytest reports as an error. The run exits 1, so a gate stops, and the report lists the three replacements to make.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Nothing heals on the second run. The baselines were never saved. In a script, use with FingerprintStore(folder) as store: or call store.save() before it ends; in pytest, check that --steero-baselines points at the same folder both times.
  • self-healing never ran: it waits 1 s .... The action's timeout is shorter than heal_after. Give it a few seconds, or lower heal_after in HealConfig.
  • no baseline fingerprint recorded for 'login.submit'. The locator never worked while wrapped under that key, so there is nothing to compare with. Run once against the version where it works.
  • Two locators share a key. The second one heals towards the first one's element. Give every wrapped locator its own key.
  • A heal clicks the right button but the test fails later. The interaction changed (a <select> became a custom list, a menu moved). Healing finds elements; it does not rewrite steps. Update the test.
  • Keeping a heal forever. Healed tests are slower (each one waits heal_after first) and depend on old baselines. Paste the suggestion in and let --steero-strict-heal enforce it.
  • Expecting healing to catch a wrong match. td:nth-child(7) that still matches the wrong cell never triggers healing. Use user-facing locators.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A healer records a fingerprint per key while a locator works, and when it stops matching, scores the page against it.
  • It heals only with a clear winner: at least 0.65, and 0.10 ahead of the runner-up; 0.80 and above is silent, below that it warns.
  • Ambiguous, low-score and destructive cases are refused, and the action fails with the reason.
  • Every heal comes with a suggested locator; heal-report.json collects them in pytest and --steero-strict-heal fails a gate until they are applied.
  • HealConfig tunes the thresholds; risk="destructive" heals only to the same id or test id.

Next: 13. Browsers and backends

docs.title: 13. Browsers and backends
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • explain why steero's main API works the same in Chrome and Firefox, and where CDP still appears
  • choose a Chrome backend (chromedriver or chromium-bidi) and know the trade-offs
  • launch Edge and release channels such as channel="chrome-beta" or firefox-nightly
  • pin browser versions with steero install chrome@<version> and STEERO_CHROME_VERSION
  • use the Chrome-only extras in steero.chromium and handle UnsupportedOnBrowser
  • know the Firefox specifics: no driver, Firefox preferences, emulation gaps, video by screencast

Time: about 35 minutes. Before this: 12. Self-healing locators. Code: examples/course/13-browsers-and-backends/

Until now you have switched browsers with one environment variable and never thought about what happens underneath. This lesson opens that box: how steero reaches each browser, how to pick the exact build you test against, and what to do with the few features only one browser has.

docs.title: One protocol, two browsers
docs.text:
Every page action in this course (navigate, click, fill, evaluate, screenshot, route) travels over WebDriver BiDi, the W3C standard protocol that Chrome, Edge and Firefox all implement. steero has one implementation of each feature, written against the standard, so a script that passes in Chrome is not a different program in Firefox.

The older Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) still exists in Chrome and Edge, and it can do a few things BiDi cannot yet: performance counters, CPU throttling, JavaScript coverage. Firefox removed CDP entirely. So steero keeps CDP out of its main API and puts those extras in one module, steero.chromium, which says plainly that it is Chrome only. If you never import steero.chromium, nothing in your script depends on CDP.

from steero import chromium

metrics = await chromium.performance_metrics(page)  # Chrome and Edge only

Coming from Playwright

Playwright drives Chromium mostly over CDP and Firefox through a patched build ("Juggler"). steero drives the stock browsers you install, over the standard. The price is that a few Chrome features only exist where CDP does, and they are marked as such.

docs.title: Chrome backends
docs.text:
steero can reach Chrome in two ways. Both end at the same BiDi connection, so the rest of your script cannot tell them apart. You pick one with backend= or the STEERO_CHROME_BACKEND environment variable.

Backend How it works Good for chromedriver (default) steero starts chromedriver, the Chrome team's own driver, matched to your Chrome version and downloaded from Chrome for Testing Google's supported path; the safest default chromium-bidi steero starts Chrome alone and loads the chromium-bidi mapper (the same code chromedriver runs) into a hidden tab no driver binary on disk; useful where you cannot run extra executables 
with launch("chrome", backend="chromium-bidi") as browser:
    ...

$env:STEERO_CHROME_BACKEND = "chromium-bidi"
python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

STEERO_CHROME_BACKEND=chromium-bidi python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

The mapper is a JavaScript file published on npm. steero downloads it on first use, checks it against npm's SHA-512 hash and caches it, just as it caches chromedriver. To fetch it ahead of time (for example on a build machine):

steero install chromium-bidi

chromium-bidi 158.0.8110-0: 1,018,728 bytes cached

STEERO_CHROMIUM_BIDI_VERSION pins another mapper version, and STEERO_CHROMIUM_BIDI_PATH points at a local mapperTab.js and skips the download. The course test runs every example on both backends (STEERO_BROWSERS=chrome,chrome:chromium-bidi,firefox), which is a cheap way to make sure a suite does not depend on one of them.

Coming from Selenium

The chromedriver backend is the driver you know, but you never download, start or match it yourself: steero reads the Chrome version, fetches the right driver and stops it when the browser closes.

docs.title: Edge and channels
docs.text:
Microsoft Edge is Chromium, so steero drives it like Chrome, through msedgedriver (downloaded the same way) or through backend="chromium-bidi":

with launch("edge") as browser:   # "msedge" works too
    print(browser.name, browser.version)   # edge 157.0.4341.42

A release channel is a separately installed build: Chrome Beta, Dev or Canary, Edge Beta, Firefox Nightly. channel= picks its executable, using Playwright's channel names:

launch("chrome", channel="chrome-beta")
launch("chrome", channel="msedge")          # switches the browser to Edge
launch("firefox", channel="firefox-nightly")

A channel that is not installed raises LaunchError, naming the environment variable to set if it lives somewhere unusual (STEERO_CHROME_BETA_PATH, STEERO_FIREFOX_NIGHTLY_PATH ...). For a binary steero does not know at all, executable_path= names it directly. steero doctor (lesson 01) lists Chrome, Firefox and Edge with their versions, so it is the first thing to run when a launch cannot find a browser.

Browser support

Edge has the same BiDi support as Chrome (same engine), and steero.chromium works in it. A channel must belong to the browser you launch: launch("firefox", channel="msedge") raises LaunchError.

docs.title: Pinned versions
docs.text:
The browser on your machine updates itself every few weeks. A suite that must keep working on the versions your users run should be tested against those versions on purpose. steero can install specific builds into its cache, without touching the system browser:

steero install chrome@154            # newest 154.x from Chrome for Testing, plus its chromedriver
steero install firefox@esr           # newest Extended Support Release
steero install firefox@157

chrome@154: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\steero\browsers\chrome-154.0.8037.92\chrome-win64\chrome.exe

Then select one with an environment variable. Nothing in your script changes:

$env:STEERO_CHROME_VERSION = "154"
python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

STEERO_CHROME_VERSION=154 python examples/course/01-getting-started/example_first_script.py

Running chrome 154.0.8037.92
Title: Sign in - steero practice site
Saved signed-in.png

STEERO_FIREFOX_VERSION does the same for Firefox. If the version is not installed, the launch fails at once with the command that fixes it:

LaunchError: STEERO_CHROME_VERSION=153 but that version is not installed; run: steero install chrome@153

STEERO_CHROME_PATH and STEERO_FIREFOX_PATH still win over a pinned version. A useful habit: run the suite against the current stable, the previous major version and, for Firefox, the ESR your users are on. The pinned browsers guide lists the limits (Chrome for Testing starts at about version 113; macOS Firefox is not installable this way).

Downloads

steero install chrome@... and firefox@... download a whole browser (well over 100 MB). The examples in this lesson never do; they only report what is already installed.

docs.title: Chrome extras
docs.text:
steero.chromium is a handful of async functions that take a Page:

Function What it gives you performance_metrics(page) Chrome's counters: Nodes, JSEventListeners, JSHeapUsedSize, LayoutCount ... set_cpu_throttling(page, rate) a CPU rate times slower (1 switches it off), for testing slow devices start_js_coverage(page) / stop_js_coverage(page) which JavaScript ran, per script heap_usage(page) the JavaScript heap's used and total bytes cdp(page, method, params) any CDP command, when you know exactly what you need

They are async only, so a script that uses them uses the async API (lesson 01). In Firefox each one raises UnsupportedOnBrowser, a SteeroError that says what is missing:

from steero import UnsupportedOnBrowser, chromium

try:
    heap = await chromium.heap_usage(page)
except UnsupportedOnBrowser as error:
    print(error)   # Chrome DevTools Protocol extras are not available in firefox

The same error comes from the main API when a browser cannot apply an option, so it is the one exception to handle when a script must run everywhere but use a feature only some browsers have. The Chromium extras guide has the full list, including the listener tools that reach objects a page keeps out of scope.

Browser support

The extras work in Chrome and Edge, on both backends. In Firefox they raise UnsupportedOnBrowser before anything is sent to the browser.

docs.title: Firefox specifics
docs.text:
Firefox needs no driver at all: it has a BiDi server built in, and steero starts Firefox with a fresh profile and connects to it directly. Three differences are worth knowing.

Preferences. Firefox is configured through preferences (the settings in about:config). prefs= writes extra ones into the fresh profile before Firefox starts:

launch("firefox", prefs={"intl.accept_languages": "fr-FR, en"})

Chrome ignores prefs=; there, use args= for command-line switches.

Emulation gaps. Firefox cannot yet apply is_mobile, has_touch, java_script_enabled=False, reduced_motion or forced_colors over BiDi. Passing one raises UnsupportedOnBrowser naming the option; steero never falls back to something that only looks right. Lesson 06 and the emulation guide have the table.

Video. Firefox records video itself (browsingContext.startScreencast) and writes a .webm. Chrome has no BiDi screencast yet, so steero captures frames and encodes them with ffmpeg when it is installed (lesson 10).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The script below opens the products page in whatever browser the course runs. In Chrome or Edge it also starts JavaScript coverage before the page loads, then prints a few metrics; in Firefox the first extra raises UnsupportedOnBrowser, and the script prints that and carries on with the part every browser can do.

"""Lesson 13: the same page in any browser, plus the Chrome-only extras where they exist.

Prints the browser's name and version. In Chrome (or Edge) it also prints a few performance
metrics and how many scripts JS coverage saw; in Firefox it shows the ``UnsupportedOnBrowser``
error those extras raise instead.

    python examples/course/13-browsers-and-backends/example_browser_info.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os

import steero
from steero import UnsupportedOnBrowser, chromium, expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        print(f"Browser: {browser.name} {browser.version}")
        page = await browser.new_page()
        try:
            # Coverage must start before the page's scripts run, so start it before goto.
            await chromium.start_js_coverage(page)
        except UnsupportedOnBrowser as error:
            print("No Chrome extras here:", error)
            await page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
            await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")
            return

        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")

        coverage = await chromium.stop_js_coverage(page)
        metrics = await chromium.performance_metrics(page)
        heap = await chromium.heap_usage(page)
        print(f"DOM nodes: {metrics['Nodes']:.0f}, event listeners: {metrics['JSEventListeners']:.0f}")
        print(f"JS heap used: {heap['used'] / 1024:,.0f} KiB")
        print(f"Scripts with coverage: {len(coverage)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

python examples/course/13-browsers-and-backends/example_browser_info.py

Browser: chrome 157.0.8103.38
DOM nodes: 103, event listeners: 4
JS heap used: 740 KiB
Scripts with coverage: 7

In Firefox:

Browser: firefox 159.0.1
No Chrome extras here: Chrome DevTools Protocol extras are not available in firefox

Two more examples cover the other launch options. example_edge_and_channels.py launches Edge and the chrome-beta channel if they are installed, and says "Skipping" for each one that is not, so it runs anywhere:

"""Lesson 13: launch Microsoft Edge and a Chrome release channel, when they are installed.

Edge is found the way Chrome is; a channel such as ``chrome-beta`` picks that channel's
executable. Anything not installed is reported and skipped, so the script always exits 0
on a machine that has Chrome.

    python examples/course/13-browsers-and-backends/example_edge_and_channels.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

# course: browsers=chrome

import os

from steero import LaunchError
from steero.launch.discover import find_browser, find_channel
from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def sign_in(browser_name: str, **options: str) -> None:
    """Sign in on the practice site and print which browser did it."""
    with launch(browser_name, headless=HEADLESS, **options) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("edge")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("secret")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, edge")
        print(f"  signed in with {browser.name} {browser.version}")


def main() -> None:
    try:
        print("Edge at", find_browser("edge"))
    except LaunchError as error:  # not installed: say so and carry on
        print("Skipping Edge:", error)
    else:
        sign_in("edge")

    try:
        family, path = find_channel("chrome-beta")
        print(f"chrome-beta ({family}) at {path}")
    except LaunchError as error:
        print("Skipping chrome-beta:", error)
    else:
        sign_in("chrome", channel="chrome-beta")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Edge at C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe
  signed in with edge 157.0.4341.42
Skipping chrome-beta: the chrome-beta channel is not installed; install it or set STEERO_CHROME_BETA_PATH to its executable

example_firefox_specifics.py (Firefox only) sets a preference and shows the error an unsupported emulation option raises:

"""Lesson 13: Firefox preferences, and an emulation option Firefox cannot apply.

``prefs=`` writes Firefox preferences into the fresh profile before Firefox starts. Here
``intl.accept_languages`` makes the browser ask for French first. Then a context with
``is_mobile=True`` (Chrome only) shows the ``UnsupportedOnBrowser`` error it raises in Firefox.

    python examples/course/13-browsers-and-backends/example_firefox_specifics.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

# course: browsers=firefox

import os

from steero import UnsupportedOnBrowser
from steero.sync_api import launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "firefox")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def main() -> None:
    prefs = {"intl.accept_languages": "fr-FR, en"}
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS, prefs=prefs) as browser:
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        languages = page.evaluate("navigator.languages")
        print("navigator.languages:", languages)
        assert languages[0] == "fr-FR", languages

        try:
            browser.new_context(is_mobile=True)
        except UnsupportedOnBrowser as error:
            print("As expected:", error)
        else:
            print("This Firefox accepted is_mobile: its BiDi support has grown since this lesson")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

navigator.languages: ['fr-FR', 'en']
As expected: is_mobile is not supported on firefox 159.0.1: the browser does not implement emulation.setViewportMetaOverride (emulation.setViewportMetaOverride)

The # course: browsers=... lines tell the course test which browsers a script is for (conventions page); you can run any of them by hand.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Run each solution from the repository root with the practice site running.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a slower CPU
docs.text:
In Chrome, time the products page at normal speed and again with set_cpu_throttling(page, 4). Page loads on a local server are so fast that the difference is small, so also time a fixed piece of JavaScript inside the page with performance.now(). Check that the throttled run is clearly slower, and switch throttling off again at the end.

Hint: page.evaluate() can run a function that returns how long a loop took.

Solution 
"""Lesson 13, exercise 1: time a page at normal speed and with the CPU four times slower.

Chrome only (``set_cpu_throttling`` is a DevTools Protocol extra). The page load is timed
from Python; a fixed piece of JavaScript work is timed inside the page with
``performance.now()``, which shows the throttling most clearly.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

# course: browsers=chrome,edge

import asyncio
import os
import time

import steero
from steero import chromium, expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

WORK = """() => {
    const t = performance.now();
    let x = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < 3e6; i++) x += i % 7;
    return performance.now() - t;
}"""


async def measure(page: steero.Page) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Seconds to load the products page, and milliseconds of in-page work."""
    started = time.perf_counter()
    await page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
    await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")
    load = time.perf_counter() - started
    work = min([await page.evaluate(WORK) for _ in range(3)])  # the best of three is the least noisy
    return load, work


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = await browser.new_page()
        await measure(page)  # warm up: the first load also starts the page's processes

        normal_load, normal_work = await measure(page)
        await chromium.set_cpu_throttling(page, 4)
        slow_load, slow_work = await measure(page)
        await chromium.set_cpu_throttling(page, 1)  # 1 switches throttling off again

        print(f"normal:    load {normal_load:.2f} s, work {normal_work:.1f} ms")
        print(f"4x slower: load {slow_load:.2f} s, work {slow_work:.1f} ms")
        print(f"the work took {slow_work / normal_work:.1f} times as long")
        assert slow_work > normal_work * 1.5, "throttling should slow the in-page work down"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

normal:    load 0.08 s, work 15.1 ms
4x slower: load 0.19 s, work 33.1 ms
the work took 2.2 times as long

The first measure() is a warm-up: the first load also starts processes and compiles code, which would make the normal run look slow. Taking the best of three runs of the loop keeps one noisy run from deciding the result. The ratio is rarely exactly 4, because throttling slows the page's main thread, not the whole machine.

docs.title: Exercise 2: two backends, one script
docs.text:
Run the lesson 01 sign-in with backend="chromedriver" and again with backend="chromium-bidi", and print how long each launch took. Do not let the script download the mapper: if it is not cached yet, print the steero install command instead.

Solution 
"""Lesson 13, exercise 2: run the lesson 01 sign-in on both Chrome backends and compare launch times.

``chromium-bidi`` needs the BiDi mapper in steero's cache. This script never downloads it:
when it is missing, the script says how to fetch it (``steero install chromium-bidi``) and
times the default backend only.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

# course: browsers=chrome

import os
import time

from steero.launch.discover import cache_dir
from steero.launch.mapper import DEFAULT_VERSION
from steero.sync_api import expect, launch

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def mapper_available() -> bool:
    """True when chromium-bidi can start without a download."""
    if os.environ.get("STEERO_CHROMIUM_BIDI_PATH"):
        return True
    version = os.environ.get("STEERO_CHROMIUM_BIDI_VERSION") or DEFAULT_VERSION
    return (cache_dir() / "chromium-bidi" / version / "mapperTab.js").is_file()


def sign_in(backend: str) -> float:
    """Launch with ``backend``, sign in, and return the seconds the launch took."""
    started = time.perf_counter()
    with launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS, backend=backend) as browser:
        launched = time.perf_counter() - started
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(BASE_URL + "login.html")
        page.get_by_label("User name").fill("ada")
        page.get_by_label("Password").fill("lovelace")
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in").click()
        expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("Welcome, ada")
    return launched


def main() -> None:
    print(f"chromedriver:  launched in {sign_in('chromedriver'):.2f} s")
    if not mapper_available():
        print("chromium-bidi: skipped, the mapper is not cached; run: steero install chromium-bidi")
        return
    print(f"chromium-bidi: launched in {sign_in('chromium-bidi'):.2f} s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chromedriver:  launched in 1.79 s
chromium-bidi: launched in 1.74 s

On a warm machine the two are close; the difference shows on the very first launch, when chromedriver is downloaded, and on machines where starting an extra executable is slow. The behaviour of the script is identical, which is the point.

docs.title: Exercise 3: skip a Chrome-only step, keep the rest
docs.text:
Write a small async helper that awaits a Chrome-only step and, in Firefox, prints which step was skipped and why, then returns None. Use it to read the heap size on the products page, then add a product to the cart, which must work in every browser.

Solution 
"""Lesson 13, exercise 3: a helper that runs a Chrome-only step, or skips it with a clear message.

The same script runs in every browser. In Chrome and Edge the step runs; in Firefox the
helper prints why it was skipped and the rest of the script carries on.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
"""

import asyncio
import os
from collections.abc import Awaitable
from typing import TypeVar

import steero
from steero import UnsupportedOnBrowser, chromium, expect

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"

T = TypeVar("T")


async def chrome_only(step: str, action: Awaitable[T]) -> T | None:
    """Await ``action``; if the browser cannot do it, print a message and return None."""
    try:
        return await action
    except UnsupportedOnBrowser as error:
        print(f"skipped {step!r}: {error}")
        return None


async def main() -> None:
    async with steero.launch(BROWSER, headless=HEADLESS) as browser:
        page = await browser.new_page()
        await page.goto(BASE_URL + "products.html")
        await expect(page.get_by_role("status")).to_have_text("3 products")

        heap = await chrome_only("heap usage", chromium.heap_usage(page))
        if heap is not None:
            print(f"heap used: {heap['used'] / 1024:,.0f} KiB")

        # The part of the check that every browser can do still runs.
        await page.get_by_role("button", name="Add Blue mug to cart").click()
        await expect(page.get_by_test_id("cart-count")).to_have_text("1")
        print(f"cart updated in {browser.name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

skipped 'heap usage': Chrome DevTools Protocol extras are not available in firefox
cart updated in firefox

Catching UnsupportedOnBrowser (and nothing wider) is what makes this safe: a real failure, such as a timeout, still raises.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes

  • Calling a steero.chromium function from sync code. It returns a coroutine and nothing happens (RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited). The extras are async: write that script with steero.launch and await.
  • Expecting prefs= to change Chrome. It is for Firefox preferences only. Chrome takes command-line switches through args=.
  • Catching SteeroError to skip a Chrome-only step. That also hides timeouts and real failures. Catch UnsupportedOnBrowser.
  • Setting STEERO_CHROME_VERSION without installing the build. The launch fails with ... that version is not installed; run: steero install chrome@<version>. Run that command.
  • Leaving STEERO_CHROME_PATH set from an earlier experiment. It outranks a pinned version and the channel lookup, so the run quietly uses another browser. steero doctor shows which executable is picked; remove the variable when you are done.
  • Passing a Chromium channel to Firefox (launch("firefox", channel="msedge")). It raises LaunchError: channel 'msedge' is an edge channel, not a firefox one, before steero even looks for the executable. Launch "chrome" or "edge" with that channel instead.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Everything in the main API is WebDriver BiDi and behaves the same in Chrome, Edge and Firefox; CDP appears only in steero.chromium.
  • Chrome has two backends, chromedriver (default) and chromium-bidi (no driver binary); pick one with backend= or STEERO_CHROME_BACKEND.
  • launch("edge"), channel="chrome-beta" and executable_path= choose the build; steero install chrome@154 with STEERO_CHROME_VERSION=154 pins a version.
  • A feature a browser lacks raises UnsupportedOnBrowser; catch exactly that to skip a step.
  • Firefox needs no driver, takes prefs=, and has a few emulation gaps listed in the guide.

Next: 14. AI agents with MCP

docs.title: 14. AI agents with MCP
docs.text:
In this lesson

You will learn to:

  • explain what the Model Context Protocol server does, and the risks of letting an agent drive a browser
  • start steero mcp for Chrome or Firefox and connect an MCP client to it
  • name the tools an agent gets (navigate, snapshot, click, type, wait, screenshot, console, tabs)
  • drive the server from a small Python client, as a test of your own setup

Time: about 25 minutes. Before this: 13. Browsers and backends. Code: examples/course/14-mcp-agents/

So far you have written every step yourself. An AI agent can also drive a browser: you ask it to "sign in and check the welcome message", and it decides which buttons to press. steero ships a server that gives such an agent a real Chrome or Firefox, with the same auto-waiting your tests get. This lesson shows what the agent sees and lets you speak the protocol yourself, so you can test the setup without any AI service.

docs.title: What MCP is
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting an AI application to tools. The application (the client: an IDE, a desktop assistant, an agent framework) starts a server program and asks it which tools it offers; the model then calls those tools by name with JSON arguments, and the server answers with text or images.

steero mcp is such a server. It speaks MCP over stdio: the client writes one JSON-RPC message per line to the server's standard input and reads one reply per line from its standard output. There is no port and no network listener. The browser starts on the first tool call and closes when the client closes the server's input.

steero mcp --browser firefox

Started by hand like this, it just waits for JSON on its input; press Ctrl+C to stop it. It is meant to be started by a client.

docs.title: Safety first
docs.text:
An agent that drives a browser acts with your machine's network access: it can open any site your browser can reach, including internal ones, and type whatever it decides into any form. steero adds no sandbox around that. So:

  • connect only agents you trust, from vendors you trust, and point them only at sites you are allowed to automate;
  • do not give it secrets it does not need; the server tells the agent not to enter secrets it was not given, but that is an instruction, not a guarantee;
  • watch it work the first few times (--headed), and review what it did;
  • run it against a practice site or a test environment before anything real.

steero mcp --help prints the same warning. The browser itself starts from a fresh, empty profile every time, so the agent never sees your own cookies or saved passwords.

docs.title: Configure a client
docs.text:
Most MCP clients read a JSON file with an mcpServers section. Where that file lives depends on the client (its documentation says); the entry for steero looks the same everywhere:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "steero": { "command": "steero", "args": ["mcp", "--browser", "firefox"] }
  }
}
Option Meaning --browser chrome or --browser firefox which browser to drive (default chrome) --headed show the window, so you can watch --backend chromium-bidi reach Chrome without chromedriver (lesson 13)

If the client cannot find steero (for example, it does not run inside your virtual environment), give the full path: "command": "C:\\path\\to\\.venv\\Scripts\\steero.exe", or "command": "/path/to/.venv/bin/python", "args": ["-m", "steero", "mcp", ...].

Coming from Playwright

Playwright's MCP server is a separate Node package. steero's is part of the Python package, has no extra dependencies, and drives stock Firefox as well as Chrome. The tool names follow the same browser_* pattern, so prompts written for one mostly work with the other.

Browser support

steero mcp --browser takes chrome, edge or firefox, and everything works the same in all three.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool Does browser_navigate open a URL; answers with a snapshot of the page browser_snapshot list the page's visible interactive elements, each with a ref (e1, e2 ...) browser_click, browser_type, browser_hover, browser_check, browser_select_option act on an element, given its ref (or a CSS selector) browser_press_key press a key or a combination such as Control+A browser_wait_for wait for text to appear (or, with gone, to disappear), or for some seconds browser_evaluate run JavaScript and return the value as JSON browser_screenshot a PNG of the viewport (full_page for the whole page), as image content browser_console_messages console output and page errors since the last call browser_tabs, browser_navigate_back, browser_close tabs, history, and closing the browser

A snapshot is how the agent "sees" the page: one line per element, its role, its name and a ref.

Page: Sign in - steero practice site
URL: http://127.0.0.1:8765/login.html
- heading "Sign in" [ref=e4]
- textbox "User name" [ref=e6]
- textbox "Password" [ref=e8]
- button "Sign in" [ref=e11]

The agent then calls browser_type with {"ref": "e6", "text": "ada"}. Refs are short, cheap for a model to repeat, and valid until the next snapshot (each snapshot numbers the page again). Every action goes through a steero locator, so it auto-waits exactly as click() does in your scripts, and a dialog that opens is dismissed so the agent is never stuck behind it. A tool that fails (an element that never appears, say) answers with isError: true and the error text, which the agent can read and react to.

docs.title: Talking to it yourself
docs.text:
You do not need an AI to try the server: any program that writes JSON lines can be the client. Three methods are enough.

  1. initialize: the handshake. The client says which protocol version it speaks; the server answers with its name, version and capabilities. The client then sends the notifications/initialized notification (no id, so no reply).
  2. tools/list: the tools, each with a JSON Schema for its arguments.
  3. tools/call: {"name": "browser_click", "arguments": {"ref": "e11"}}; the reply holds content (a list of text or image parts) and isError.

On the wire, a request and its reply look like this:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "browser_navigate", "arguments": {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/login.html"}}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Page: Sign in - steero practice site\n..."}], "isError": false}}

The lesson's folder has a small client, mcp_client.py, that starts python -m steero mcp as a subprocess and does exactly this. Each request gets a number, and a reader thread matches each reply to it with a deadline, so a lost reply fails in seconds instead of hanging:

"""Lesson 14: a minimal MCP client that starts ``steero mcp`` and talks JSON-RPC to it over stdio.

Not an example on its own: the lesson's scripts import it. It does what an AI agent's host
program does, without the AI: one JSON message per line on the server's stdin, one reply per
line on its stdout, every request numbered so its reply can be matched.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (edge)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import queue
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
from types import TracebackType
from typing import Any


class McpError(Exception):
    """The server answered a request with a JSON-RPC error."""


class McpClient:
    """Start ``steero mcp`` as a subprocess and call its tools.

    Args:
        browser: ``chrome``, ``edge`` or ``firefox``.
        headed: Show the browser window.
        command: The whole command line that starts the server, used as given (``browser`` and
            ``headed`` are then ignored). Default: ``python -m steero mcp --browser <browser>``.
    """

    def __init__(self, browser: str = "chrome", *, headed: bool = False, command: list[str] | None = None):
        args = command or [sys.executable, "-m", "steero", "mcp", "--browser", browser,
                           *(["--headed"] if headed else [])]
        # stderr is inherited: the server logs warnings there, never on stdout.
        self.process = subprocess.Popen(args, stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
        self._lines: queue.Queue[bytes] = queue.Queue()
        self._next_id = 0
        threading.Thread(target=self._read, daemon=True).start()

    def _read(self) -> None:
        assert self.process.stdout is not None
        for line in self.process.stdout:
            self._lines.put(line)
        self._lines.put(b"")  # end of output: the server has exited

    def _send(self, message: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
        assert self.process.stdin is not None
        self.process.stdin.write((json.dumps(message) + "\n").encode())
        self.process.stdin.flush()

    def request(self, method: str, params: dict[str, Any] | None = None, timeout: float = 60) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Send a request and return its ``result``; wait at most ``timeout`` seconds."""
        self._next_id += 1
        self._send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": self._next_id, "method": method, "params": params or {}})
        while True:
            try:
                line = self._lines.get(timeout=timeout)
            except queue.Empty:
                raise TimeoutError(f"no reply to {method} within {timeout} s") from None
            if not line:
                raise ConnectionError("the MCP server exited")
            reply: dict[str, Any] = json.loads(line)
            if reply.get("id") != self._next_id:
                continue  # not the answer to this request
            if "error" in reply:
                raise McpError(f"{method}: {reply['error']['message']}")
            result: dict[str, Any] = reply["result"]
            return result

    def initialize(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """The MCP handshake: ``initialize``, then the ``notifications/initialized`` notification."""
        result = self.request("initialize", {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {},
                                             "clientInfo": {"name": "course-client", "version": "1"}})
        self._send({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"})  # a notification: no id, no reply
        return result

    def call(self, tool: str, **arguments: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Call a tool and return its result (``content`` and ``isError``)."""
        return self.request("tools/call", {"name": tool, "arguments": arguments})

    def text(self, tool: str, **arguments: Any) -> str:
        """Call a tool that answers with text; raise if the tool reported an error."""
        result = self.call(tool, **arguments)
        text = "\n".join(part["text"] for part in result["content"] if part["type"] == "text")
        if result.get("isError"):
            raise McpError(f"{tool} failed: {text}")
        return text

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Close stdin, which tells the server to close the browser and exit."""
        assert self.process.stdin is not None
        self.process.stdin.close()
        try:
            self.process.wait(timeout=60)
        finally:
            if self.process.poll() is None:
                self.process.kill()

    def __enter__(self) -> McpClient:
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None,
                 tb: TracebackType | None) -> None:
        self.close()

The client closes the server by closing its standard input. The server then closes the browser and exits, so nothing is left running.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The script plays the agent's part with fixed steps: list the tools, open the sign-in page, find the refs in the snapshot, type, click, wait for the welcome message and read it back.

"""Lesson 14: drive ``steero mcp`` the way an AI agent would, from a small Python client.

Starts the server, lists its tools, opens the sign-in page, reads the snapshot to find the
fields' refs, types into them, clicks Sign in and waits for the welcome message.

    python examples/course/14-mcp-agents/example_mcp_sign_in.py

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (steero mcp drives Edge too)
"""

import os
import re

from mcp_client import McpClient

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def ref(snapshot: str, role: str, name: str) -> str:
    """The ref (``e3``) of the element with this role and name in a snapshot."""
    match = re.search(rf'- {role} "{re.escape(name)}" \[ref=(e\d+)\]', snapshot)
    assert match, f"no {role} {name!r} in the snapshot:\n{snapshot}"
    return match.group(1)


def main() -> None:
    with McpClient(BROWSER, headed=not HEADLESS) as client:
        info = client.initialize()
        print("Server:", info["serverInfo"]["name"], info["serverInfo"]["version"])
        tools = client.request("tools/list")["tools"]
        print("Tools:", ", ".join(tool["name"] for tool in tools))

        snapshot = client.text("browser_navigate", url=BASE_URL + "login.html")
        print(snapshot)

        client.text("browser_type", ref=ref(snapshot, "textbox", "User name"), text="ada")
        client.text("browser_type", ref=ref(snapshot, "textbox", "Password"), text="lovelace")
        client.text("browser_click", ref=ref(snapshot, "button", "Sign in"))
        client.text("browser_wait_for", text="Welcome, ada")

        status = client.text("browser_evaluate", script="document.getElementById('status').textContent")
        print("Status:", status)
        assert "Welcome, ada" in status


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python examples/course/14-mcp-agents/example_mcp_sign_in.py

Server: steero 1.0.0rc4
Tools: browser_navigate, browser_snapshot, browser_click, browser_type, browser_press_key, ...
Page: Sign in - steero practice site
URL: http://127.0.0.1:8765/login.html
- link "Practice site" [ref=e1]
- link "Sign in" [ref=e2]
- link "Products" [ref=e3]
- heading "Sign in" [ref=e4]
- label "User name" [ref=e5]
- textbox "User name" [ref=e6]
- label "Password" [ref=e7]
- textbox "Password" [ref=e8]
- label "Remember me" [ref=e9]
- checkbox "Remember me" [ref=e10] [unchecked]
- button "Sign in" [ref=e11]
Status: "Welcome, ada"

Notice that the header link and the submit button are both called "Sign in"; the snapshot tells them apart by role, and so does the ref() helper. browser_wait_for is what makes the last step reliable: the welcome text appears half a second after the click, and the wait returns as soon as it does. browser_evaluate returns JSON, which is why the status is printed in quotes.

docs.title: Exercise 1: press Enter, then take a picture
docs.text:
Sign in as grace without clicking the button: let browser_type press Enter after the password. Wait for the welcome message, then call browser_screenshot and save the PNG it returns as mcp-signed-in.png.

Hint: the screenshot's content part has type: "image" and base64 data.

Solution 
"""Lesson 14, exercise 1: sign in by pressing Enter, wait for the welcome, and save a screenshot.

``browser_type`` with ``submit=True`` presses Enter after typing, so no click is needed.
``browser_screenshot`` answers with image content: base64 PNG data, decoded and saved here.

Author: Pandiyaraj Karuppasamy
Date: Nov-07-2026
Modified: Nov-07-2026 (steero mcp drives Edge too)
"""

import base64
import os
import re

from mcp_client import McpClient

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")
BROWSER = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_BROWSER", "chrome")
HEADLESS = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_HEADED") != "1"


def ref(snapshot: str, role: str, name: str) -> str:
    """The ref (``e3``) of the element with this role and name in a snapshot."""
    match = re.search(rf'- {role} "{re.escape(name)}" \[ref=(e\d+)\]', snapshot)
    assert match, f"no {role} {name!r} in the snapshot:\n{snapshot}"
    return match.group(1)


def main() -> None:
    with McpClient(BROWSER, headed=not HEADLESS) as client:
        client.initialize()
        snapshot = client.text("browser_navigate", url=BASE_URL + "login.html")
        client.text("browser_type", ref=ref(snapshot, "textbox", "User name"), text="grace")
        client.text("browser_type", ref=ref(snapshot, "textbox", "Password"), text="hopper", submit=True)
        client.text("browser_wait_for", text="Welcome, grace")

        result = client.call("browser_screenshot")
        image = result["content"][0]
        assert image["type"] == "image" and image["mimeType"] == "image/png", image.keys()
        png = base64.b64decode(image["data"])
        assert png.startswith(b"\x89PNG"), "not a PNG"
        with open("mcp-signed-in.png", "wb") as file:
            file.write(png)
        print(f"Saved mcp-signed-in.png ({len(png):,} bytes)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Checking the first bytes (\x89PNG) before saving catches the case where a tool answered with an error text instead of an image.

import os

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("STEERO_COURSE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8765/")

Console: [error] boot console error
